# `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`

### Purpose

This interface defines the read-only query contract for repositories in the `DataAccessLayer` namespace. It exists so that the rest of the codebase can depend on a database-agnostic set of query operations rather than a specific ORM, letting `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` supply the Hibernate-based implementation.

### Role in the Codebase

`IRepository<TKey>` sits at the core of the data access abstraction. It is implemented by `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`, which extends it with write capability (`Save`) and a unit-of-work, so this interface is deliberately query-only. `IRepositoryFactory` in the same directory also constrains the repositories it hands out to this interface. If it were removed, the Hibernate layer and the factory contract would both lose their base contract.

Note the split in responsibilities: `IRepository<TKey>` covers reading, while `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` adds `Save<TEntity>` and `UnitOfWork`. Code that only reads entities can depend on `IRepository<TKey>` alone.

### Relationships

- **`IEntity<TKey>`** (same directory, `DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs`): the marker interface every entity must implement — a single `TKey Id { get; }` property. Every method here constrains `TEntity` to `class, IEntity<TKey>` on top of it.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepository<TKey>`**: the concrete implementation, reached through `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`, which adds `IDisposable` plus `Save` and `UnitOfWork` to this contract.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** and **`IRepositoryFactory`**: factories that produce repositories bound to this contract.
- **Callers**: `BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs` wires `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`, so the business layer is the layer that consumes repositories created from this contract.

### Behavior & Details

The generic parameter `TKey` (constrained to `struct`) is the identifier type for entities stored in this repository. The `in` (contravariant) variance declaration is unusual for an interface with no parameter-only positions; in practice it restricts assignability rather than adding flexibility, so do not rely on variance when substituting `TKey` types.

All seven members are constrained the same way: `TEntity : class, IEntity<TKey>`. There are no `TKey`-typed parameters on any member — `TKey` only flows through `TEntity`'s `Id`.

The methods group into three patterns:

- **Deferred queryables** — `GetQueryable<TEntity>(Expression<Func<TEntity, bool>> predicate)` and the parameterless `GetQueryable<TEntity>()`. These return `IQueryable<TEntity>`, so the expression tree is not evaluated at the call site; the consuming context (an active session in the Hibernate implementation) executes the query when it is enumerated or passed on to further LINQ operations. This is the escape hatch for callers who need to compose additional queries.
- **Single-result lookups** — `Single<TEntity>(criteria)`, `SingleOrDefault<TEntity>(criteria)`, and `FindOne<TEntity>(criteria)`. `Single` and `SingleOrDefault` follow the standard LINQ naming: `Single` returns `TEntity` (and throws if zero or more than one match), `SingleOrDefault` returns `TEntity?` (nullable, so it can represent "no match"). `FindOne` is a sibling of the same idea, also returning `TEntity?` — its distinction from `SingleOrDefault` is not encoded in the contract and lives in whichever implementation and calling convention the codebase uses.
- **Collection results** — `Find<TEntity>(criteria)` and `GetAll<TEntity>()`, both returning `IEnumerable<TEntity>`. `GetAll` has no predicate; `Find` narrows by expression.

Because the return types for `Find`, `GetAll`, and the `GetQueryable` overloads are `IQueryable`/`IEnumerable` rather than concrete lists, the interface does not commit to eager vs. deferred execution at this level — that depends on the implementation (the Hibernate-backed one) and on how the caller enumerates the result.

A few caveats worth knowing before you implement or extend this:

- No `IDisposable` here. `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` adds it, so code that holds a repository directly against `IRepository<TKey>` cannot dispose it — disposal is an `IHibernateRepository` concern.
- `TKey` is contravariant (`in`) despite never appearing in a parameter position. This is legal but almost certainly unintentional; treat it as if there were no variance modifier.
- `Single`/`SingleOrDefault`/`FindOne` overlap heavily; pick whichever name your implementation actually differentiates, rather than assuming the LINQ semantics for all three.

### Rough edges

- The `in` variance on `TKey` is unearned (no input positions) and may mislead readers about substitutability.
- `FindOne` and `SingleOrDefault` have near-identical signatures, and the interface gives no signal of how they differ in behaviour.
- No write path and no lifecycle (`IDisposable`) are part of this contract — a consumer holding only `IRepository<TKey>` cannot save or release resources; both live one layer down in `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`.

# DataAccessException.cs

`DataAccessLayer/DataAccessException.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `DataAccessException`, the exception type the data access layer uses to surface persistence failures. It exists so that consumers of the data access layer can distinguish "something went wrong talking to the data store" from any other kind of exception, without having to inspect underlying driver or ORM exceptions.

### Role in the Codebase

`DataAccessException` is the shared failure signal of the `DataAccessLayer` project. It is a thin marker exception with no logic of its own — its value is purely in the type. Callers that depend on data access can `catch (DataAccessException)` to handle any persistence-layer failure uniformly, regardless of which repository or provider produced it. If the class were removed, that catch point would disappear and callers would have to handle raw ORM/driver exceptions instead.

### Relationships

- `DataAccessException` inherits from `System.Exception` (the standard .NET exception base class); nothing beyond the constructor is overridden.
- It currently has one throw site in the repository: `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs` wraps any failure while building the Hibernate session factory with `throw new DataAccessException("Error initializing Hibernate repository factory", e)`, preserving the original failure as the inner exception.
- No code in the repository currently catches `DataAccessException`; today it is a one-directional contract — thrown by the data access layer, awaiting a consumer.

### Behavior & Details

The class has a single constructor, `DataAccessException(string message, Exception inner)`, which forwards both arguments straight to the base `Exception` constructor. Two consequences follow:

- **There is no parameterless constructor and no message-only constructor.** Callers must always supply a message and an inner exception. Code that wants to throw `DataAccessException` without an underlying cause (e.g. `throw new DataAccessException("msg")`) will not compile — adding such a constructor is a deliberate extension point if that ever becomes needed.
- **The original failure is preserved.** Because the second argument is always passed as the inner exception, the stack trace and message of the root cause (e.g. a SQL or NHibernate error) remain accessible via `InnerException` after the exception propagates up.

The class has no properties, state, or other members; serializing or inspecting it behaves exactly like a plain `Exception`.

Rough edges: the only constructor forces an inner exception to be present, which is fine for wrapping but makes the type awkward to use for purely programmatic data-access failures (validation, misconfiguration) where no underlying exception exists.

# DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs

## Purpose

`IUnitOfWork` is the provider-agnostic contract for managing database transactions in this codebase. It exists so that business logic (e.g., `UserService` in `BusinessLayer/`) can begin, commit, and roll back transactions without knowing which ORM or data access implementation is actually being used.

## Role in the Codebase

This file sits in the `DataAccessLayer` directory alongside other abstraction interfaces (`IRepository<TKey>`, `IRepositoryFactory`). It defines the transactional "unit" boundary for all data access: a caller starts a transaction, performs one or more repository operations, then commits or rolls back as a single atomic unit.

The concrete implementation is `HibernateUnitOfWork` (in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/`), which wraps an NHibernate `IStatelessSession`. A thinner sub-interface, `IHibernateUnitOfWork`, extends `IUnitOfWork` to add an overload of `BeginTransaction` that accepts an explicit `IsolationLevel`.

If this interface were removed, there would be no provider-agnostic way to express transactional boundaries, and callers would be forced to depend on the NHibernate-specific implementation directly.

## Relationships

- **Inherited by:** `IHibernateUnitOfWork` (DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateUnitOfWork.cs) — adds `BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel isolationLevel)`.
- **Implemented by:** `HibernateUnitOfWork` (DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateUnitOfWork.cs) — the only concrete implementation in the repository.
- **Exposed through:** `IHibernateRepository.UnitOfWork` property, which returns an `IHibernateUnitOfWork`.
- **Consumed by:** `UserService` (BusinessLayer/UserService.cs) calls `repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction()`, `CommitTransaction()`, and `RollBackTransaction()` to wrap user-save operations in a transaction.

`IUnitOfWork` itself extends `System.IDisposable` (standard .NET), so a unit of work is expected to release its underlying session/transaction resources when disposed.

## Behavior & Details

The interface declares four members:

| Member | Contract |
|---|---|
| `bool IsInTransaction { get; }` | Read-only flag: `true` when a transaction has been opened and not yet committed or rolled back. |
| `void BeginTransaction()` | Opens a new transaction. The `HibernateUnitOfWork` implementation starts with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted` by default and throws `InvalidOperationException` if a transaction is already open. |
| `void CommitTransaction()` | Commits the open transaction. Throws `InvalidOperationException` if no transaction is active. On failure, the implementation rolls back before rethrowing. |
| `void RollBackTransaction()` | Rolls back the open transaction. Throws `InvalidOperationException` if no transaction is active. |

### Typical usage pattern

```csharp
using var repository = _repositoryFactory.Create();
repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction();
try
{
    await repository.Save(entity);
    repository.UnitOfWork.CommitTransaction();
}
catch
{
    repository.UnitOfWork.RollBackTransaction();
    throw;
}
```

Callers (such as `UserService.AddUser`) are responsible for the try/catch and for deciding whether to rethrow or wrap the exception. The unit of work itself does not swallow errors.

### Rough edges

- The `CommitTransaction` failure path in `HibernateUnitOfWork` calls `RollBackTransaction()`, but if that rollback also throws, the original exception is lost (the rollback exception propagates instead). This is an implementation detail outside this interface, but it is relevant to anyone relying on the "commit or throw" contract.
- `Dispose` on `HibernateUnitOfWork` sets `_isDisposed = true` only when a transaction existed at disposal time, which means calling `Dispose` twice with no transaction open leaves the flag unset. Again, this lives in the implementation, not the contract.

# DataAccessLayer/SortOrder.cs

### Purpose

`DataAccessLayer/SortOrder.cs` defines a small public enum, `SortOrder`, with two members — `Ascending` and `Descending` — intended to express the direction in which query results should be sorted. It is a shared vocabulary for the data access layer: code that issues queries can refer to a sort direction by this type rather than by strings or booleans.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a leaf data type in the `DataAccessLayer` project, which otherwise holds the persistence abstractions (`IEntity<TKey>`, `Entity<TKey>`, `IRepository<TKey>`, `IRepositoryFactory`, `IUnitOfWork`) plus `DataAccessException`. This enum is the only sort-related type in the project. It has no logic of its own and no dependencies.

### Relationships

- No usings and no references to other code in the repository; it is fully self-contained.
- Nothing in the repository currently uses it. The `IRepository<TKey>` interface in `IRepository.cs` exposes query methods (`GetQueryable`, `Find`, `GetAll`, …) that return unordered `IQueryable`/`IEnumerable` results and take no ordering parameter; `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` adds only `Save` and a `UnitOfWork`. So the enum is presently a definition awaiting consumers rather than part of a live code path.
- Removing it would break compilation of any project that references it, but today nothing does.

### Behavior & Details

- `public enum SortOrder { Ascending, Descending }` — an un-decorated C# enum, so the members get the default underlying `int` values: `Ascending = 0`, `Descending = 1`. `Ascending` is therefore also the value `default(SortOrder)` resolves to.
- Because it is in the `DataAccessLayer` namespace, consumers can use it as `DataAccessLayer.SortOrder.Descending` or with a `using DataAccessLayer;` directive.

### Rough edges

The enum has no current callers in the repository — no interface, repository implementation, or query API accepts a `SortOrder` — so its intended usage is only implied by its name and location.

# DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs

### Purpose

This file defines `IEntity<TKey>`, the marker contract for anything the data access layer treats as an entity: a type that has an `Id` of a struct type. It exists so that the generic repository and unit-of-work types can constrain their `TEntity` parameters to "things with an identity" without knowing the concrete shape of each domain entity.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the base contract of the `DataAccessLayer` project, sitting next to the abstract base class `Entity<TKey>` (in `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs`) that implements it. Every repository operation in this project is gated on this contract — for example `IRepository<TKey>.GetQueryable<TEntity>(...)` and `FindOne<TEntity>(...)` in `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs` all declare `where TEntity : class, IEntity<TKey>`, as does `HibernateRepository` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`. If this interface were removed, those constraints and `Entity<TKey>`'s implementation clause would stop compiling.

### Relationships

- Implemented by `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs`'s `Entity<TKey>`, which is the abstract base class concrete domain entities are expected to derive from.
- Referenced as a generic constraint throughout `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`, `IRepositoryFactory.cs`, `IUnitOfWork.cs`, and the Hibernate implementation, so the data-access layer can be written once against any entity type.

## Purpose

It exists so that consumers of the data access layer can obtain repositories through a factory abstraction instead of instantiating them directly, which decouples business-layer code from the mechanics of opening sessions.

## Role in the Codebase

The interface is the top of a small inheritance chain in the `DataAccessLayer` project:

2. `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs` — binds `TRepository` to `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`, so callers only write `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`.

The concrete implementation is `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`; the composed instance is `RepositoryFactory` in `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`.

- **Extends nothing**; its constraint references `IRepository<TKey>` from `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`, the generic query API (`GetQueryable`, `Single`, `Find`, `GetAll`, etc.) that created repositories implement.

# `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `Entity<TKey>`, the abstract base class that gives every persisted entity in the system its identity. It exists so that all domain entities share a single, uniform `Id` property with a consistent contract, without each entity having to declare its own key.

### Role in the Codebase

`DataAccessLayer` is a small contract-and-abstraction project: interfaces for repositories (`IRepository.cs`, `IRepositoryFactory.cs`, `IUnitOfWork.cs`), the entity marker interface `IEntity<TKey>` (`IEntity.cs`), plus `DataAccessException` and `SortOrder`. This class is the concrete half of the entity-identity contract: `IEntity<TKey>` declares the interface, and `Entity<TKey>` is the base class real entities inherit from. If it were removed, concrete entities (e.g. `Entity.Hibernate/User.cs`, `User : Entity<int>`) would lose their shared `Id` implementation and would have to define keys individually.

### Relationships

- **`IEntity<TKey>`** (defined in `DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs`) — the interface this class implements. It declares only `TKey Id { get; }` and has an `out` variance modifier, so `IEntity<int>` values flow into read-only collections and repository queries.
- **Subclasses in the entity projects** — e.g. `User : Entity<int>` in `Entity.Hibernate/User.cs` is the pattern: each concrete entity picks a struct key type and inherits `Id`.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`** — the repository methods are constrained to `IEntity<TKey>` (the interface, not this class), so anything exposing an `Id` of the right key type works with the data-access layer, but this class is the intended way for entities to satisfy that constraint.

### Behavior & Details

- `Entity<TKey>` is abstract, so it can only be subclassed. The `where TKey : struct` constraint restricts key types to value types (e.g. `int`, `Guid`).
- The constructor is `protected` and sets `Id = default!` (the C# null-forgiving operator applied to `default(TKey)`, e.g. `0` for `int`). Subclasses must be constructible without arguments (see `User`'s comment about NHibernate requiring a parameterless constructor), and that requirement chains from here.
- `Id` is `public virtual` with a `protected set` — meaning only the class itself or derived classes can assign it, never application code or the repositories from outside the hierarchy. Declaring it `virtual` leaves room for a persistence provider or subclass to override the accessor if needed, though the known subclasses (`User`) do not.
- `[Serializable]` on the class marks it for binary/serialization compatibility, and `[Browsable(false)]` on `Id` keeps the key property out of designer/property-grid tooling.
- Nothing is stored or cached: there is no state beyond the key, no side effects, and no failure modes of its own. A new `User` therefore starts with `Id == 0` until the provider assigns a real key.

### Rough edges

`IEntity<TKey>`'s `Id` setter is intentionally absent, yet `Entity<TKey>` marks `Id` `virtual` — a derived class could in principle override the property with a public setter, breaking the "identity is not settable from outside" contract. Nothing in this codebase does so, but the compiler will not stop a subclass from doing it.

# `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`

### Purpose

This interface defines the read-only query contract for repositories in the `DataAccessLayer` namespace. It exists so that the rest of the codebase can depend on a database-agnostic set of query operations rather than a specific ORM, letting `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` supply the Hibernate-based implementation.

### Role in the Codebase

`IRepository<TKey>` sits at the core of the data access abstraction. It is implemented by `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`, which extends it with write capability (`Save`) and a unit-of-work, so this interface is deliberately query-only. `IRepositoryFactory` in the same directory also constrains the repositories it hands out to this interface. If it were removed, the Hibernate layer and the factory contract would both lose their base contract.

Note the split in responsibilities: `IRepository<TKey>` covers reading, while `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` adds `Save<TEntity>` and `UnitOfWork`. Code that only reads entities can depend on `IRepository<TKey>` alone.

### Relationships

- **`IEntity<TKey>`** (same directory, `DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs`): the marker interface every entity must implement — a single `TKey Id { get; }` property. Every method here constrains `TEntity` to `class, IEntity<TKey>` on top of it.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepository<TKey>`**: the concrete implementation, reached through `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`, which adds `IDisposable` plus `Save` and `UnitOfWork` to this contract.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** and **`IRepositoryFactory`**: factories that produce repositories bound to this contract.
- **Callers**: `BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs` wires `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`, so the business layer is the layer that consumes repositories created from this contract.

### Behavior & Details

The generic parameter `TKey` (constrained to `struct`) is the identifier type for entities stored in this repository. The `in` (contravariant) variance declaration is unusual for an interface with no parameter-only positions; in practice it restricts assignability rather than adding flexibility, so do not rely on variance when substituting `TKey` types.

All seven members are constrained the same way: `TEntity : class, IEntity<TKey>`. There are no `TKey`-typed parameters on any member — `TKey` only flows through `TEntity`'s `Id`.

The methods group into three patterns:

- **Deferred queryables** — `GetQueryable<TEntity>(Expression<Func<TEntity, bool>> predicate)` and the parameterless `GetQueryable<TEntity>()`. These return `IQueryable<TEntity>`, so the expression tree is not evaluated at the call site; the consuming context (an active session in the Hibernate implementation) executes the query when it is enumerated or passed on to further LINQ operations. This is the escape hatch for callers who need to compose additional queries.
- **Single-result lookups** — `Single<TEntity>(criteria)`, `SingleOrDefault<TEntity>(criteria)`, and `FindOne<TEntity>(criteria)`. `Single` and `SingleOrDefault` follow the standard LINQ naming: `Single` returns `TEntity` (and throws if zero or more than one match), `SingleOrDefault` returns `TEntity?` (nullable, so it can represent "no match"). `FindOne` is a sibling of the same idea, also returning `TEntity?` — its distinction from `SingleOrDefault` is not encoded in the contract and lives in whichever implementation and calling convention the codebase uses.
- **Collection results** — `Find<TEntity>(criteria)` and `GetAll<TEntity>()`, both returning `IEnumerable<TEntity>`. `GetAll` has no predicate; `Find` narrows by expression.

Because the return types for `Find`, `GetAll`, and the `GetQueryable` overloads are `IQueryable`/`IEnumerable` rather than concrete lists, the interface does not commit to eager vs. deferred execution at this level — that depends on the implementation (the Hibernate-backed one) and on how the caller enumerates the result.

A few caveats worth knowing before you implement or extend this:

- No `IDisposable` here. `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` adds it, so code that holds a repository directly against `IRepository<TKey>` cannot dispose it — disposal is an `IHibernateRepository` concern.
- `TKey` is contravariant (`in`) despite never appearing in a parameter position. This is legal but almost certainly unintentional; treat it as if there were no variance modifier.
- `Single`/`SingleOrDefault`/`FindOne` overlap heavily; pick whichever name your implementation actually differentiates, rather than assuming the LINQ semantics for all three.

### Rough edges

- The `in` variance on `TKey` is unearned (no input positions) and may mislead readers about substitutability.
- `FindOne` and `SingleOrDefault` have near-identical signatures, and the interface gives no signal of how they differ in behaviour.
- No write path and no lifecycle (`IDisposable`) are part of this contract — a consumer holding only `IRepository<TKey>` cannot save or release resources; both live one layer down in `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`.

# DataAccessException.cs

`DataAccessLayer/DataAccessException.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `DataAccessException`, the exception type the data access layer uses to surface persistence failures. It exists so that consumers of the data access layer can distinguish "something went wrong talking to the data store" from any other kind of exception, without having to inspect underlying driver or ORM exceptions.

### Role in the Codebase

`DataAccessException` is the shared failure signal of the `DataAccessLayer` project. It is a thin marker exception with no logic of its own — its value is purely in the type. Callers that depend on data access can `catch (DataAccessException)` to handle any persistence-layer failure uniformly, regardless of which repository or provider produced it. If the class were removed, that catch point would disappear and callers would have to handle raw ORM/driver exceptions instead.

### Relationships

- `DataAccessException` inherits from `System.Exception` (the standard .NET exception base class); nothing beyond the constructor is overridden.
- It currently has one throw site in the repository: `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs` wraps any failure while building the Hibernate session factory with `throw new DataAccessException("Error initializing Hibernate repository factory", e)`, preserving the original failure as the inner exception.
- No code in the repository currently catches `DataAccessException`; today it is a one-directional contract — thrown by the data access layer, awaiting a consumer.

### Behavior & Details

The class has a single constructor, `DataAccessException(string message, Exception inner)`, which forwards both arguments straight to the base `Exception` constructor. Two consequences follow:

- **There is no parameterless constructor and no message-only constructor.** Callers must always supply a message and an inner exception. Code that wants to throw `DataAccessException` without an underlying cause (e.g. `throw new DataAccessException("msg")`) will not compile — adding such a constructor is a deliberate extension point if that ever becomes needed.
- **The original failure is preserved.** Because the second argument is always passed as the inner exception, the stack trace and message of the root cause (e.g. a SQL or NHibernate error) remain accessible via `InnerException` after the exception propagates up.

The class has no properties, state, or other members; serializing or inspecting it behaves exactly like a plain `Exception`.

Rough edges: the only constructor forces an inner exception to be present, which is fine for wrapping but makes the type awkward to use for purely programmatic data-access failures (validation, misconfiguration) where no underlying exception exists.

# DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs

## Purpose

`IUnitOfWork` is the provider-agnostic contract for managing database transactions in this codebase. It exists so that business logic (e.g., `UserService` in `BusinessLayer/`) can begin, commit, and roll back transactions without knowing which ORM or data access implementation is actually being used.

## Role in the Codebase

This file sits in the `DataAccessLayer` directory alongside other abstraction interfaces (`IRepository<TKey>`, `IRepositoryFactory`). It defines the transactional "unit" boundary for all data access: a caller starts a transaction, performs one or more repository operations, then commits or rolls back as a single atomic unit.

The concrete implementation is `HibernateUnitOfWork` (in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/`), which wraps an NHibernate `IStatelessSession`. A thinner sub-interface, `IHibernateUnitOfWork`, extends `IUnitOfWork` to add an overload of `BeginTransaction` that accepts an explicit `IsolationLevel`.

If this interface were removed, there would be no provider-agnostic way to express transactional boundaries, and callers would be forced to depend on the NHibernate-specific implementation directly.

## Relationships

- **Inherited by:** `IHibernateUnitOfWork` (DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateUnitOfWork.cs) — adds `BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel isolationLevel)`.
- **Implemented by:** `HibernateUnitOfWork` (DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateUnitOfWork.cs) — the only concrete implementation in the repository.
- **Exposed through:** `IHibernateRepository.UnitOfWork` property, which returns an `IHibernateUnitOfWork`.
- **Consumed by:** `UserService` (BusinessLayer/UserService.cs) calls `repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction()`, `CommitTransaction()`, and `RollBackTransaction()` to wrap user-save operations in a transaction.

`IUnitOfWork` itself extends `System.IDisposable` (standard .NET), so a unit of work is expected to release its underlying session/transaction resources when disposed.

## Behavior & Details

The interface declares four members:

| Member | Contract |
|---|---|
| `bool IsInTransaction { get; }` | Read-only flag: `true` when a transaction has been opened and not yet committed or rolled back. |
| `void BeginTransaction()` | Opens a new transaction. The `HibernateUnitOfWork` implementation starts with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted` by default and throws `InvalidOperationException` if a transaction is already open. |
| `void CommitTransaction()` | Commits the open transaction. Throws `InvalidOperationException` if no transaction is active. On failure, the implementation rolls back before rethrowing. |
| `void RollBackTransaction()` | Rolls back the open transaction. Throws `InvalidOperationException` if no transaction is active. |

### Typical usage pattern

```csharp
using var repository = _repositoryFactory.Create();
repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction();
try
{
    await repository.Save(entity);
    repository.UnitOfWork.CommitTransaction();
}
catch
{
    repository.UnitOfWork.RollBackTransaction();
    throw;
}
```

Callers (such as `UserService.AddUser`) are responsible for the try/catch and for deciding whether to rethrow or wrap the exception. The unit of work itself does not swallow errors.

### Rough edges

- The `CommitTransaction` failure path in `HibernateUnitOfWork` calls `RollBackTransaction()`, but if that rollback also throws, the original exception is lost (the rollback exception propagates instead). This is an implementation detail outside this interface, but it is relevant to anyone relying on the "commit or throw" contract.
- `Dispose` on `HibernateUnitOfWork` sets `_isDisposed = true` only when a transaction existed at disposal time, which means calling `Dispose` twice with no transaction open leaves the flag unset. Again, this lives in the implementation, not the contract.

- The constructor is `protected` and sets `Id = default!` (the C# null-forgiving operator applied to `default(TKey)`, e.g. `0` for `int`). Subclasses must be constructible without arguments (see `User`'s comment about NHibernate requiring a parameterless constructor), and that requirement chains from here.
- `Id` is `public virtual` with a `protected set` — meaning only the class itself or derived classes can assign it, never application code or the repositories from outside the hierarchy. Declaring it `virtual` leaves room for a persistence provider or subclass to override the accessor if needed, though the known subclasses (`User`) do not.
- `[Serializable]` on the class marks it for binary/serialization compatibility, and `[Browsable(false)]` on `Id` keeps the key property out of designer/property-grid tooling.
- Nothing is stored or cached: there is no state beyond the key, no side effects, and no failure modes of its own. A new `User` therefore starts with `Id == 0` until the provider assigns a real key.

### Rough edges

`IEntity<TKey>`'s `Id` setter is intentionally absent, yet `Entity<TKey>` marks `Id` `virtual` — a derived class could in principle override the property with a public setter, breaking the "identity is not settable from outside" contract. Nothing in this codebase does so, but the compiler will not stop a subclass from doing it.
children.summary:
### Purpose

The `DataAccessLayer` project defines the abstract contracts for data persistence in this codebase. It provides the core interfaces for querying, managing transactions, and defining entity identities, allowing the application to remain decoupled from specific Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) providers.

These files belong together because they form a dependency-free foundation: they contain no logic, only definitions. By keeping the abstraction layer separate from implementation details (like NHibernate, which lives in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`), higher-level business logic can depend on these stable contracts without needing to know how the data is actually stored or retrieved.

### Software Components

This directory contains four distinct functional areas, all defined as interfaces or base types to enforce loose coupling:

**Entity Identity**
This group defines what counts as a "entity" for the persistence layer.
*   [IEntity](DataAccessLayer/IEntity.md) (`IEntity.cs`): The marker interface requiring a read-only `Id` of type `TKey`.
*   [Entity](DataAccessLayer/Entity.md) (`Entity.cs`): The abstract base class that implements `IEntity`, providing a standard `Id` property that concrete domain models (like `User`) inherit from.

**Querying**
This group defines how data is retrieved.
*   [IRepository](DataAccessLayer/IRepository.md) (`IRepository.cs`): The primary read-only contract. It exposes methods for finding single entities (`FindOne`, `Single`) and collections (`Find`, `GetAll`), as well as `IQueryable` access for composed LINQ queries. It is strictly query-oriented; it does not include save or delete operations.

**Factory & Lifecycle**
This group defines how repositories are instantiated.
*   [IRepositoryFactory](DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.md) (`IRepositoryFactory.cs`): The contract for creating and dropping repository instances. It abstracts the creation of stateless sessions, ensuring that each repository instance is independent.

**Transactions & Errors**
This group defines operational control and failure signaling.
*   [IUnitOfWork](DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.md) (`IUnitOfWork.cs`): The contract for managing transactional boundaries (`Begin`, `Commit`, `Rollback`). It ensures that business operations can be treated as atomic units regardless of the underlying provider.
*   [DataAccessException](DataAccessLayer/DataAccessException.md) (`DataAccessException.cs`): A wrapper exception type that standardizes how persistence errors are propagated to consumers, hiding the underlying ORM/driver specifics.
*   [SortOrder](DataAccessLayer/SortOrder.md) (`SortOrder.cs`): A simple enum (`Ascending`/`Descending`) intended as a shared vocabulary for sorting, though it is currently unused by the other interfaces in this directory.

### Relationships

The components in this directory form a strict dependency hierarchy where the factory produces repositories, repositories expose the unit of work, and all entities conform to the entity contract.

`IRepositoryFactory` is the entry point for consumers. It creates instances of `IRepository` (specifically `IHibernateRepository` in the concrete layer). Once a repository is created, it exposes an `IUnitOfWork` instance, which the caller uses to wrap database operations in a transaction. All query methods in `IRepository` and the identity checks in `IEntity` rely on the `TKey` generic parameter being a `struct`, ensuring consistent key handling across the layer.

`DataAccessException` acts as the unified error boundary. While defined here, it is typically thrown by the concrete Hibernate implementations to wrap lower-level driver errors, allowing business layers to catch a single type for all persistence failures.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph DataAccessLayer
        EF[IRepositoryFactory]
        ER[IRepository]
        EU[IUnitOfWork]
        EI[IEntity]
        EC[Entity]
        EX[DataAccessException]
        SO[SortOrder]
    end

    EF -->|Creates| ER
    ER -->|Exposes| EU
    EC -->|Implements| EI
    ER -.->|Constrains TEntity| EI
    EX -.->|Thrown by| EF
```

*Note: `SortOrder` is currently isolated from the other components in this directory as no interface currently accepts it as a parameter.*

### Rough edges

*   `IRepositoryFactory` includes a `Drop()` method that has no working implementation in the concrete layers, making it effectively unusable for shutdown logic.
*   `SortOrder` is defined but not referenced by any other interface or class in this directory, leaving its intended usage ambiguous.

# DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs

### Purpose

This file defines `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`, the contract for a factory that produces Hibernate-based repositories. It exists to give callers a stable interface for requesting NHibernate-backed repositories while hiding the session factory and configuration details inside the concrete implementation.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the Hibernate-specific factory contract inside the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` namespace. The generic, engine-agnostic contract is `IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`, which declares `Create()` and `Drop()` and constrains `TRepository` to `IRepository<TKey>`. This interface specializes that contract to the Hibernate repository type, so the business layer can ask for a factory without depending on any concrete data-access implementation.

### Relationships

- **`IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`): the base interface. It declares `Create()` and `void Drop()`. This interface inherits both; `Drop()` carries over unchanged, and `Create()` is hidden via `new` with a more specific return type of `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` instead of the base `TRepository` type argument.
- **`IHibernateRepository<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`): the repository type returned by `Create()`. It extends `IRepository<TKey>` and `IDisposable` and adds `Save<TEntity>` and a `UnitOfWork` property.
- **`HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`): the concrete implementation. It builds the NHibernate `ISessionFactory` in its constructor, and its `Create()` returns a `HibernateRepository<TKey>` wrapping a stateless session. Because `TRepository` is an out-variance (`out TRepository`) position, that implementation satisfies this interface.
- **`BusinessLayer.IRepositoryFactory`** (`BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`): a non-generic marker interface that simply extends `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`. This is the form the business layer would actually hold and resolve, so this interface is what business-layer code indirectly depends on.

### Behavior & Details

- `TKey` is constrained to `struct`, matching the base `IRepositoryFactory`.
- The `new IHibernateRepository<TKey> Create()` declaration **hides** rather than overrides the base `Create()` (interfaces cannot override). A caller holding an `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` reference gets the specific `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` return type; a caller holding only the base `IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>` reference gets the base return type and must cast if it wants the Hibernate-specific members like `Save` or `UnitOfWork`. The concrete class bridges the two by providing an explicit implementation of the base `Create()` that simply delegates to the public one.

# `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IModelContext.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `IModelContext`, a small two-property contract that carries the database connection string and the list of mapping assemblies needed to configure NHibernate. It exists so that consumers in the data-access layer can receive this configuration through dependency injection rather than reading `App.config` or hard-coding assembly names themselves.

### Role in the Codebase

`IModelContext` is the configuration seam between the composition root (the `BusinessLayer` project) and the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` project. The data-access layer knows how to build an NHibernate `ISessionFactory` given a connection string and mapping assemblies, but it does not know *where* those values come from. The `BusinessLayer` project supplies them: `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs` exports a concrete `ModelContext` (built on `ModelContextBase`) with `[Export(typeof(IModelContext))]`, pulling the connection string from `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]` and the mapping assemblies from a hard-coded array.

### Relationships

- **`ModelContextBase`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/ModelContextBase.cs`): the abstract base class in the same project that implements `IModelContext`. Concrete contexts (like `BusinessLayer.ModelContext`) inherit from it, which stores the constructor-supplied values in the two read-only properties.
- **`BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`**: the main consumer. Its `[ImportingConstructor]` takes an `IModelContext` and forwards `context.ConnectionString` and `context.MappingAssemblies` to `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`'s base constructor.
- **`BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs`**: the concrete implementation that MEF exports for this interface.
- **`HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`): receives the two values and uses them with FluentNHibernate to configure the database, load Fluent mappings from the named assemblies, run a schema update, and build the `ISessionFactory`.

### Behavior & Details

- **`MappingAssemblies`** (`string[]`): the names of the assemblies that contain FluentNHibernate mapping files. `SessionFactoryBuilder` and `HibernateRepositoryFactory` each iterate over this array, call `Assembly.Load(name)`, and register the mappings found in each assembly. A caller adding a new entity-mapping assembly therefore only needs to update the concrete context, not the data-access layer.
- **`ConnectionString`** (`string`): passed to `MsSqlConfiguration.MsSql2012.ConnectionString(...)` along with `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver`, i.e. this interface assumes a SQL Server database.
- Both members are read-only getters; the interface is implemented once in `ModelContextBase`, which assigns the values in its constructor. There is no default implementation, no state, and no lifetime management — it is a pure data contract.

Rough edges: `SessionFactoryBuilder.BuildSessionFactory` duplicates the entire session-factory configuration logic of `HibernateRepositoryFactory`'s constructor (including the `SchemaUpdate` call), so `SessionFactoryBuilder` and `HibernateRepositoryFactory` can drift apart when NHibernate configuration changes. Also, `HibernateRepositoryFactory` has a static `IsInitialized` flag that throws `InvalidOperationException("Already initialized")` if a second factory is ever constructed, meaning the injected `IModelContext` is effectively usable by exactly one factory instance per process.

# Documentation

**File:** `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`

### Purpose

`HibernateRepository<TKey>` is the NHibernate-backed implementation of the repository pattern in this data access layer. It gives business-logic code LINQ-to-NHibernate queries plus a single insert operation over any entity type that implements `IEntity<TKey>`, and it exposes a unit of work for transaction control.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is the concrete repository consumed through `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` (defined in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`). Instances are created by `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>.Create()`, which hands out one repository per `IStatelessSession` opened from the shared `ISessionFactory`. If this class were removed, the factory in `HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs` would have nothing to return, and any code typed against `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` or `IRepository<TKey>` would lose its NHibernate implementation.

### Relationships

- **`IHibernateRepository<TKey>`** (same directory): the direct interface implemented here. It extends `IDisposable` and `IRepository<TKey>` (from `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`), which is why this class carries the query methods (`GetQueryable`, `Single`, `Find`, etc.) plus the `Save` method and `UnitOfWork` property that only the interface `IHibernateRepository` declares.
- **`IEntity<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs`): the entity marker interface requiring a struct `Id`. All generic methods here are constrained to `class, IEntity<TKey>`, so only mapped entities with an identity can be queried or saved.
- **`HibernateUnitOfWork`** (same directory): created lazily by the `UnitOfWork` property and wrapping the same `IStatelessSession`, so transaction begin/commit/rollback act on this repository's session.
- **`NHibernate` / `NHibernate.Linq`**: `IStatelessSession` for execution and the LINQ provider for translating the `IQueryable` chains.
- **Callers**: anything resolving `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` — e.g. code going through `IRepositoryFactory` (`BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`) which is rooted at `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` — would rely on this class.

### Behavior & Details

- **Stateless session semantics.** The repository holds a single `IStatelessSession` for its lifetime. With stateless sessions NHibernate performs no identity map or dirty checking, which is why the class exposes only `InsertAsync` (in `Save<TEntity>`) for writes — there is no `Update` or `Delete`; updates must go through the session/`HibernateUnitOfWork` directly.

- **Query methods.** `GetQuery<TEntity>()` (private) wraps `_session.Query<TEntity>()`, the NHibernate.Linq entry point. Everything else is a thin LINQ expression over that:
  - `GetQueryable(predicate)` — filtered query, not yet executed.
  - `GetQueryable()` — unfiltered, as `IQueryable`.
  - `Single` / `SingleOrDefault` — execute immediately, throwing / returning null on zero-or-many / zero matches respectively.
  - `Find` — deferred filtered `IEnumerable`; `FindOne` — `FirstOrDefault`, so null on no match rather than an exception.
  - `GetAll` — deferred full-table enumeration; `GetAllAsync` — awaited materialization to a `List<TEntity>`.
  Queries are only sent to the database when enumerated, so `GetQueryable`/`Find`/`GetAll` return nothing until consumed.

- **`UnitOfWork` property.** Uses the null-coalescing assignment (`??=`) to create exactly one `HibernateUnitOfWork` per repository, always bound to this repository's session. Because `Dispose()` disposes `_unitOfWork`, disposing a repository also tears down any live unit of work.

- **`Dispose()`.** Guarded by `_disposed` so double-disposal is a no-op. It disposes the unit of work if one was created. Note it does **not** dispose `_session` — the session is owned by the factory's `OpenStatelessSession()` call, so callers disposing the repository leave the session open (see below).

- **`Save<TEntity>` is marked `async` but contains no `await`.** It simply calls `await _session.InsertAsync(entity)` — the method does actually await, so the warning only applies if you'd expect it to compose further; as written it performs one async insert.

### Rough edges

- `Dispose()` disposes the unit of work but never the underlying `IStatelessSession`, so disposing the repository can leak the session that `HibernateRepositoryFactory.Create()` opened for it.
- `GetAll<TEntity>` and `GetAllAsync<TEntity>` materialize the entire table with no paging, so they are risky on large entities.

### Purpose

`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateUnitOfWork.cs` defines `HibernateUnitOfWork`, the NHibernate-backed unit of work for this data access layer. It wraps a single `IStatelessSession`'s transaction lifecycle — begin, commit, rollback, dispose — so repository consumers can bracket their database operations in a transaction without dealing with NHibernate's `ITransaction` directly.

### Role in the Codebase

This is the concrete `IUnitOfWork` implementation for the NHibernate persistence layer, paired with the sibling `HibernateRepository<TKey>` in the same directory. The repository's `UnitOfWork` property creates it on demand: `_unitOfWork ??= new HibernateUnitOfWork(_session)` — i.e., each repository instance lazily creates one unit of work over the stateless session the factory (`HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`) opened for it. If removed, `HibernateRepository`'s `UnitOfWork` property and `IUnitOfWork` would have no concrete implementation to hand out.

### Relationships

- **`IHibernateUnitOfWork`** (same directory): the interface this class implements. It extends `IUnitOfWork` (defined in `DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs`, which declares `IsInTransaction`, `BeginTransaction()`, `RollBackTransaction()`, `CommitTransaction()`, and `IDisposable`) and adds one member, `BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel isolationLevel)`.
- **`IUnitOfWork`** (`DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs`): the base interface; its members are implemented verbatim here.
- **`IDataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepository<TKey>`**: the main caller — it owns a `readonly IStatelessSession` and passes it to the unit of work's constructor.
- **NHibernate** (external library): the `IStatelessSession` and `ITransaction` types and their `BeginTransaction`/`Commit`/`Rollback` semantics come from the NHibernate assembly, not this repository.

### Behavior & Details

- **Constructor** takes an `IStatelessSession` and stores it. No transaction is started at construction time; one must call `BeginTransaction` first.
- **`BeginTransaction()`** delegates to the overload with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted`.
- **`BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel)`** calls `_session.BeginTransaction(isolationLevel)` and stores the result in `_transaction`. It throws `InvalidOperationException` if a transaction is already running, so at most one transaction can be active per unit of work.
- **`CommitTransaction()`** commits, then releases (disposes and nulls) the transaction. If the commit throws, it rolls back and rethrows the original exception — the rollback here is defensive cleanup around a failed commit.
- **`RollBackTransaction()`** throws `InvalidOperationException` when no transaction is running; otherwise it rolls back and releases the transaction.
- **`IsInTransaction`** is simply `_transaction != null`, so it is true from the call to `BeginTransaction` until commit or rollback completes.
- **`Dispose()`** is virtual. Note that it only disposes the current transaction — it does not roll it back. A disposed unit of work with an uncommitted transaction therefore silently discards it; nothing is rolled back on the database. It also does not clear `_transaction` to null afterward, and `_isDisposed` is only set when a transaction was pending at disposal time.

### Rough edges

- The `CommitTransaction` pre-check error message says "Cannot roll back a transaction..." even though the method commits — a copy/paste leftover that will mislead anyone reading the exception.
- `Dispose()` does not set `_isDisposed` when no transaction is active, and it doesn't null `_transaction`, so `_isDisposed` and the actual state of the object are not reliably consistent.
- The class is not thread-safe, and `_transaction` has no `volatile`/locking; this is fine as long as each unit of work is confined to one thread of use, but nothing enforces that.

# `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/ModelContextBase.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `ModelContextBase`, an abstract base class that packages the two pieces of configuration NHibernate needs to build a session factory: a SQL Server connection string and a list of assembly names that contain the fluent mapping files. It is the shared half of the data-access configuration for the NHibernate layer.

### Role in the Codebase

`ModelContextBase` is a thin base class in the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` namespace. It implements the `IModelContext` interface (defined in `IModelContext.cs`, same directory), which exposes exactly two properties: `ConnectionString` and `MappingAssemblies`. The class stores whatever is passed to its constructor and exposes it read-only — it performs no validation, no I/O, and no database work.

Its job is to give the BusinessLayer a common contract for "here is where and how to talk to the database" without the business layer having to know about NHibernate's internals.

### Relationships

- **Implements `IModelContext`** (same directory, `IModelContext.cs`) — the interface declares the same two read-only properties, so `ModelContextBase` is essentially the reference implementation.
- **Extended by `ModelContext`** in `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs`. That class is a single-line concrete subclass:

  ```csharp
  public class ModelContext()
      : ModelContextBase(ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]!, ["Entity.Hibernate"]);
  ```

  It pulls the connection string from `App.config`/`Web.config` and points the mapping assemblies at `Entity.Hibernate`. It is MEF-exported as `IModelContext`.
- **Consumed indirectly by `RepositoryFactory`** in `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`, which takes an `IModelContext` in its importing constructor and forwards `context.ConnectionString` and `context.MappingAssemblies` to its base, `HibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`. That factory then builds an `ISessionFactory` using those values.
- Note the sibling static helper `SessionFactoryBuilder` in the same directory does essentially the same thing with the same two inputs, but it is **not** the one wired up by the business layer — `HibernateRepositoryFactory` contains its own inline FluentNHibernate configuration.

### Behavior & Details

- The constructor is `protected`, so the class can only be instantiated through subclasses. It copies the connection string as-is and turns the mapping-assemblies array into a (temporarily growable) `List<string>` before freezing it back into the `MappingAssemblies` array. Nothing is verified: an empty list or a misspelled assembly name will surface later, as an `Assembly.Load` failure, inside `HibernateRepositoryFactory`'s constructor.
- Both properties are get-only, set once at construction, so a context instance is effectively immutable once created.

### Rough edges

- The `List<string>` in the constructor is only used to carry a commented-out initializer `{ /*"DataAccessLayer", "DataAccessLayer.Hibernate" */}`. The list adds no behavior — `list.ToArray()` on an empty list just returns the original array. If the commented assemblies are ever re-enabled, only the comment would need to change.
- `SessionFactoryBuilder` in the same directory duplicates the NHibernate bootstrapping that `HibernateRepositoryFactory` already does inline, with the same inputs. Nothing in the business layer appears to call `SessionFactoryBuilder`, so it is currently dead parallel code, and the connection-string/mapping-assemblies pair exists in two places that can drift.

# DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs

### Purpose

`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs` defines `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`, the NHibernate-specific contract that extends the data layer's generic `IRepository<TKey>` (`DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`) with two Hibernate concerns: an explicit `Save<TEntity>` method and a `UnitOfWork` property that exposes the unit of work backed by the same session.

### Role in the Codebase

The generic `IRepository<TKey>` in the `DataAccessLayer` namespace defines only query operations (`GetQueryable`, `Single`, `Find`, `GetAll`, and so on). Callers who want to persist through NHibernate need an interface that also declares saving and transaction access; that is this interface. It is implemented by `HibernateRepository<TKey>` in the same directory (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`), and produced by factories implementing `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`). Domain/application code can depend on `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` rather than the concrete class, or on plain `IRepository<TKey>` when it only needs reads.

### Relationships

- Inherits `IRepository<TKey>` from `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs` — all read/query members come from that interface and are not restated here.
- Inherits `IDisposable` from `System`.
- `IEntity<TKey>` (referenced in the `Save` constraint) is defined in `DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs` as a marker requiring a `TKey Id` property; abstract base class `Entity<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs` implements it.
- `IHibernateUnitOfWork` is defined in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateUnitOfWork.cs` and implemented by `HibernateUnitOfWork` in the same directory.

### Behavior & Details

- `TKey` is constrained to `struct` and marked `in` (contravariant), so a repository typed on a derived key can be used where a base-key repository is expected.
- `Save<TEntity>(TEntity entity)` is the only persistence operation declared. In the sole implementation, `HibernateRepository.Save`, it calls `IStatelessSession.InsertAsync(entity)`. Because the session is a *stateless* NHibernate session, `Save` is an immediate insert — there is no identity map or dirty checking. If an entity already exists in the database, a second `Save` will produce a duplicate-key error; this interface has no `Update` or `Delete` members at all.
- `UnitOfWork { get; }` exposes the `IHibernateUnitOfWork` bound to the repository's session. The implementation lazily creates a `HibernateUnitOfWork(_session)` on first access, so the caller controls transaction scope (`BeginTransaction`, `CommitTransaction`, `RollBackTransaction`) around any work performed through that repository. `Save` executes within the active transaction on that session.
- `Dispose` (inherited from `IDisposable`) disposes the associated unit of work, and by extension any uncommitted transaction on it.

### Rough edges

The `UnitOfWork` property on the *interface* is a lazy, mutable cache in the implementation: once a unit of work is created for a repository, the repository effectively has a committed scope of work for its lifetime, which can surprise callers who obtain several repositories from the factory expecting independent transactions.

# `SessionFactoryBuilder.cs`

**Path:** `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/SessionFactoryBuilder.cs`

## Purpose

`SessionFactoryBuilder` is a static helper that builds an NHibernate `ISessionFactory` from a connection string and a list of mapping-assembly names. It exists to centralise the Fluent NHibernate configuration (SQL Server 2012, the SqlClient driver, Fluent mapping discovery, and schema auto-update) in one place, as a reusable alternative to the inline configuration in `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`.

## Role in the Codebase

It sits in the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` project alongside `HibernateRepository<TKey>`, `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`, `HibernateUnitOfWork`, and the `IModelContext`/`ModelContextBase` types. It is intended as a shared factory for the session infrastructure that repositories (`HibernateRepository<TKey>`) and the unit of work depend on.

In practice, it is currently dead code: `BuildSessionFactory` is not called anywhere in the repository. The same configuration is instead duplicated inline in the constructor of `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` (via the `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs` → `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs` chain, where `IModelContext.ConnectionString` and `MappingAssemblies` are passed to the factory's constructor). If you want new code to use this class, nothing stops you from calling `SessionFactoryBuilder.BuildSessionFactory(...)` directly — it is public. If you remove the file, nothing breaks today, but the duplicated configuration in `HibernateRepositoryFactory` remains the only working path.

## Relationships

- Depends on external libraries only: Fluent NHibernate (`Fluently.Configure()`, `MsSqlConfiguration.MsSql2012`), NHibernate (`ISessionFactory`, `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver`), and `NHibernate.Tool.hbm2ddl.SchemaUpdate`. No other project file is referenced.
- `mappingAssemblies` are resolved at runtime with `Assembly.Load(mappingAssembly)`, so the entries are assembly names, not file paths. The live counterpart in this codebase passes `["Entity.Hibernate"]` (see `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs`), so the mapping assemblies contain Fluent NHibernate maps such as `UserMap`.
- Its output, an `ISessionFactory`, is the same type `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` holds and uses via `_sessionFactory.OpenStatelessSession()` to create `HibernateRepository<TKey>` instances.

## Behavior & Details

`BuildSessionFactory(string connectionString, string[] mappingAssemblies)`:

1. Configures the database with `MsSqlConfiguration.MsSql2012`, the supplied `connectionString`, `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver`, and `ShowSql()` (SQL statements are logged to the console/stdout).
2. For each name in `mappingAssemblies`, loads the assembly and adds its Fluent mappings via `FluentMappings.AddFromAssembly`.
3. Runs `SchemaUpdate(cfg).Execute(false, true)` through `ExposeConfiguration`. This auto-updates the database schema to match the mappings on every build — the `true` flag means updates are executed, `false` means no script is written to disk.
4. Returns the result of `.BuildSessionFactory()`.

Caveats:

- **Schema mutation at construction time.** `SchemaUpdate` runs as a side effect of building the factory, so calling this method in a production or test environment will issue `ALTER` statements against the target database. The duplicated inline version in `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` has the same behaviour, so the whole project assumes an auto-evolving schema.
- **No error wrapping.** Exceptions from `Assembly.Load` or `BuildSessionFactory` propagate raw to the caller. By contrast, `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` wraps initialisation failures in a `DataAccessException`.
- **`ShowSql()` is hardcoded on.** There is no way to suppress SQL logging through this method.

## Rough edges

- The entire Fluent NHibernate configuration is duplicated between `SessionFactoryBuilder.BuildSessionFactory` and the `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` constructor, and only the factory's copy is actually used by the application. The two could diverge (they already differ in ordering: `SessionFactoryBuilder` registers mappings before the `SchemaUpdate` step, the factory registers them after) with no compile-time signal.

# `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateUnitOfWork.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `IHibernateUnitOfWork`, the NHibernate-specific unit-of-work contract. It exists so callers can depend on a way to control transactions with an explicit `System.Data.IsolationLevel`, which the generic base contract does not provide.

### Role in the Codebase

The interface lives in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` alongside its implementation `HibernateUnitOfWork` (see `HibernateUnitOfWork.cs`) and the repository types that expose it. It is a small extension point: it narrows the generic `IUnitOfWork` contract (defined in `DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs`) for the NHibernate stack. If it were removed, `HibernateUnitOfWork` could no longer be consumed generically, and callers that need a non-default isolation level would have no typed way to ask for one.

### Relationships

- **Extends** `IUnitOfWork` from the `DataAccessLayer` namespace (`DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs`). That base declares `IsInTransaction`, `BeginTransaction()`, `RollBackTransaction()`, `CommitTransaction()`, and (via `IDisposable`) disposal. Everything from the base is inherited by reference; this interface only adds one member.
- **Implemented by** `HibernateUnitOfWork`, which takes an NHibernate `IStatelessSession` and owns an `ITransaction`.
- **Exposed by** `HibernateRepository<TKey>` through its `UnitOfWork` property (declared on `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`), which lazily creates a `HibernateUnitOfWork` sharing the repository's session. So a repository is the natural entry point for obtaining the unit of work.
- **Consumed by business-layer code** — for example `BusinessLayer/UserService.cs` calls `repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction()` before its operations.

### Behavior & Details

The single added member is:

```csharp
void BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel isolationLevel);
```

- It starts a transaction at the caller-specified `System.Data.IsolationLevel`. The base interface's parameterless `BeginTransaction()` remains available for the default case; `HibernateUnitOfWork`'s parameterless method simply delegates to this one with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted`, so this overload is the single source of truth for actually opening the transaction.
- The contract for the inherited members comes from `IUnitOfWork`: `IsInTransaction` reports whether a transaction is open, and `RollBackTransaction()`/`CommitTransaction()` end it. The implementation throws `InvalidOperationException` if you begin a second transaction before finishing the first, or try to commit/rollback with none running.
- Callers that need a stricter or looser isolation level than `ReadCommitted` (for example `Serializable` for a read-modify-write sequence) program against this interface rather than `IUnitOfWork` to reach the overload.

### Rough edges

- The base contract in `IUnitOfWork` has no way to express an isolation level, so every provider-specific unit-of-work interface in this codebase would have to add its own overload; there is no shared mechanism for it.

### Purpose

`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.csproj` is the project file for the NHibernate-backed implementation of the data access abstractions. It is build configuration, not application logic: it declares the target framework and the NuGet packages and project references that let the sibling classes in this directory talk to a SQL Server database through NHibernate.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the compilation unit for the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` project, which sits alongside `DataAccessLayer` (the interface-only abstraction: `IRepository<T>`, `IUnitOfWork`, etc.). Every class in this directory — `HibernateRepository`, `HibernateRepositoryFactory`, `HibernateUnitOfWork`, `SessionFactoryBuilder` and the `IHibernate*` interfaces — is compiled from the settings in this file. Without it, none of that code builds; removing the `ProjectReference` to `DataAccessLayer.csproj` specifically would break compilation of the types that implement its interfaces.

### Relationships

- **`..\DataAccessLayer\DataAccessLayer.csproj`** — the only project reference. The Hibernate types implement the abstractions defined there (`IRepository<T>`, `IEntity<T>`, `IUnitOfWork`, `DataAccessException`), so this project depends on that one.
- **NuGet packages**, all used by the project's code rather than by this file itself:
  - `NHibernate` 5.6.0 and `FluentNHibernate` 3.4.1 — the ORM; `SessionFactoryBuilder` uses FluentNHibernate's `Fluently.Configure()` to build the session factory, and the repository/unit-of-work types use `ISession`.
  - `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` 7.0.0 — the ADO.NET driver, wired in via NHibernate's `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver` in `SessionFactoryBuilder`.

Consumers of the resulting assembly are any projects that want the concrete NHibernate data access layer (for example the `Entity.Hibernate` mapping project or application layers that resolve `IHibernateRepositoryFactory`).

### Behavior & Details

- Targets `net10.0`, matching the companion `DataAccessLayer.csproj`.
- Enables `ImplicitUsings` and `Nullable`, so all code in the project gets implicit global usings and nullable-reference-type checking.
- No output type, no custom build steps, no property overrides — a stock class-library project with three package references and one project reference.

### Rough edges

`SessionFactoryBuilder` calls `SchemaUpdate` at session factory construction, so the schema is auto-updated every time the factory is built — including in any non-development deployment of this project. That behavior is declared in code, not controlled by anything in this project file, but it's worth knowing when reasoning about what shipping this project entails.

# `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`, the class that builds the NHibernate `ISessionFactory` once for the application and then mints repository instances from it. It exists so that repository creation can be decoupled from the costly one-time NHibernate bootstrap (database configuration, schema update, mapping assembly loading) — the bootstrap happens in the constructor, and every subsequent repository is just a new stateless session.

It implements `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` (same folder), which in turn derives from `DataAccessLayer.IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>` defined in `DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`. That base interface declares `TRepository Create()` and `void Drop()`; this class adds the concrete `new IHibernateRepository<TKey> Create()` signature from the derived interface.

### Role in the Codebase

Inside `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`, this class is the entry point to the data layer. The business layer never touches NHibernate directly; it gets repositories through the factory chain:

- `BusinessLayer.RepositoryFactory` (in `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`) inherits `HibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` and implements `IRepositoryFactory` (i.e. `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`), passing `context.ConnectionString` and `context.MappingAssemblies` from an `IModelContext` into the base constructor. It is exported via MEF (`[Export(typeof(IRepositoryFactory))]`).
- Consumers such as `BusinessLayer.UserService` depend on `IRepositoryFactory` and call `_repositoryFactory.Create()` inside a `using` block per operation.

If this class were removed, `BusinessLayer.RepositoryFactory` would have no base class to bootstrap from, and no repository could be created. Note the factory itself is created only once in the process — a second construction attempt is an error (see below).

### Relationships

- **`IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`) — the interface implemented here.
- **`HibernateRepository<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`) — what `Create()` returns; it wraps the `IStatelessSession` this factory opens, exposing `GetQueryable`, `Find`, `Save`, a lazily created `UnitOfWork` (`HibernateUnitOfWork`), and `Dispose()`.
- **`IModelContext`** (`IModelContext.cs` / `ModelContextBase.cs`) — the source of the `connectionString` and `mappingAssemblies` arguments, supplied by the caller (`RepositoryFactory`) rather than read from configuration here.
- **FluentNHibernate / NHibernate** (external libraries) — `Fluently.Configure()`, `MsSqlConfiguration`, `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver`, `SchemaUpdate` are all from those packages.

### Behavior & Details

**Constructor** `HibernateRepositoryFactory(string connectionString, string[] mappingAssemblies)`:

- **Static `IsInitialized` guard.** A second call to any constructor throws `InvalidOperationException("Already initialized")`. The flag is `static`, so this is process-wide: the application is designed to have exactly one session factory.
- **Database configuration** is hardcoded to SQL Server 2012 via `MsSqlConfiguration.MsSql2012`, using the `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver` and `.ShowSql()` (SQL statements echoed to the log).
- **Schema auto-update:** `ExposeConfiguration(cfg => new SchemaUpdate(cfg).Execute(false, true))` runs an NHibernate schema *update* against the database on every factory construction, before the session factory is built. This mutates the database schema to match the mappings.
- **Mappings:** for each assembly name in `mappingAssemblies`, `Assembly.Load(assembly)` loads it by string name and all its Fluent NHibernate mappings are added. The assembly names are whatever `IModelContext` provides (e.g. `"DataAccessLayer.Hibernate"`).
- **Failure:** any exception during this setup is wrapped in `DataAccessException("Error initializing Hibernate repository factory", e)`. Note the static flag is set only after success, so a failed construction allows a retry — but a successful one permanently blocks further construction for the process lifetime.

**`Create()`** returns `new HibernateRepository<TKey>(_sessionFactory.OpenStatelessSession())`. Each repository gets its **own stateless session** — stateless sessions hold no identity map or first-level cache, so every repository instance is independent and must be disposed by the caller (the business layer does this with `using var repository = ...`). The factory holds only the `_sessionFactory`; repositories are not tracked or pooled.

**Explicit interface implementation.** `IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>.Create()` is implemented explicitly and simply delegates to `Create()`, satisfying the base `DataAccessLayer.IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>` contract through the interface hierarchy.

**`Drop()`** throws `NotImplementedException` — the schema-teardown half of the interface contract is a stub; there is no way to drop the schema through this factory.

### Rough edges

- The session factory construction logic here (connection string, `SchemaUpdate`, loading mappings by assembly name) duplicates `SessionFactoryBuilder.BuildSessionFactory` in the same folder, except the factory's version also runs the schema update. The two can drift.
- `Drop()` is unimplemented, and `Create()` returns a stateless session with no disposal tracking — callers must remember to dispose each repository, and there is nothing in the factory to catch them if they don't.

# DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs

### Purpose

This file defines `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`, the contract for a factory that produces Hibernate-based repositories. It exists to give callers a stable interface for requesting NHibernate-backed repositories while hiding the session factory and configuration details inside the concrete implementation.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the Hibernate-specific factory contract inside the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` namespace. The generic, engine-agnostic contract is `IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`, which declares `Create()` and `Drop()` and constrains `TRepository` to `IRepository<TKey>`. This interface specializes that contract to the Hibernate repository type, so the business layer can ask for a factory without depending on any concrete data-access implementation.

### Relationships

- **`IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`): the base interface. It declares `Create()` and `void Drop()`. This interface inherits both; `Drop()` carries over unchanged, and `Create()` is hidden via `new` with a more specific return type of `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` instead of the base `TRepository` type argument.
- **`IHibernateRepository<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`): the repository type returned by `Create()`. It extends `IRepository<TKey>` and `IDisposable` and adds `Save<TEntity>` and a `UnitOfWork` property.
- **`HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`): the concrete implementation. It builds the NHibernate `ISessionFactory` in its constructor, and its `Create()` returns a `HibernateRepository<TKey>` wrapping a stateless session. Because `TRepository` is an out-variance (`out TRepository`) position, that implementation satisfies this interface.
- **`BusinessLayer.IRepositoryFactory`** (`BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`): a non-generic marker interface that simply extends `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`. This is the form the business layer would actually hold and resolve, so this interface is what business-layer code indirectly depends on.

### Behavior & Details

- `TKey` is constrained to `struct`, matching the base `IRepositoryFactory`.
- The `new IHibernateRepository<TKey> Create()` declaration **hides** rather than overrides the base `Create()` (interfaces cannot override). A caller holding an `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` reference gets the specific `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` return type; a caller holding only the base `IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>` reference gets the base return type and must cast if it wants the Hibernate-specific members like `Save` or `UnitOfWork`. The concrete class bridges the two by providing an explicit implementation of the base `Create()` that simply delegates to the public one.
