### Purpose

The `Mvvm` project serves as the framework-agnostic core of the application's MVVM architecture. It provides the abstract base classes, interfaces, and shared types that define how ViewModels behave, how Views connect to them, and how application modules communicate with the user interface.

The contents belong together because they form the contract layer between the business logic (feature modules like `UserManagement`) and the specific UI technologies (WPF or WinForms). By centralizing the `ViewModelBase` hierarchy, the `IView` contract, and the `IMessageService` abstraction here, the project ensures that feature code remains testable and UI-agnostic, while the host applications only need to implement the specific glue code for their respective frameworks.

### Software Components

The components in this directory group into three functional layers:

**View-Model Base Hierarchy**
The foundation of the library is the inheritance chain starting at [ViewModelBase](Mvvm/ViewModelBase.md). It extends CommunityToolkit's `ObservableObject` to provide property change notification, design-mode detection, and a parent-child tree structure for managing nested ViewModels. Derived from this are three specialized bases:
*   [ValidatableViewModelBase](Mvvm/ValidatableViewModelBase.md) adds support for `FluentValidation` and surfaces errors via `INotifyDataErrorInfo`.
*   [DisposableViewModelBase](Mvvm/DisposableViewModelBase.md) implements the standard dispose pattern for ViewModels that manage unmanaged or external resources.
*   [MainViewModelBase](Mvvm/MainViewModelBase.md) handles the lifecycle of the application's main window, including icon loading and shutdown logic.

**View and ViewModel Contracts**
The interfaces define the boundary between the model and the view:
*   [IViewModel](Mvvm/IViewModel.md) is the root marker interface for all ViewModels, extending `INotifyPropertyChanged`.
*   [IMainViewModel](Mvvm/IMainViewModel.md) adds window-specific controls like `CloseWindow()` and `Shutdown()` to the ViewModel contract.
*   [IDisposableViewModel](Mvvm/IDisposableViewModel.md) marks ViewModels that must be explicitly disposed.
*   [IView](Mvvm/IView.md) defines the minimal view contract, primarily through the `DataContext` property which serves as the binding point for the ViewModel.
*   [IDialogView](Mvvm/IDialogView.md) and [IMainView](Mvvm/IMainView.md) extend `IView` with specific behaviors for dialogs and the main application window, respectively.

**Messaging and Module Lifecycle**
*   [IMessageService](Mvvm/IMessageService.md) abstracts the UI framework's message boxes, allowing ViewModels to display warnings, errors, and questions without referencing WPF or WinForms types directly.
*   [MessageResult](Mvvm/MessageResult.md) is an enum that standardizes the return values of user interactions (Yes/No/Cancel) across different UI frameworks.
*   [IModuleController](Mvvm/IModuleController.md) defines the lifecycle contract (`Initialize`, `Run`, `Shutdown`) for application modules, allowing hosts to start and stop features uniformly.

### Relationships

The dependency structure follows a strict layering: concrete application code depends on these abstractions, but these abstractions do not depend on the specific UI host. The `ViewModelBase` class is the central hub; it implements `IViewModel` and is the parent to the specialized bases. For instance, a concrete ViewModel like `UserViewModel` might derive from `MainViewModelBase` (which derives from `ViewModelBase`) and implement `IMainViewModel`.

The messaging subsystem relies on the [MessageResult](Mvvm/MessageResult.md) enum to translate platform-specific results into a common type. The `IModuleController` interface is the entry point for the host applications (WPF/WinForms), which use MEF to discover and drive the lifecycle of these modules. The `Common` project is a dependency for `Mvvm` (specifically for `ExtendedGuard` in `ViewModelBase`), but no other external dependencies exist within the `Mvvm` project itself beyond the NuGet packages for CommunityToolkit and FluentValidation.

# Mvvm.Console/Mvvm.Console.csproj

### Purpose

This is the MSBuild project file for the `Mvvm.Console` library. It defines a class library targeting `net10.0-windows` that provides a console-based implementation of the `IMessageService` abstraction from the `Mvvm` project — i.e., the way view models display messages, warnings, errors, and yes/no questions to a console user.

It exists so the solution can have a platform-specific messaging backend for console hosts, parallel to the WPF and WinForms equivalents.

### Role in the Codebase

This project file is the build manifest for a one-class library (`Mvvm.Console.MessageService`). It is referenced by:

- `ConsoleApp1/ConsoleApp1.csproj` — the console application that composes and runs the view models.
- `Demo.slnx` — the solution file, which includes it as a project.

If the project were removed, `ConsoleApp1` could not build (it has a direct `ProjectReference`), and the console host would have no `IMessageService` export for MEF to discover.

### Relationships

- **`Mvvm/Mvvm.csproj`** — project reference. The `Mvvm` project defines `IMessageService` (in `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`) and `MessageResult`; this library implements that interface.
- **`System.ComponentModel.Composition` (NuGet, 10.0.6)** — the MEF package that supplies the `[Export]` attribute used by `MessageService`. The same package version is also referenced by the `Mvvm` project itself, which declares the `[Import]` side.
- **Consumers:** `ConsoleApp1` pulls in this project so that MEF can discover `MessageService` and inject it wherever `IMessageService` is imported.

### Behavior & Details

- **Target framework `net10.0-windows`:** the same TFM as the other projects in the solution. No `OutputType` element is present, so MSBuild defaults to a class library (`Library`).
- **`ImplicitUsings` / `Nullable`:** enabled for this project, matching the rest of the solution's projects.
- **Two `ItemGroup` blocks:** one for the MEF NuGet package, one for the project reference. Nothing else (no output type, no content, no analyzers).

There is no build-time logic, packaging, or conditional behavior in this file beyond the above.

# Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs

### Purpose
This file defines `MessageService`, the console-host implementation of `IMessageService` (defined in `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`). It exists so that ViewModels in the library can display messages and warnings, and ask the user yes/no/ok-cancel questions, without knowing which UI technology is hosting the application. In a console app, the "display" part is coloured `Console.WriteLine` output; the question part is not implemented in a console host.

### Role in the Codebase
It is one of three sibling implementations of the same contract: `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs` (this file), `Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs`, and `Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs`. The `Mvvm` project defines only the interface, enum, and base ViewModel; each host-specific project contributes its own `MessageService`. The `Mvvm.Console` project contains nothing else but this service and its `.csproj`, so its entire reason to exist is to provide this export. If it were removed, any console application composing `IMessageService` from this assembly would fail to resolve the dependency (or would have to bring in the WPF/WinForms implementation instead).

### Relationships
- **`IMessageService`** (`Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`): the interface implemented here. All nine members, including the three question methods, are required by it.
- **`MessageResult`** (`Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`): the enum returned by the question methods.
- **MEF**: the `[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]` attribute (from `System.ComponentModel.Composition`) makes this class discoverable for dependency injection. Callers depend on the interface, not this class. For example, `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs` declares `IMessageService MessageService` as a settable property and calls `MessageService.ShowError("User data is invalid!")`. Which concrete `MessageService` is supplied depends on which `Mvvm.*` assembly the host application composes.
- **Tests**: `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` does not use this class; it mocks `IMessageService` directly.

### Behavior & Details
All output is formatted as `{caption} | {message}`.

- `ShowMessage` prints to standard output in white; the single-argument overload delegates with the caption `"Message"`.
- `ShowWarning` prints to standard output in yellow; the single-argument overload uses the caption `"Warning"`.
- `ShowError` prints to standard **error** (`Console.Error`) in red — the only method that does this — with the caption `"Error"`.
- Each two-argument method sets `Console.ForegroundColor` and never restores the previous colour, so the console stays coloured as the last method that ran.
- `ShowYesNoCancelQuestion`, `ShowYesNoQuestion`, and `ShowOkCancelQuestion` each throw `NotImplementedException`. They exist only to satisfy the interface.

### Rough edges
- The question methods are unimplementable in a plain console host (no modal dialog), so they throw; any ViewModel calling a question method in a console app crashes at runtime rather than degrading gracefully.
- `ShowMessage` and `ShowWarning` permanently change the console foreground colour as a side effect of writing one line.

### Purpose

`Mvvm.Console` is a .NET class library that provides a console-based implementation of the `IMessageService` interface defined in the `Mvvm` project. Its sole responsibility is to enable ViewModels to display messages, warnings, and errors to a console user via colored text output. This directory exists to allow console applications to host the shared Mvvm infrastructure without requiring WPF or WinForms dependencies, serving as one of three sibling implementations (alongside `Mvvm.Wpf` and `Mvvm.Winforms`) for the same contract.

### Software Components

The library consists of two primary artifacts:

*   **`MessageService`**: Defined in [MessageService.cs](Mvvm.Console/MessageService.md), this class is the core component. It is decorated with `[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]` to make it discoverable via MEF. It implements the `ShowMessage`, `ShowWarning`, and `ShowError` methods by writing to `Console.Out` or `Console.Error` with specific foreground colors (white, yellow, and red, respectively). The three question methods (`ShowYesNoCancelQuestion`, `ShowYesNoQuestion`, `ShowOkCancelQuestion`) are present to satisfy the interface but throw `NotImplementedException`, as modal dialogs are not feasible in a standard console host.
*   **Project Definition**: Defined in [Mvvm.Console.csproj](Mvvm.Console/Mvvm.Console.md), this file configures the library to target `net10.0-windows` and establishes the dependency on the `Mvvm` project for the interface definition and on `System.ComponentModel.Composition` for MEF support.

### Relationships

`Mvvm.Console` depends strictly on the `Mvvm` project to satisfy the `IMessageService` contract. It does not reference other host-specific projects (`Mvvm.Wpf` or `Mvvm.Winforms`), ensuring that a console host remains lightweight. Conversely, consumer projects like `ConsoleApp1` reference `Mvvm.Console` to allow MEF to inject the console-specific `MessageService` into ViewModels that import `IMessageService`. The dependency direction is strictly outward from the consumer to this library, and from this library to the core `Mvvm` abstraction.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Mvvm.Console"
        MS[MessageService]
        CSP[Mvvm.Console.csproj]
    end

    subgraph "Mvvm"
        IMS[IMessageService]
        MR[MessageResult]
    end

    subgraph "External"
        MEF[System.ComponentModel.Composition]
        CONS[ConsoleApp1]
    end

    CSP -->|references| MEF
    CSP -->|project reference| IMS
    MS -->|implements| IMS
    MS -->|uses| MEF
    MS -->|uses| MR
    CONS -->|references| CSP
    CONS -->|MEF injection target| MS
```

### Rough edges

*   The question methods in [MessageService](Mvvm.Console/MessageService.md) throw `NotImplementedException` rather than providing a fallback, meaning any ViewModel attempting to show a question in a console app will crash at runtime.
*   The `ShowMessage` and `ShowWarning` methods permanently alter the console foreground color and do not restore the previous color, which can affect subsequent non-Mvvm output in the console.

# Mvvm.Winforms.csproj

## Purpose

This is the project file (build definition) for the `Mvvm.Winforms` class library. It configures how the WinForms flavor of the MVVM layer compiles: it targets `net10.0-windows`, enables the Windows Forms runtime (`UseWindowsForms`), and enables nullable references and implicit usings.

The project contains exactly one source file, `MessageService.cs`, a WinForms implementation of the `IMessageService` interface from the `Mvvm` project — so this csproj is what makes that single type buildable and consumable as a library.

## Role in the Codebase

- The only build configuration for `Mvvm.Winforms`; without it the folder is just a directory of C# files with no assembly to compile into.
- By setting `UseWindowsForms=true`, it gives `MessageService.cs` access to `MessageBox` and the related WinForms types it uses.
- Declares the sole project dependency: `..\Mvvm\Mvvm.csproj`. That project provides the `IMessageService` interface (and, transitively, `Common`), so this project is a thin WinForms adapter over the framework-agnostic MVVM core.
- It is referenced as a `ProjectReference` by host applications that want MVVM on WinForms (e.g. `WinFormsApp1` in the solution).

## Relationships

- Depends on the `Mvvm` project (`..\Mvvm\Mvvm.csproj`), which defines `IMessageService` and the MVVM infrastructure (`CommunityToolkit.Mvvm`, `CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics`, `FluentValidation`) that the consuming side uses.
- No NuGet package references of its own — everything comes transitively through the `Mvvm` project.

# Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs

## Purpose

`MvvmApplication` is the base `Application` class for WPF hosts of this codebase's MVVM framework. It exists so a WPF app's `App` class (see `WpfApp1/App.xaml.cs`, which is literally `public partial class App : MvvmApplication` with no body) gets a full application lifecycle for free: composition-container creation, module discovery via MEF, ordered module startup, teardown on exit, and a global exception policy — without any of that code appearing in the consuming app.

It's the WPF counterpart of what `WinFormsApp1/Program.cs` and `ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` do imperatively (both call `CompositionHelper.CreateCompositionContainer(...)` and drive the same `Initialize()` → `Run()` → `Shutdown()` sequence themselves).

## Role in the Codebase

The `Mvvm.Wpf` project is a small library (this file plus `MessageService.cs`) that WPF applications reference. `MvvmApplication` is the piece an app plugs into by making its `App.xaml` root element `mvvm:MvvmApplication` (as `WpfApp1/App.xaml` does) and its code-behind derive from it. The app then supplies behaviour through ME

F exports in its own assemblies rather than code in `App`. Removing it would force every WPF host to re-implement container creation, the two-phase module start, reverse-order shutdown, and the exception handlers.

## Relationships

- **`System.Windows.Application`** (WPF framework type) — the base class. `MvvmApplication` adds nothing visible to WPF itself; it only overrides `OnStartup` and `OnExit` and adds constructors.
- **`Common.Composition.CompositionHelper`** (`Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs`) — builds the `CompositionContainer`. It scans the folder containing the *Common* assembly for files with assembly extensions, skips names in `ignoreAssemblies` (case-insensitive), and additionally loads whatever is passed in `moduleAssemblies` via `Assembly.LoadFrom`. A container failure here is caught and only `Console.WriteLine`d, so a WPF app gets no UI feedback from it.
- **`Mvvm.IModuleController`** (`Mvvm/IModuleController.cs`) — the contract with the app's modules: `Initialize()`, `Run()`, `Shutdown()`. Modules opt in with `[Export(typeof(IModuleController))]`, e.g. `WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController` (which in `Run()` shows the main view, and in `Shutdown()` closes it).
- **`Common.ExitCodes`** (`Common/ExitCodes.cs`) — supplies `ExitCodes.Error` (-1) for the two fatal startup paths.
- **Consumers** — WPF app `App` classes derived from it (the `App` in `WpfApp1`), typically via XAML, since WPF instantiates `Application` from XAML rather than from a constructor call.

## Behavior & Details

**Constructors.** The primary constructor takes `string[] moduleAssemblies`, `string[] ignoreAssemblies`, and an optional `SearchOption` (default `TopDirectoryOnly`), all stored as properties. The two public overloads delegate with an empty `moduleAssemblies`; one takes no arguments, the other only `ignoreAssemblies`. So the default behavior is: scan the app's own directory, exclude nothing, no explicitly named extra assemblies.

Note the parameter order is `moduleAssemblies` *then* `ignoreAssemblies`. The single-array overload is therefore `MvvmApplication(string[] ignoreAssemblies, ...)` — if a caller passes one array, it is treated as *ignore* names, not as assemblies to load. Easy to get backwards.

**Startup (`OnStartup`).** In order:

1. Register the two exception handlers (see below).
2. Create the `CompositionContainer` via `CompositionHelper`.
3. `GetExportedValues<IModuleController>()`. If that throws `ReflectionTypeLoadException`, each loader exception is written to `Console` and the app exits with `ExitCodes.Error` (console output is invisible in a WPF app, so this is effectively a silent early exit).
4. If zero modules were exported, show a "No module found." `MessageBox` and exit with `ExitCodes.Error`.
5. Call `Initialize()` on every module, then — in a second pass — `Run()` on every module. The split means every module is fully initialized before any module's `Run()` executes, which lets a module's `Run()` assume other modules' `Initialize()` already happened.

**Shutdown (`OnExit`).** `ModuleControllers.Reverse().Shutdown()` — modules shut down in the opposite order they started. Then `Container.Dispose()`. If startup failed before any modules ran, this loop is a no-op and the container (possibly null, if `OnStartup` returned before assigning it) is disposed only if non-null.

**Exception handling.** Two handlers cover the usual WPF split:

- `AppDispatcherUnhandledException` catches exceptions on the UI thread, calls the shared handler, then sets `e.Handled = true` — so the app survives any non-terminating UI exception.
- `AppDomain.UnhandledException` catches everything else; it cannot prevent termination.

Both funnel into `HandleException`, which `Trace.TraceError`s the exception and — only when not terminating — shows a modal error box. The UI string here is German ("Es ist ein Fehler aufgetreten." / "Fehler") while the no-modules message above is English, so localisation is inconsistent within the class.

There's a comment claiming the handlers are skipped in Debug mode so the debugger can break on exceptions; the code actually registers them unconditionally, so in Debug a WPF app will still show the error box and swallow UI exceptions rather than breaking.

## Rough edges

- The comment above the handler registration doesn't match the code: handlers are registered in all configurations, so the "don't handle in Debug" intent isn't implemented.
- The `ReflectionTypeLoadException` path reports to `Console`, which a WPF app has no console for — the user sees only a sudden exit.
- The single-`string[]` overload takes `ignoreAssemblies`, the opposite of what the parameter order in the primary constructor suggests; a reader of the signature alone will guess wrong.
- Error message language is mixed (German dialog, English "No module found.").

### Purpose
`Mvvm.Wpf/Mvvm.Wpf.csproj` is the MSBuild project file for the `Mvvm.Wpf` library — the WPF-specific half of this repository's Mvvm framework. It defines how the project's two classes, `MvvmApplication` and `MessageService`, are compiled. The project exists to make the framework's module-based, MEF-composed application shell available for WPF, complementing the sibling `Mvvm` core project and the `Mvvm.Winforms` / `Mvvm.Console` variants.

### Relationships
- References `..\Mvvm\Mvvm.csproj` — the framework core. Both projects pin `System.ComponentModel.Composition` 10.0.6 (the MEF package), which `MvvmApplication` uses to build its `CompositionContainer` and discover `IModuleController` exports.

# Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs

### Purpose

`Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs` defines the WPF implementation of `IMessageService` (declared in `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`), a small abstraction over native message boxes. It exists so that view models can show informational, warning, error, and question dialogs without referencing WPF types. View models depend on the interface; this class is what actually displays the `System.Windows.MessageBox` at runtime.

### Role in the Codebase

This is a platform adapter inside the `Mvvm.Wpf` project. That project is the WPF host layer of an MEF-based modular application: `MvvmApplication.cs` in the same folder builds a `CompositionContainer` from assemblies at startup, and every exported type in the loaded assemblies becomes available for import. `MessageService` is marked `[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]`, so the container wires it into anything that carries an `[Import]` of `IMessageService` — for example the `MessageService` property in `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`, which calls `MessageService.ShowError(...)` when validation fails.

The `Mvvm.Wpf` namespace is not imported in this file, which is why this file doesn't see the interface — it comes from the `Mvvm` namespace via the project reference in `Mvvm.Wpf.csproj`. The same pattern exists for other UI stacks: `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs` and `Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs` export equivalent implementations for their own platforms. A given application only loads the host assembly for the stack it runs on, so its container resolves to exactly one of these exports.

### Relationships

- **Implements** `IMessageService` (`Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`) — the nine members here are exactly the interface's members.
- **Returns** `MessageResult` (`Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`), a plain enum that mirrors WPF's `MessageBoxResult` values (`None`, `OK`, `Cancel`, `Abort`, `Retry`, `Ignore`, `Yes`, `No`, `TryAgain`, `Continue`), so callers never see a WPF type.
- **Consumed via MEF**: view models and other components pull it in with `[Import] public IMessageService MessageService { get; set; }`. Unit tests instead mock the interface directly (see `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs`).
- Depends on `System.Windows.MessageBox` from WPF — this is the only place the WPF dependency shows up in the type's surface, which is the point of the abstraction.

### Behavior & Details

The class is a thin, stateless wrapper. Every method maps one-to-one onto a `MessageBox.Show` call with `MessageBoxButton.OK` for the informational family, and the appropriate button set for questions.

- **Informational methods** (`ShowMessage`, `ShowWarning`, `ShowError`) return `void`. Each has a two-argument form and a one-argument overload that supplies a default caption: `"Message"`, `"Warning"`, and `"Error"` respectively. Icons are `None`, `Warning`, and `Error`; button is always `OK`.
- **Question methods** return `MessageResult`. There are no caption overloads here — every question method requires an explicit caption.
  - `ShowYesNoCancelQuestion` — buttons `YesNoCancel`, default result `Cancel`.
  - `ShowYesNoQuestion` — buttons `YesNo`, default result `No` (pressed via the `E` key or as a default button behavior in WPF).
  - `ShowOkCancelQuestion` — buttons `OkCancel`, default result `Cancel`.

Each question method casts the raw WPF `MessageBoxResult` to the local `MessageResult` enum. Both enums use identical numeric values, so the cast is safe in practice, but it means the two enums must stay in lockstep — a value added to WPF's enum that isn't mirrored in `MessageResult` would be silently lost in the cast.

A subtle detail: WPF's `MessageBox.Show` returns `MessageBoxResult.None` if the box is dismissed by some path that doesn't map to a button (rare, but possible in some dialog interactions). In that case the question methods return `MessageResult.None`, not the declared default — the `Cancel`/`No` parameters are only the *default button*, not a fallback return value. Callers that treat "not affirmative" as the safe branch should check `!= MessageResult.OK` / `!= MessageResult.Yes` rather than assuming the default is always returned.

There is no logging, no async surface, and no customization point (font, owner window, modal-vs-modeless) — the class is deliberately opaque: it only answers "show this message, get back this result."

### Rough edges

- The `MessageBoxResult` → `MessageResult` cast couples the two enums silently; a future divergence in WPF's enum values would corrupt results without a compile-time error.
- Question methods lack the one-argument caption overloads their informational counterparts have, so callers writing `ShowYesNoQuestion("...", "…")` must always pass the caption — an asymmetry easy to trip over.

# Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs

### Purpose

`Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs` defines the WPF implementation of `IMessageService` (declared in `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`), a small abstraction over native message boxes. It exists so that view models can show informational, warning, error, and question dialogs without referencing WPF types. View models depend on the interface; this class is what actually displays the `System.Windows.MessageBox` at runtime.

### Role in the Codebase

This is a platform adapter inside the `Mvvm.Wpf` project. That project is the WPF host layer of an MEF-based modular application: `MvvmApplication.cs` in the same folder builds a `CompositionContainer` from assemblies at startup, and every exported type in the loaded assemblies becomes available for import. `MessageService` is marked `[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]`, so the container wires it into anything that carries an `[Import]` of `IMessageService` — for example the `MessageService` property in `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`, which calls `MessageService.ShowError(...)` when validation fails.

The `Mvvm.Wpf` namespace is not imported in this file, which is why this file doesn't see the interface — it comes from the `Mvvm` namespace via the project reference in `Mvvm.Wpf.csproj`. The same pattern exists for other UI stacks: `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs` and `Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs` export equivalent implementations for their own platforms. A given application only loads the host assembly for the stack it runs on, so its container resolves to exactly one of these exports.

### Relationships

- **Implements** `IMessageService` (`Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`) — the nine members here are exactly the interface's members.
- **Returns** `MessageResult` (`Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`), a plain enum that mirrors WPF's `MessageBoxResult` values (`None`, `OK`, `Cancel`, `Abort`, `Retry`, `Ignore`, `Yes`, `No`, `TryAgain`, `Continue`), so callers never see a WPF type.
- **Consumed via MEF**: view models and other components pull it in with `[Import] public IMessageService MessageService { get; set; }`. Unit tests instead mock the interface directly (see `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs`).
- Depends on `System.Windows.MessageBox` from WPF — this is the only place the WPF dependency shows up in the type's surface, which is the point of the abstraction.

### Behavior & Details

The class is a thin, stateless wrapper. Every method maps one-to-one onto a `MessageBox.Show` call with `MessageBoxButton.OK` for the informational family, and the appropriate button set for questions.

- **Informational methods** (`ShowMessage`, `ShowWarning`, `ShowError`) return `void`. Each has a two-argument form and a one-argument overload that supplies a default caption: `"Message"`, `"Warning"`, and `"Error"` respectively. Icons are `None`, `Warning`, and `Error`; button is always `OK`.
- **Question methods** return `MessageResult`. There are no caption overloads here — every question method requires an explicit caption.
  - `ShowYesNoCancelQuestion` — buttons `YesNoCancel`, default result `Cancel`.
  - `ShowYesNoQuestion` — buttons `YesNo`, default result `No` (pressed via the `E` key or as a default button behavior in WPF).
  - `ShowOkCancelQuestion` — buttons `OkCancel`, default result `Cancel`.

Each question method casts the raw WPF `MessageBoxResult` to the local `MessageResult` enum. Both enums use identical numeric values, so the cast is safe in practice, but it means the two enums must stay in lockstep — a value added to WPF's enum that isn't mirrored in `MessageResult` would be silently lost in the cast.

A subtle detail: WPF's `MessageBox.Show` returns `MessageBoxResult.None` if the box is dismissed by some path that doesn't map to a button (rare, but possible in some dialog interactions). In that case the question methods return `MessageResult.None`, not the declared default — the `Cancel`/`No` parameters are only the *default button*, not a fallback return value. Callers that treat "not affirmative" as the safe branch should check `!= MessageResult.OK` / `!= MessageResult.Yes` rather than assuming the default is always returned.

There is no logging, no async surface, and no customization point (font, owner window, modal-vs-modeless) — the class is deliberately opaque: it only answers "show this message, get back this result."

### Rough edges

- The `MessageBoxResult` → `MessageResult` cast couples the two enums silently; a future divergence in WPF's enum values would corrupt results without a compile-time error.
- Question methods lack the one-argument caption overloads their informational counterparts have, so callers writing `ShowYesNoQuestion("...", "…")` must always pass the caption — an asymmetry easy to trip over.

### Purpose

The `Mvvm.Wpf` project serves as the WPF-specific host layer for the repository's MEF-based MVVM framework. Its primary responsibility is to provide a ready-made application shell that handles container composition, module lifecycle management, and global exception handling, allowing WPF applications to focus on business logic rather than bootstrapping infrastructure.

Its contents belong together because they form a complete WPF binding for the shared `Mvvm` core: one component (`MvvmApplication`) manages the application startup and shutdown, while the other (`MessageService`) abstracts the platform-specific UI messaging. Together, they allow WPF hosts to plug into the framework via XAML inheritance and MEF exports, mirroring the patterns established in the `Mvvm.Console` and `Mvvm.Winforms` sibling projects.

### Software Components

This directory contains two distinct functional components, each defined in its own C# file:

*   **Application Lifecycle Management**: `MvvmApplication.cs` defines the base `Application` class that WPF apps inherit from. It encapsulates the complex startup sequence, including scanning assemblies for MEF exports, creating the composition container, and executing the ordered `Initialize` and `Run` phases of all modules. It also manages the reverse-order shutdown and registers global exception handlers for both the UI dispatcher and the application domain.
*   **UI Message Abstraction**: `MessageService.cs` implements the `IMessageService` interface from the core `Mvvm` project. It acts as a thin adapter that translates interface method calls into native `System.Windows.MessageBox` invocations. By exporting itself via MEF, it ensures that any view model importing `IMessageService` is wired to this WPF-specific implementation without needing to reference WPF types directly.

### Relationships

The two components operate independently but within the same MEF-composition context established by the application host. `MvvmApplication` is the entry point that constructs the environment in which `MessageService` becomes available.

1.  **Bootstrapping and Dependency Injection**: `MvvmApplication.OnStartup` uses `CompositionHelper` to build a `CompositionContainer`. This container scans loaded assemblies for types decorated with `[Export]`. `MessageService` is one such exported type (`[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]`). Consequently, any other module or view model that declares `[Import] IMessageService` will be injected with an instance of `Mvvm.Wpf.MessageService` at runtime.
2.  **Isolation of Concerns**: `MvvmApplication` does not directly interact with `MessageService` for its core logic. It uses `Console.WriteLine` for fatal startup errors (a known limitation in WPF) and a hardcoded `MessageBox` for the "No module found" scenario. This separation means `MessageService` is only utilized by the *content* modules (view models) discovered during the startup process, not by the shell itself for its internal errors.
3.  **Project Structure**: The `Mvvm.Wpf.csproj` file ties these components together by referencing the core `Mvvm` project (for interfaces like `IMessageService` and `IModuleController`) and enabling WPF support. It ensures that both the application base class and the message service are compiled into a single library assembly for WPF hosts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Mvvm.Wpf Project"
        MA[MvvmApplication]
        MS[MessageService]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Mvvm Project"
        IMC[IModuleController]
        IMS[IMessageService]
    end
    
    subgraph "WPF Framework"
        App[System.Windows.Application]
        MB[System.Windows.MessageBox]
    end
    
    MA -->|Inherits from| App
    MA -->|Imports/Uses| IMC
    MS -->|Implements| IMS
    MS -->|Calls| MB
    
    MA -.->|Discovers via MEF| MS
    MS -.->|Exported to| MA
```

### Rough edges

*   **Inconsistent Error Reporting**: `MvvmApplication` reports fatal startup errors (like reflection failures) to the `Console`, which is invisible in WPF applications, resulting in a silent exit. In contrast, the "No module found" error uses a `MessageBox`.
*   **Language Mismatch**: The error dialog shown by `MvvmApplication` when an unhandled exception occurs is in German ("Es ist ein Fehler aufgetreten."), while the "No module found" message is in English.
*   **Enum Coupling**: `MessageService` relies on a direct cast between WPF's `MessageBoxResult` and the core project's `MessageResult` enum. These must maintain identical numeric values to avoid silent data corruption, a fragile dependency not enforced by the compiler.

- [MessageService.cs](Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.md)
- [Mvvm.Wpf.csproj](Mvvm.Wpf/Mvvm.Wpf.md)
- [MvvmApplication.cs](Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.md)

### Role in the Codebase

It is not a build or deployment tool — it simply defines how the two C# files in `TestProject1/` (`UserViewModelTest.cs` and `MSTestSettings.cs`) are compiled into a test project. Those tests exercise `UserManagement.ViewModel.UserViewModel` (and its `ShowUsersViewModel` / `AddUserViewModel` children), using mocks of `IUserService` and `IMessageService`.

If the file is removed, the solution has no test project: the `UserViewModelTest` and `MSTestSettings` sources would compile nowhere.

### Relationships

- **`Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk` 18.4.0** — the test host; required for MSTest to be discoverable by `dotnet test`.
- **`MSTest` 4.2.1** — the test framework, supplying the `[TestClass]`, `[TestMethod]`, `[DataRow]`, `[TestInitialize]`, `[TestCleanup]`, `Assert`, and assembly-level `Parallelize` attributes used by the test sources.
- **`Moq` 4.20.72** — mocking library; `Mock<IUserService>` and `Mock<IMessageService>` in `UserViewModelTest.cs` depend on it. Note the test file also uses `CommunityToolkit.Mvvm` (`WeakReferenceMessenger`) — it reaches it transitively through the `UserManagement` project reference, not a direct package here.
- **Project references** — `..\BusinessLayer\BusinessLayer.csproj` (provides `IUserService` and `BusinessLayerException`, the type the tests verify) and `..\UserManagement\UserManagement.csproj` (provides `UserViewModel`, `ShowUsersViewModel`, `AddUserViewModel`, and `IMessageService`).
- **Global using** — `<Using Include="Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting" />` adds the MSTest namespace to every source file in the project, so the test classes don't need explicit `using` directives for `TestClassAttribute` etc.
- **Test discovery** — `MSTestSettings.cs` carries `[assembly: Parallelize(...)]`, which only takes effect because this project references MSTest.

### Behavior & Details

- `TargetFramework` is `net10.0-windows`, so the tests build and run only on Windows with the .NET 10 SDK.
- `Nullable` is enabled and `LangVersion` is `latest`; the test sources already use the null-forgiving operator (`= null!`) accordingly.
- The `<Using Include="...">` item is the only non-standard element: it is the MSBuild mechanism that makes `Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting` implicitly available project-wide, so `MSTestSettings.cs` (a one-line file with no `using`) still resolves the `Parallelize` assembly attribute.

### Rough edges

The assembly-level `[assembly: Parallelize(Scope = ExecutionScope.MethodLevel)]` in `MSTestSettings.cs` and the class-level `[DoNotParallelize]` in `UserViewModelTest.cs` are mutually exclusive at class scope — the class attribute wins for this class, so the assembly attribute currently has nothing to apply to. It would only matter if a future test class didn't opt out.

### Purpose

`TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` is the unit-test suite for the user-management ViewModels in the `UserManagement` project. It defines one MSTest class, `UserViewModelTest`, which exercises two pieces of behaviour in the real `UserViewModel` object graph: adding a user (with input validation and error surfacing, in `AddUserViewModel`) and loading the active user list (in `ShowUsersViewModel`). The `IUserService` and `IMessageService` dependencies are mocked with Moq so the tests verify the ViewModels' orchestration logic without touching a database or showing real dialogs.

### Role in the Codebase

The `TestProject1` project is the solution's test project (MSTest on `net10.0-windows`, Moq, referencing `BusinessLayer` and `UserManagement`). This class is its only test. The ViewModels under test are `MefExported` composition parts — normally wired up by MEF imports at runtime — so the tests construct them by hand and assign the `UserService`/`MessageService` properties directly, which is why the properties exist as settable `[Import]` properties in the source. Removing this file loses the coverage of the add-user validation path, the successful add path (collection update + field clearing), and the initial load path.

### Relationships

- **`UserViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`): the object under test. It is a `MainViewModelBase` that exposes `AddUserViewModel` and `ShowUsersViewModel` (MefImported in the app; instantiated manually here).
- **`AddUserViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`): derives from `ValidatableViewModelBase<IUser>` with a `UserValidator` (FluentValidation rule: `FirstName` and `LastName` must be non-empty). `SaveUserAsync()` — exposed as `SaveUserCommand` via `[RelayCommand]` — validates, calls `MessageService.ShowError("User data is invalid!")` if invalid, otherwise calls `UserService.AddUser`, sends a `UserChangedMessage` over `WeakReferenceMessenger`, and clears the name fields.
- **`ShowUsersViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`): registers for `UserChangedMessage` in its constructor (an `Added` message appends to `Users`); `OnLoadedAsync` — exposed as `LoadedCommand` — fetches `UserService.GetActiveUsers()` and populates its `Users` collection.
- **`IUserService`** (`BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`): mocked; provides `GetActiveUsers()` and `AddUser(UserDto)`.
- **`IMessageService`** (`Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`): mocked; the tests verify the exact `ShowError` call.
- **`UserChangedMessage` / `WeakReferenceMessenger`** (`UserManagement.Messaging`, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm): the messaging channel that makes `AddUserViewModel` and `ShowUsersViewModel` cooperate.

### Behavior & Details

**Test setup and isolation.** `[DoNotParallelize]` on the class keeps all four tests in the same class from running concurrently (MSTest otherwise parallelizes at method level per the assembly-level `Parallelize` attribute in `MSTestSettings.cs`). This matters because `Teardown` calls `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default.UnregisterAll(...)` on the shared static messenger for both child ViewModels; if tests ran in parallel, one test's teardown could unregister the other test's ViewModels and silently break its messaging assertions.

**`CanSaveUser_ValidatesInputsCorrectly`** — data-driven over four cases: empty first name, empty last name, and both whitespace-only variants. It sets the fields, stubs `AddUser` and `SaveUserAsync`, and asserts that `MessageService.ShowError("User data is invalid!")` is called once and the service is never called. Note that the whitespace cases only pass because the fields go through the `[ObservableProperty]` generated properties, whose change notifications (with their `NotifyCanExecuteChangedFor`/validation hooks) make validation treat `"   "` as invalid; in `ValidatableViewModelBase` the error is tracked per property, and `ValidateAllProperties` inside `SaveUserAsync` runs the FluentValidation `NotEmpty` rule against the current property value.

**`SaveUserAsync_WhenSuccessful_AddsUserToCollectionAndClearsFields`** — the happy path. After calling `SaveUserAsync`, it verifies three effects: the service received a `UserDto` with the exact names; the user appears in `ShowUsersViewModel.Users` (this happens through the `UserChangedMessage` posted by `SaveUserAsync` and handled by `ShowUsersViewModel`'s constructor-time messenger registration — so the test implicitly covers the messaging contract); and `FirstName`/`LastName` are reset to `string.Empty`.

**`SaveUserAsync_WhenServiceThrows_RethrowsExceptionAndDoesNotAddUser`** — `AddUser` is stubbed to throw a `BusinessLayerException` (with an inner `Exception`, mirroring the catch clause in `SaveUserAsync` that rethrows only `BusinessLayerException`). It asserts the exception propagates out of the command unchanged, with its message, and that `Users` remains empty — i.e., the failure path neither swallows the error nor leaves stale UI state.

**`OnLoadedAsync_FetchesActiveUsers_AndPopulatesCollection`** — stubs `GetActiveUsers` with two `UserDto`s, executes `LoadedCommand`, and asserts the service was called once and `Users` contains both entries in order. It does not exercise the `UserChangedMessage` path (messages sent by `SaveUserAsync` are the other way around).

### Rough edges

- The `UserService` mock in the validation test stubs `AddUser` although the method under test never reaches it — harmless but misleading; `VerifyNoOtherCalls` is the real assertion.
- In `SaveUserAsync_WhenSuccessful_...`, the comment says `//await _viewModel.SaveUserCommand.ExecuteAsync(null);` — a commented-out call on `UserViewModel`, which has no such command (it lives on `AddUserViewModel`). It is dead code that could confuse a future reader.
- The whitespace `[DataRow]` cases depend on the generated property setters doing their notification/validation dance; if `SaveUserAsync` were refactored to validate a different object, or the properties changed shape, these cases could behave differently than the test names imply.

# TestProject1/MSTestSettings.cs

## Purpose

This file is MSTest's **module-level settings file**. Its single line,

```csharp
[assembly: Parallelize(Scope = ExecutionScope.MethodLevel)]
```

tells the MSTest runner (MSTest 4.2.1, per `TestProject1.csproj`) to run the test **methods** in this assembly concurrently, using a separate execution context per method.

That is the only configuration this assembly carries: no explicit worker count, no `MaxConcurrency` — the runner defaults apply.

## Role in the Codebase

This is not a source file with logic; it is build-time test-runner configuration for the `TestProject1` unit test project. MSTest looks for a file named `MSTestSettings.cs` in the test assembly and applies any `[assembly: ...]` attributes it finds there, so the file name is what makes it work — it cannot be arbitrarily renamed or merged into `UserViewModelTest.cs` (an assembly attribute could technically live anywhere in the assembly, but the conventional, discoverable location is this file). If it were removed, all tests in the project would fall back to MSTest's default: sequential execution, no parallelization.

## Relationships

- **Consumed by the MSTest framework**, not by application code. No class in the project imports or references anything from this file; it compiles into assembly-level attributes that the test runner reads at discovery/execution time.
- **Scope of effect: the `UserViewModelTest` class** in `UserViewModelTest.cs` — the only test class in the project. That class is annotated `[DoNotParallelize]`, which opts its methods out of the parallelization enabled here. So in practice, as the project stands today, the setting has **no observable effect**: every test in the assembly is excluded from parallel execution.

## Behavior & Details

- `ExecutionScope.MethodLevel` means each `[TestMethod]` gets its own isolated context and may run in parallel with methods from other classes. A coarser scope, `ClassLevel`, would run methods within a class serially and classes in parallel; the finer method-level scope is the most aggressive option.
- `[DoNotParallelize]` at class level (as `UserViewModelTest` uses) is the supported escape hatch, and is appropriate here: the test class relies on MSTest's per-test `TestInitialize`/`TestCleanup` cycle and shares static, mutable infrastructure — `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default` (a `CommunityToolkit.Mvvm` static singleton) — which concurrent tests could interleave on. So opting out is deliberate and correct, but it does make the assembly-level `Parallelize` setting currently inert.
- A caveat if you ever add more test classes: the `[Parallelize]` setting applies assembly-wide from the moment any class does **not** carry `[DoNotParallelize]`. New tests that touch shared statics (messenger registries, caches, file system) will silently start running concurrently, and any shared-state assumption will surface as flaky tests rather than a compile error.

### Rough edges

- As currently written, the file's only directive is fully neutralized by `[DoNotParallelize]` on the sole test class — the two files contradict each other, and it is unclear which is intended to be the default policy (parallel where possible, or sequential by default).

# TestProject1/MSTestSettings.cs

## Purpose

This file is MSTest's **module-level settings file**. Its single line,

```csharp
[assembly: Parallelize(Scope = ExecutionScope.MethodLevel)]
```

tells the MSTest runner (MSTest 4.2.1, per `TestProject1.csproj`) to run the test **methods** in this assembly concurrently, using a separate execution context per method.

That is the only configuration this assembly carries: no explicit worker count, no `MaxConcurrency` — the runner defaults apply.

## Role in the Codebase

This is not a source file with logic; it is build-time test-runner configuration for the `TestProject1` unit test project. MSTest looks for a file named `MSTestSettings.cs` in the test assembly and applies any `[assembly: ...]` attributes it finds there, so the file name is what makes it work — it cannot be arbitrarily renamed or merged into `UserViewModelTest.cs` (an assembly attribute could technically live anywhere in the assembly, but the conventional, discoverable location is this file). If it were removed, all tests in the project would fall back to MSTest's default: sequential execution, no parallelization.

## Relationships

- **Consumed by the MSTest framework**, not by application code. No class in the project imports or references anything from this file; it compiles into assembly-level attributes that the test runner reads at discovery/execution time.
- **Scope of effect: the `UserViewModelTest` class** in `UserViewModelTest.cs` — the only test class in the project. That class is annotated `[DoNotParallelize]`, which opts its methods out of the parallelization enabled here. So in practice, as the project stands today, the setting has **no observable effect**: every test in the assembly is excluded from parallel execution.

## Behavior & Details

- `ExecutionScope.MethodLevel` means each `[TestMethod]` gets its own isolated context and may run in parallel with methods from other classes. A coarser scope, `ClassLevel`, would run methods within a class serially and classes in parallel; the finer method-level scope is the most aggressive option.
- `[DoNotParallelize]` at class level (as `UserViewModelTest` uses) is the supported escape hatch, and is appropriate here: the test class relies on MSTest's per-test `TestInitialize`/`TestCleanup` cycle and shares static, mutable infrastructure — `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default` (a `CommunityToolkit.Mvvm` static singleton) — which concurrent tests could interleave on. So opting out is deliberate and correct, but it does make the assembly-level `Parallelize` setting currently inert.
- A caveat if you ever add more test classes: the `[Parallelize]` setting applies assembly-wide from the moment any class does **not** carry `[DoNotParallelize]`. New tests that touch shared statics (messenger registries, caches, file system) will silently start running concurrently, and any shared-state assumption will surface as flaky tests rather than a compile error.

### Rough edges

- As currently written, the file's only directive is fully neutralized by `[DoNotParallelize]` on the sole test class — the two files contradict each other, and it is unclear which is intended to be the default policy (parallel where possible, or sequential by default).

### Purpose

`TestProject1` is the unit test project for the solution, specifically validating the ViewModels within the `UserManagement` module. It exists to verify that user management logic—such as adding users with validation and loading user lists—behaves correctly without relying on a real database or UI dialogues. The contents belong together because they form a single MSTest assembly that targets the `UserViewModel` object graph, using Moq to mock external dependencies like `IUserService` and `IMessageService`.

### Software Components

The directory contains two source files that define the test execution environment and the test logic itself.

`UserViewModelTest.cs` is the primary component, containing the `UserViewModelTest` class. This class orchestrates the manual construction of `UserViewModel`, `AddUserViewModel`, and `ShowUsersViewModel`, bypassing the normal MEF composition. It uses Moq to stub out `IUserService` and `IMessageService`, allowing it to test specific behaviors such as input validation errors, successful user addition with state clearing, and error propagation when the service throws exceptions. The tests also verify the messaging contract via `WeakReferenceMessenger` to ensure that adding a user updates the active user list in `ShowUsersViewModel`.

`MSTestSettings.cs` is a configuration component that defines assembly-level test runner attributes. It sets the default parallelization scope for the test assembly.

### Relationships

The relationship between these files is one of configuration versus execution, though there is a notable conflict in their current intent. `TestProject1.csproj` defines the project structure, linking the source files to the MSTest and Moq libraries and referencing the production `BusinessLayer` and `UserManagement` projects.

`MSTestSettings.cs` applies an assembly-level `[Parallelize]` attribute, intending to allow test methods to run concurrently. However, `UserViewModelTest.cs` explicitly applies `[DoNotParallelize]` to its test class. This is a deliberate design choice to protect shared static state, specifically the `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default` instance, which is manipulated in the test teardown. Because the only test class in the assembly opts out of parallelization, the assembly-level setting in `MSTestSettings.cs` currently has no observable effect. The two files thus establish a tension: one enables a feature the other immediately disables.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Test Assembly"
        CSProj[TestProject1.csproj]
        Settings[MSTestSettings.cs]
        TestClass[UserViewModelTest.cs]
    end

    subgraph "Production Code (References)"
        UserMgmt[UserManagement]
        BizLayer[BusinessLayer]
    end

    CSProj -->|compiles| Settings
    CSProj -->|compiles| TestClass
    CSProj -->|references| UserMgmt
    CSProj -->|references| BizLayer
    
    Settings -->|configures runner| TestClass
    TestClass -->|instantiates| UserMgmt
    TestClass -->|mocks interfaces from| BizLayer
    
    style TestClass fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

### Rough edges

The assembly-level parallelization enabled in `MSTestSettings.cs` is currently inert because the sole test class in `UserViewModelTest.cs` explicitly disables it with `[DoNotParallelize]`. This creates ambiguity about the intended default policy for the project, as the configuration file suggests parallel execution while the only consumer prevents it.

# UserManagement.csproj

`UserManagement/UserManagement.csproj`

## Purpose

This file is the SDK-style project file for the `UserManagement` library. It is build configuration, not application code: it declares the target framework, nullable/implicit-usings settings, and the dependencies needed to compile the view models, models, and messages in the `UserManagement` directory. The project itself holds the view-model layer for user management (`ViewModel/`, `Model/`, `Messaging/`, `Design/`), written UI-framework-agnostic so several host apps can consume it.

## Role in the Codebase

It is a class library — there is no `OutputType` of `Exe` or `WinExe`, so it compiles to a DLL rather than an executable. It is not an entry point. Removing it would break every project that references it: `WpfApp1`, `WinFormsApp1`, `ConsoleApp1`, and `TestProject1` all declare a `ProjectReference` to `..\UserManagement\UserManagement.csproj`, so their builds would fail to resolve the `UserManagement` namespace.

## Relationships

- **Project references (dependencies):**
  - `..\BusinessLayer\BusinessLayer.csproj` — supplies `IUserService`, which the view models import via MEF (`[Import] public IUserService UserService`) and call, e.g. `UserService.GetActiveUsers()` in `ShowUsersViewModel`.
  - `..\DataAccessLayer.Hibernate\DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.csproj` — transitively provides the `Entity.Hibernate` entity types that `UserManagement` code references.
  - `..\Logging\Logging.csproj` — supplies `ILoggingService`, likewise consumed via `[Import]`.
  - `..\Mvvm\Mvvm.csproj` — supplies `ViewModelBase`, the base class of the view models in this project.
- **Package reference:** `System.ComponentModel.Composition` 10.0.6 — the MEF implementation used for `[Export]`/`[Import]` composition of the view models.
- **Consumers:** the four host/test projects listed above compile this DLL into their apps; the WPF and WinForms hosts pair it with their own `Mvvm.Wpf`/`Mvvm.Winforms` projects to render the view models.

## Behavior & Details

- `TargetFramework` is `net10.0-windows`, which is what makes this library consumable only by Windows-targeted apps — matching the Windows-only hosts that reference it.
- `ImplicitUsings` and `Nullable` are both enabled, so the C# sources in the project rely on compiler-inferred usings and nullable reference type checks.
- The `System.ComponentModel.Composition` package is required because .NET no longer ships MEF in the base class libraries; without this reference the `[Export]`/`[Import]` attributes used throughout `ViewModel/` would not resolve.
- There are no custom build targets, no `OutputType`, and no content items — the project relies entirely on default SDK compilation of the `.cs` files in its directory tree.

### Rough edges

- The project references `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` even though its own sources import `Entity.Hibernate` types; the reference appears to exist to make those entity types available, which couples this view-model layer to the persistence stack transitively.

children.summary:
### Purpose

The `UserManagement` directory is a UI-framework-agnostic C# class library that implements the user management feature using the MVVM pattern. It provides the view models, data models, and messaging contracts required to display and manage users in Windows-based host applications. These components belong together because they form a self-contained feature module that can be consumed by multiple hosts (WPF, WinForms, Console) without exposing framework-specific dependencies.

### Software Components

The library is structured into four distinct layers, each with a specific responsibility:

*   **View Models (`ViewModel/`)**: The core logic layer. It contains the [UserViewModel](UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.md) (the root shell), [AddUserViewModel](UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.md) (for creating users), and [ShowUsersViewModel](UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.md) (for listing users). Each view model follows an interface-implementation pattern to support MEF-based dependency injection.
*   **Data Models (`Model/`)**: A lightweight data binding layer. It defines the [UserModel](UserManagement/Model/UserModel.md) class, which exposes observable properties for user details (First/Last Name) to the UI, keeping the view models decoupled from persistence entities.
*   **Messaging (`Messaging/`)**: The event contract layer. It defines [UserChangedMessage](UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.md) and [UserChangeType](UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangeType.md), allowing view models to communicate state changes (like "User Added") via a messenger pattern without direct coupling.
*   **Design Stubs (`Design/`)**: Design-time support. This contains view model subclasses that populate the WPF XAML designer with hard-coded sample data, ensuring the UI renders visibly in editors where MEF composition is unavailable.

The project configuration in [UserManagement.csproj](UserManagement/UserManagement.md) ties these together, defining the .NET 10 Windows target and referencing external layers like `BusinessLayer` and `Mvvm`.

### Relationships

The components interact through a combination of MEF dependency injection and event messaging. `UserViewModel` acts as the composition root, importing `IAddUserViewModel` and `IShowUsersViewModel` from the MEF container. At runtime, these resolve to the concrete implementations in the same folder.

Communication between sibling view models is decoupled. When `AddUserViewModel` saves a user, it broadcasts a `UserChangedMessage` via `WeakReferenceMessenger`. `ShowUsersViewModel` subscribes to this message and updates its user collection in response. The `Design/` subdirectory mirrors this structure but replaces MEF injection with direct instantiation to feed the visual designer.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "UserManagement"
        subgraph "ViewModel"
            UV[UserViewModel]
            AUV[AddUserViewModel]
            SUV[ShowUsersViewModel]
        end
        
        subgraph "Model"
            UM[UserModel]
        end
        
        subgraph "Messaging"
            UCM[UserChangedMessage]
        end
        
        subgraph "Design"
            DUV[DesignUserViewModel]
        end
    end
    
    UV -->|MEF Imports| AUV
    UV -->|MEF Imports| SUV
    
    AUV -->|Creates| UM
    AUV -->|Sends| UCM
    SUV -->|Receives| UCM
    SUV -->|Updates| UM
    
    DUV -.->|Design-time instantiation of| UV
```

### Rough edges

The `ShowUsersViewModel` only handles `Added` user change events; `Updated` and `Deleted` events throw `NotImplementedException`, meaning the UI cannot currently reflect modifications or removals. Additionally, the `UserModel` lacks an `Id` property, which prevents the view model from uniquely identifying users to apply these future updates or deletions.

## Contents

- [Design/](UserManagement/Design.md)
- [Messaging/](UserManagement/Messaging.md)
- [Model/](UserManagement/Model.md)
- [ViewModel/](UserManagement/ViewModel.md)

### Purpose

`UserManagement/Design/DesignAddUserViewModel.cs`

`DesignAddUserViewModel` exists so the "add user" form renders with plausible sample content in a designer or preview tool. It subclasses the real `AddUserViewModel` and overrides only the constructor to pre-fill `FirstName` and `LastName` with `"Sample"` and `"User"`. This is a WPF design-time stub, not runtime application code.

### Role in the Codebase

It lives in the `UserManagement/Design/` folder alongside `DesignShowUsersViewModel` and `DesignUserViewModel`, a sibling design-time stub for each of the real view models in `UserManagement/ViewModel/`. Its parent `AddUserViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`) is a partial class; the XAML designer generates a second partial for design purposes, and this subclass is what the designer instantiates in place of it.

The sole consumer is the XAML designer itself. `WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml` designates `DesignUserViewModel` via `d:DesignInstance`, and `DesignUserViewModel`'s constructor constructs a `DesignAddUserViewModel` for its `AddUserViewModel` property. At runtime nothing instantiates this class.

### Relationships

- Inherits `AddUserViewModel` from `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`, which in turn extends `ValidatableViewModelBase<IUser>` and exports `IAddUserViewModel`. `DesignAddUserViewModel` adds no members beyond the constructor, so it inherits all behavior: the `FirstName`/`LastName` observable properties, validation, and `SaveUserAsync`.
- Used only by `DesignUserViewModel` (same folder), which sets it as the `AddUserViewModel` property when the designer builds the view hierarchy.

### Behavior & Details

The constructor sets the two inherited properties to non-empty values so the text fields are visibly populated and the inherited `SaveUserCommand` appears executable in the designer. Because these assignments go through the inherited property setters, `OnFirstNameChanged`/`OnLastNameChanged` run and call `ValidateProperty`; the constructor does not touch the injected `UserService`, `LoggingService`, or `MessageService`, which remain null (`null!`) and are only ever used inside `SaveUserAsync` — which the designer does not invoke.

One caveat: `IsDesignTimeCreatable=True` in `UserView.xaml` only guarantees constructability, not safety. If any designer action ever executes `SaveUserAsync`, the null-injected services would throw — but a plain designer preview only builds the object graph and binds properties, so this never happens in practice.

### Purpose

`UserManagement/Design/DesignUserViewModel.cs` defines `DesignUserViewModel`, a design-time stand-in for the real `UserViewModel`. The WPF XAML designer cannot run the application's MEF composition, so the designer's `[Import]`-wired child view models (`AddUserViewModel`, `ShowUsersViewModel`) would be `null` if it instantiated `UserViewModel` directly. This class exists so the XAML designer can create a `UserViewModel` that is actually populated with sample data, letting developers see the user view laid out with content.

### Role in the Codebase

It is one of three files in `UserManagement/Design/` that provide designer-only view models (alongside `DesignShowUsersViewModel` and `DesignAddUserViewModel`). The class is never used at runtime — the only reference to it is in `WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml`:

```xml
d:DataContext="{d:DesignInstance Type=design:DesignUserViewModel, IsDesignTimeCreatable=True}"
```

The `d:` namespace means this `DesignInstance` markup applies only inside the designer. Removing this file (and its two siblings) would not change runtime behaviour at all; the designer would simply show the user view empty, with no child view models or demo data.

### Relationships

- **Base type:** `UserViewModel` (in `UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`), which extends `MainViewModelBase` and implements `IUserViewModel`. It exposes the two child view model properties `AddUserViewModel` (`IAddUserViewModel`) and `ShowUsersViewModel` (`IShowUsersViewModel`), marked `[Import]` for MEF composition. `DesignUserViewModel` inherits these and does not override or add anything of its own beyond the constructor.
- **Constructs:** `DesignShowUsersViewModel` and `DesignAddUserViewModel`, both in the same `UserManagement/Design/` namespace. The former seeds its `Users` collection with three fake `UserModel` entries; the latter sets `FirstName`/`LastName` to "Sample User".
- **Consumed by:** the XAML designer via `UserView.xaml`; no production code path references it.

### Behavior & Details

The entire behaviour is the constructor, which assigns the two child view model properties that `UserViewModel` leaves as `null!` until MEF fills them:

```csharp
ShowUsersViewModel = new DesignShowUsersViewModel();
AddUserViewModel = new DesignAddUserViewModel();
```

Because the designer cannot run composition, these direct instantiations substitute for the `[Import]` wiring. No commands, bindings, or logic are redefined here — at design time the view shows the designer's demo data through these children.

Note that this class does not itself carry MEF exports; unlike `UserViewModel`, it is not `[Export]`-ed, consistent with its designer-only role.

### Purpose

`UserManagement/Design/DesignShowUsersViewModel.cs` defines `DesignShowUsersViewModel`, a design-time-only subclass of `ShowUsersViewModel` whose sole job is to give the XAML editor fake data. When a designer (Visual Studio, Blend) opens `UserView.xaml`, the designer instantiates this class instead of the real ViewModel, and it seeds the user list with three hard-coded demo users so the "Current Users" `ListView` renders with sample rows rather than appearing empty.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is never used by the running application. The production code path composes `ShowUsersViewModel` via MEF (`[Export(typeof(IShowUsersViewModel))]` in `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`) and loads real data from `IUserService`. The design class exists purely to make the view previewable in the XAML Designer. Removing it would not affect the application at runtime — the XAML would simply show no users in the designer preview.

### Relationships

- **`ShowUsersViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`) — the parent class, an MEF-exported MVVM ViewModel that exposes `Users`, an `ObservableCollection<UserModel>`, and a `LoadedCommand` that fetches active users from `IUserService`. The design subclass inherits all of this, including the constructor's `UserChangedMessage` messenger registration, and reuses the inherited `Users` collection.
- **`UserModel`** (`UserManagement/Model/UserModel.cs`) — a simple `ObservableObject` with `FirstName`/`LastName` properties; the demo rows are built from it.
- **`DesignUserViewModel`** (`UserManagement/Design/DesignUserViewModel.cs`) — the sibling design-time class that composes this one: its constructor assigns `ShowUsersViewModel = new DesignShowUsersViewModel()`, alongside `DesignAddUserViewModel`.
- **`UserView.xaml`** (`WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml`) — the consumer. Its `d:DataContext` uses `d:DesignInstance Type=design:DesignUserViewModel, IsDesignTimeCreatable=True`, so the designer instantiates `DesignUserViewModel` (and therefore this class) only at design time. Because `IsDesignTimeCreatable` is set, the constructor runs in the designer.

### Behavior & Details

The entire logic is the parameterless constructor: it adds three fixed `UserModel` entries — Jane Doe, John Smith, and Alice Johnson — to the inherited `Users` collection. No other members are defined.

One behavioral note: the inherited `ShowUsersViewModel` constructor registers a `UserChangedMessage` handler on `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default`. Since the design-time instance runs the real constructor, that registration happens in the designer as well — harmless in practice (the designer will not raise those messages), but worth knowing if you ever reason about messenger subscribers. The inherited `LoadedCommand` is also present on the design instance; the XAML only invokes it via an `EventTrigger` on `Loaded`, which does not fire in the designer, so the real `IUserService` lookup (whose `[Import]` would be unpopulated) is never triggered at design time.

Because the designer cannot run composition, these direct instantiations substitute for the `[Import]` wiring. No commands, bindings, or logic are redefined here — at design time the view shows the designer's demo data through these children.

Note that this class does not itself carry MEF exports; unlike `UserViewModel`, it is not `[Export]`-ed, consistent with its designer-only role.

### Purpose

`UserManagement/Design/DesignShowUsersViewModel.cs` defines `DesignShowUsersViewModel`, a design-time-only subclass of `ShowUsersViewModel` whose sole job is to give the XAML editor fake data. When a designer (Visual Studio, Blend) opens `UserView.xaml`, the designer instantiates this class instead of the real ViewModel, and it seeds the user list with three hard-coded demo users so the "Current Users" `ListView` renders with sample rows rather than appearing empty.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is never used by the running application. The production code path composes `ShowUsersViewModel` via MEF (`[Export(typeof(IShowUsersViewModel))]` in `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`) and loads real data from `IUserService`. The design class exists purely to make the view previewable in the XAML Designer. Removing it would not affect the application at runtime — the XAML would simply show no users in the designer preview.

### Relationships

- **`ShowUsersViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`) — the parent class, an MEF-exported MVVM ViewModel that exposes `Users`, an `ObservableCollection<UserModel>`, and a `LoadedCommand` that fetches active users from `IUserService`. The design subclass inherits all of this, including the constructor's `UserChangedMessage` messenger registration, and reuses the inherited `Users` collection.
- **`UserModel`** (`UserManagement/Model/UserModel.cs`) — a simple `ObservableObject` with `FirstName`/`LastName` properties; the demo rows are built from it.
- **`DesignUserViewModel`** (`UserManagement/Design/DesignUserViewModel.cs`) — the sibling design-time class that composes this one: its constructor assigns `ShowUsersViewModel = new DesignShowUsersViewModel()`, alongside `DesignAddUserViewModel`.
- **`UserView.xaml`** (`WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml`) — the consumer. Its `d:DataContext` uses `d:DesignInstance Type=design:DesignUserViewModel, IsDesignTimeCreatable=True`, so the designer instantiates `DesignUserViewModel` (and therefore this class) only at design time. Because `IsDesignTimeCreatable` is set, the constructor runs in the designer.

### Behavior & Details

The entire logic is the parameterless constructor: it adds three fixed `UserModel` entries — Jane Doe, John Smith, and Alice Johnson — to the inherited `Users` collection. No other members are defined.

One behavioral note: the inherited `ShowUsersViewModel` constructor registers a `UserChangedMessage` handler on `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default`. Since the design-time instance runs the real constructor, that registration happens in the designer as well — harmless in practice (the designer will not raise those messages), but worth knowing if you ever reason about messenger subscribers. The inherited `LoadedCommand` is also present on the design instance; the XAML only invokes it via an `EventTrigger` on `Loaded`, which does not fire in the designer, so the real `IUserService` lookup (whose `[Import]` would be unpopulated) is never triggered at design time.

### Purpose

The `UserManagement/Design` directory contains view model subclasses that exist solely to support the WPF XAML designer. Because the designer cannot execute the application’s MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework) composition, it cannot populate the child view models of the main `UserViewModel` with real data. These classes provide hard-coded, sample data so that `UserView.xaml` renders with visible content in visual editors like Visual Studio or Blend, rather than appearing empty.

### Software Components

This directory contains three source code files, each acting as a "design-time" stub for a corresponding production view model located in `UserManagement/ViewModel/`. These are not runtime components; they are never instantiated by the running application.

*   **`DesignUserViewModel.cs`**: This is the root design-time model. It subclasses `UserViewModel` and overrides the constructor to manually instantiate its two child view models (`AddUserViewModel` and `ShowUsersViewModel`). In production, these children are injected via MEF; here, they are replaced with their design-time counterparts to ensure the view hierarchy is fully populated in the designer.
*   **`DesignAddUserViewModel.cs`**: This subclasses `AddUserViewModel`. Its only role is to pre-fill the `FirstName` and `LastName` properties with "Sample" and "User" so that the add-user form appears filled out in the designer preview.
*   **`DesignShowUsersViewModel.cs`**: This subclasses `ShowUsersViewModel`. Its constructor seeds the `Users` collection with three hard-coded demo users (Jane Doe, John Smith, Alice Johnson) so that the user list renders with sample rows.

### Relationships

The relationship between these components is strictly hierarchical and directional, mirroring the production view model tree but replacing MEF-injected dependencies with direct instantiations.

`UserView.xaml` references [DesignUserViewModel](UserManagement/Design/DesignUserViewModel.md) via `d:DesignInstance`. When the designer loads the view, it constructs `DesignUserViewModel`. This class then constructs [DesignShowUsersViewModel](UserManagement/Design/DesignShowUsersViewModel.md) and [DesignAddUserViewModel](UserManagement/Design/DesignAddUserViewModel.md).

Crucially, these design classes inherit from their production counterparts in `UserManagement/ViewModel/`. They do not redefine commands or bindings; they rely entirely on the base class behavior. The only difference is the constructor logic that injects fake data. Because they inherit from the production classes, they also inherit side effects like messenger subscriptions, though these are harmless in the designer context as no messages are dispatched.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    XAML["UserView.xaml"] -->|d:DesignInstance| DUV["DesignUserViewModel"]
    
    subgraph "UserManagement/Design"
        DUV -->|constructs| DSUV["DesignShowUsersViewModel"]
        DUV -->|constructs| DAVM["DesignAddUserViewModel"]
    end

    subgraph "UserManagement/ViewModel (Production Base)"
        UV["UserViewModel"] 
        SSV["ShowUsersViewModel"]
        AUV["AddUserViewModel"]
    end

    DUV -.->|inherits from| UV
    DSUV -.->|inherits from| SSV
    DAVM -.->|inherits from| AUV

    classDef design fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
    classDef prod fill:#ff9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
    class DUV,DSUV,DAVM design
    class UV,SSV,AUV prod
```

The design-time classes execute the real constructors of their base classes. This means that side effects present in the production constructors (such as registering message handlers in `ShowUsersViewModel`) are also triggered in the designer. While currently harmless because the designer does not dispatch these messages, this creates a coupling where changes to the production constructor's side effects could inadvertently affect the design-time behavior or cause unexpected interactions if the designer environment were ever to simulate message sending.
