# `UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangeType.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `UserChangeType`, the enum that classifies *what happened* to a user whenever one is changed. It exists so that the messaging layer can carry the kind of change (`Added`, `Updated`, `Deleted`) alongside the affected `UserModel` in a single message, letting recipients react differently to each kind.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a small shared vocabulary type for the `UserManagement/Messaging` namespace, whose other member is `UserChangedMessage`. The enum is the discriminating field of that message: `UserChangedMessage` wraps a `UserChangeType` plus a `UserModel`, and recipients branch on it. Remove it and `UserChangedMessage` cannot express which of the three operations occurred.

### Relationships

- **Defined alongside:** `UserChangedMessage` (`UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.cs`) — takes a `UserChangeType` in its constructor, exposes it as its `UserChangeType` property, and its convenience constructor defaults a new user to `UserChangeType.Added`.
- **Producer:** `AddUserViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`) sends `new UserChangedMessage(UserChangeType.Added, userModel)` through `WeakReferenceMessenger` after a successful save.
- **Consumer:** `ShowUsersViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`) registers a handler for `UserChangedMessage` and switches on `message.UserChangeType`, adding to its `Users` collection on `Added`.

### Behavior & Details

Three members, all implicitly valued:

- `Added` — a user was created.
- `Updated` — an existing user changed.
- `Deleted` — a user was removed.

Because it is a plain enum, `exhaustive` handling is up to the receiver. Note that `ShowUsersViewModel`'s handler currently only implements `Added`; the `Updated` and `Deleted` cases throw `NotImplementedException`, so a recipient registered for all message kinds will crash on those two if they are ever sent. As of the code in this repository, only `Added` is actually sent, so the other two members are reserved for use that has not been implemented yet.

### Rough edges

`Updated` and `Deleted` exist as values, but the only registered consumer (`ShowUsersViewModel`) throws `NotImplementedException` for both, and no code currently sends either — so these members describe operations the messaging layer cannot yet handle end to end.

### Purpose

`UserChangedMessage` (`UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.cs`) is a message class that announces a change to a user — added, updated, or deleted — to other parts of the UserManagement module. It exists so that screens displaying user data can stay in sync with the user service without directly referencing it: a view model performs the change and sends a message; any view model that cares receives it through the CommunityToolkit `WeakReferenceMessenger`.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is the messaging contract of the `UserManagement/Messaging` folder, alongside its sibling `UserChangeType` enum (`UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangeType.cs`), which defines the three operations: `Added`, `Updated`, `Deleted`. It is a data model for events, not logic — its entire job is to carry a `UserModel` plus the kind of change that happened to it. Removing it would break both the sender (`AddUserViewModel`) and the receiver (`ShowUsersViewModel`), which both reference it directly.

### Relationships

- **Base type:** `ValueChangedMessage<UserModel>` from the external CommunityToolkit.Mvvm library. It supplies the `Value` property holding the `UserModel`, so `UserChangedMessage` only adds the change-type dimension.
- **`UserChangeType`** (same folder) — the enum naming the operation.
- **`UserModel`** (`UserManagement/Model/UserModel.cs`) — the payload, an `ObservableObject`-based model of a user.
- **Sender:** `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs` builds the message after creating a user:
  ```csharp
  WeakReferenceMessenger.Default.Send(new UserChangedMessage(UserChangeType.Added, userModel));
  ```
- **Receiver:** `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs` registers in its constructor and reacts by appending `message.Value` to its `Users` collection when the type is `Added`.

### Behavior & Details

- The primary primary-constructor takes the change type and the user. The convenience constructor that takes only a `UserModel` defaults to `UserChangeType.Added`. Any call site relying on "no type" therefore silently publishes an `Added` event — use the explicit constructor for anything else.
- `UserChangeType` is a read-only property (`{ get; }`) initialized once via the primary constructor; the message is immutable.
- `message.Value` (inherited from `ValueChangedMessage<UserModel>`) carries the user payload.

### Rough edges

`ShowUsersViewModel`'s handler throws `NotImplementedException` for `Updated` and `Deleted`, so only the `Added` path is actually handled today despite the enum advertising all three. Also, the single-argument constructor defaulting to `Added` can mask intent if a future sender forgets to pass the type.

### Purpose

The `UserManagement/Messaging` directory defines the event contract for user changes within the module. It contains two files that work together to allow view models to communicate user state changes (add, update, delete) to other parts of the application without direct dependencies.

These files belong together because they form the minimal data structure required for this communication: the message payload and the enum that classifies the type of change.

### Software Components

The directory consists of two tightly coupled components:

- **`UserChangedMessage`** ([UserChangedMessage.cs](UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.md)): This is the message class that travels through the system. It extends `ValueChangedMessage<UserModel>` from the CommunityToolkit.Mvvm library to carry a specific `UserModel` instance. It adds a `UserChangeType` property to specify what operation occurred. It provides two constructors: one that accepts both the type and the user, and a convenience constructor that defaults to `Added` if only a user is provided.
- **`UserChangeType`** ([UserChangeType.cs](UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangeType.md)): This enum defines the three possible operations: `Added`, `Updated`, and `Deleted`. It serves as the discriminator within the message, allowing recipients to determine how to handle the event.

### Relationships

The relationship between the two files is direct and mandatory. `UserChangedMessage` cannot exist or function without `UserChangeType`, as it uses the enum to define the nature of the event it carries.

External components interact with this directory as follows:
- **Senders**: `AddUserViewModel` creates an instance of `UserChangedMessage` with `UserChangeType.Added` and sends it via `WeakReferenceMessenger` after a successful user creation.
- **Receivers**: `ShowUsersViewModel` registers to listen for `UserChangedMessage`. It inspects the `UserChangeType` to decide how to update its UI. Currently, it only handles `Added` events, appending the new user to its collection. It throws a `NotImplementedException` for `Updated` and `Deleted` events.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "UserManagement/Messaging"
        M[UserChangedMessage]
        T[UserChangeType]
    end

    subgraph "External ViewModels"
        Sender[AddUserViewModel]
        Receiver[ShowUsersViewModel]
    end

    Sender -->|Creates and Sends| M
    Receiver -->|Registers and Handles| M
    M -->|Contains| T
```

### Rough edges

The `UserChangeType` enum defines `Updated` and `Deleted` states, but the current implementation does not support them end-to-end. `ShowUsersViewModel` explicitly throws an exception for these types, and no code currently sends them, meaning these enum values are effectively unused placeholders.

- [UserChangedMessage.cs](UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.md)

# UserManagement/Model/UserModel.cs

### Purpose

`UserModel` is the view-side representation of a user: a tiny MVVM model holding just a `FirstName` and a `LastName`, shaped for data binding in the UserManagement module. It exists so the UI layer can display and pass around user display data without touching the persistence layer's types (like `UserDto` or the Hibernate entities). The `[ObservableProperty]` attributes from CommunityToolkit.Mvvm make each field into an auto-generated public property that raises `PropertyChanged`, so bound controls refresh when a value changes.

### Role in the Codebase

This is the only file in `UserManagement/Model/`, making it the module's sole data model. It is a display object, not an entity — the UserManagement project has no storage logic of its own, so this class carries no validation or persistence concerns. Removing it would break the view model, messaging, and WinForms view layers described below, since they all hold and render `UserModel` instances.

### Relationships

- **Base class:** `ObservableObject` from the external `CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.ComponentModel` package (the package is referenced in the `Mvvm` project, and this class is marked `partial` because the toolkit's source generator fills in the rest).
- **`UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`** — keeps an `ObservableCollection<UserModel>` of displayed users. It creates the instances by mapping `User` objects from `UserService.GetActiveUsers()` into `new UserModel { FirstName = ..., LastName = ... }`, and appends to it when it receives a `UserChangedMessage` of type `Added`.
- **`UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`** — after saving a new user via `UserService.AddUser`, it constructs a `UserModel` from the form fields and sends it out as `UserChangedMessage(UserChangeType.Added, userModel)` so `ShowUsersViewModel` picks it up.
- **`UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.cs`** — wraps a `UserModel` (it extends `ValueChangedMessage<UserModel>`), so messages about user changes always carry a `UserModel`.
- **`UserManagement/Design/DesignShowUsersViewModel.cs`** — creates hardcoded `UserModel` instances to give the XAML designer demo data.
- **`WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.cs`** — binds the user list box to `ShowUsersViewModel.Users` and formats each `UserModel` as `"{FirstName} {LastName}"` in its `lstUsers.Format` handler.

### Behavior & Details

Two private fields, `_firstName` and `_lastName`, both defaulting to `string.Empty`. The `[ObservableProperty]` source generator turns each into a public `string` property named `FirstName` / `LastName` and emits the property-change notifications — that generated code is what every consumer actually accesses, including object-initializer syntax like `new UserModel { FirstName = "Jane", LastName = "Doe" }`.

There is no other logic: no validation, no `Equals`/`GetHashCode` overrides, and the two fields do not reference each other. Instances are short-lived display objects — typically constructed fresh per user by `ShowUsersViewModel` or `AddUserViewModel` rather than shared long-term.

### Rough edges

The model is a flat copy of data with no identity (no `Id` property), so nothing in the UI can distinguish two users by anything but name. This is directly implicated by `ShowUsersViewModel`, where the `Updated` and `Deleted` cases of its message handler are `NotImplementedException` — without an identifier there is no natural way to locate the row to update or remove once those message types are actually sent.

### Purpose

`UserManagement/Model` defines the view-model data structures for the UserManagement module. It contains the [UserModel](UserManagement/Model/UserModel.md) class, which serves as the primary data binding object for the UI layer. By separating display logic from persistence entities like `UserDto`, it ensures the UI remains decoupled from the backend storage details.

### Software Components

The directory holds a single source file, `UserModel.cs`. This file defines the [UserModel](UserManagement/Model/UserModel.md) class, which extends `ObservableObject` from CommunityToolkit.Mvvm. **File:** `UserManagement/ViewModel/IAddUserViewModel.cs`

### Purpose

`IAddUserViewModel` is the contract for the "add a new user" screen in the User Management module. It tells the rest of the application (and the WPF designer) what the add-user view model exposes: the editable user fields, the command that saves, and the services it needs to save correctly. It exists so callers can depend on the view model by interface and so the concrete view model is unit-testable and designer-friendly.

### Role in the Codebase

This is the interface half of the add-user view model pair. The concrete implementation is `AddUserViewModel` in the same `ViewModel` directory, which is exported via MEF (`[Export(typeof(IAddUserViewModel))]`) and discovered through this interface. The sibling interfaces `IUserViewModel`, `IShowUsersViewModel` follow the same "interface + implementation" convention; `IAddUserViewModel` is the one that owns the create-user form. Remove it and `AddUserViewModel` has nothing to implement, and consumers that take the interface can no longer compile.

### Relationships

- **Extends two parents:**
  - `IUser` (defined in `Dto/IUser.cs`) — contributes `FirstName` and `LastName` as `string` properties. This makes the view model itself carry the user data being entered.
  - `INotifyDataErrorInfo` (from `System.ComponentModel`) — the WPF standard validation surface that lets the UI bind per-property validation errors.

- **Members and their implementation sites** (in `AddUserViewModel`):
  - `UserService` — an `IUserService` (defined in `BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`) injected via MEF. Used to persist the user.
  - `LoggingService` — an `ILoggingService` injected via MEF.
  - `SaveUserCommand` — an `IAsyncRelayCommand` (from `CommunityToolkit.Mvvm.Input`). The implementation generates this automatically from `SaveUserAsync()` by stripping the `Async` suffix.

### Purpose

It exists so that composition-root code and host views can depend on a stable interface rather than the concrete `UserViewModel` class. # `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`

### Purpose

`ShowUsersViewModel` is the ViewModel for the "show users" part of the user-management feature. It holds the list of users the UI displays (`Users`), fetches that list from the business layer on load, and keeps the list updated when other parts of the app add users via the `UserChangedMessage` messenger.

### Role in the Codebase

It lives in `UserManagement/ViewModel/` alongside the other feature ViewModels (`UserViewModel`, `AddUserViewModel`) and is the concrete implementation of `IShowUsersViewModel` (defined in `UserManagement/ViewModel/IShowUsersViewModel.cs`). It is exported from the MEF composition container via `[Export(typeof(IShowUsersViewModel))]`, which is how `UserViewModel`'s `[Import] public IShowUsersViewModel ShowUsersViewModel` property gets populated. `UserViewModel` in turn exports itself as the main view model (`IUserViewModel` / `IMainViewModel`), so this class is one of the child view models the shell views bind to:

- `WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml` binds a `ListView` to `ShowUsersViewModel.Users` and invokes `LoadedCommand` in a `DataTrigger`.
- `WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.cs` binds a `ListBox` through a `BindingSource` to `Users` and executes `LoadedCommand` on the form's `Load` event.
- `ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` calls `ShowUsersViewModel.OnLoadedAsync()` directly, then prints `Users`.
- `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` instantiates it and tests both `OnLoadedAsync` and the message handler.
- `UserManagement/Design/DesignShowUsersViewModel.cs` subclasses it to seed demo data for the XAML designer.

Removing it would break the user list in both WPF and WinForms shells, the console app, and the test project.

### Relationships

- **Base class:** `ViewModelBase` (in `Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs`), itself extending CommunityToolkit Mvvm's `ObservableObject` and implementing `IViewModel`. This class inherits the observable-property machinery and the child-view-model lifecycle helpers; it overrides none of them.
- **`[Import]` dependencies** (injected by MEF at composition time):
  - `IUserService` (`BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`) — used for `GetActiveUsers()`, which returns `Task<List<UserDto>>`.
  - `ILoggingService` (`Logging`) — imported but currently never used in this class.
- **`UserModel`** (`UserManagement/Model/UserModel.cs`) — the observable view-model item with `FirstName`/`LastName` properties, stored in `Users`.
- **`UserChangedMessage`** (`UserManagement/Messaging/UserChangedMessage.cs`) — a `ValueChangedMessage<UserModel>` carrying a `UserChangeType`. Sent by `AddUserViewModel` (line 66 of that file) after a successful add.
- **`UserDto`** (`Dto`) — the business-layer user returned by `IUserService`; only `FirstName` and `LastName` are copied into `UserModel`.

### Behavior & Details

- **`Users`** — a read-only `ObservableCollection<UserModel>`, initialized inline. The only mutation paths are `OnLoadedAsync` (initial population) and the messenger handler (appending new users).
- **Constructor** — registers `this` as a recipient of `UserChangedMessage` on `WeakReferenceMessenger.Default` (registration is weakly referenced, so the VM must stay alive externally for messages to arrive — composition keeps it alive). The switch on `message.UserChangeType` currently handles only `Added` (appends `message.Value` to `Users`); `Updated` and `Deleted` throw `NotImplementedException`, so sending either would crash the recipient.
- **`OnLoadedAsync`** — marked `[RelayCommand]`, so the source generator produces `LoadedCommand` (an `IAsyncRelayCommand`) that the WPF view triggers on load and `UserForm` executes on the form's `Load`. It calls `await UserService.GetActiveUsers()` and adds one `UserModel` per returned `UserDto`, mapping only first and last name. It appends to the existing collection rather than clearing it first, so running the load twice duplicates entries. Errors from the service propagate to the caller of the command (e.g., the console app or the test).

### Rough edges

- The `LoggingService` import is declared but never used.
- `OnLoadedAsync` appends without clearing `Users`, so re-running the load command duplicates the whole list; only the initial load is expected by the current callers.
- The `Updated` and `Deleted` branches of the message handler throw `NotImplementedException`; nothing else in the codebase sends those types today, but it means the "list of users" cannot stay in sync with updates or deletions yet.

### Purpose

`IShowUsersViewModel` is the contract for the view model that displays the list of active users in the UserManagement module. It exists so that the parent view model (`IUserViewModel`) can hold a reference to the "show users" pane through an abstraction rather than the concrete `ShowUsersViewModel` class — the concrete class is resolved at runtime via MEF composition.

### Role in the Codebase

This file is part of the `UserManagement/ViewModel` folder, where each view model follows the pair pattern: an interface in its own file, and a concrete class that implements it and is exported with `[Export(typeof(...))]`. `IUserViewModel` declares a `ShowUsersViewModel` property of this interface type, so the main user-management view model composes the sub-views by their interfaces and MEF hands back the concrete implementations. If this interface were removed, `IUserViewModel` and `UserViewModel` would lose the type they use to hold the show-users pane.

### Relationships

- **Implemented by** `ShowUsersViewModel` (same folder), which additionally inherits from `ViewModelBase` and is tagged `[Export(typeof(IShowUsersViewModel))]`, so it is this interface's only implementation in the codebase.
- **Consumed by** `IUserViewModel` and `UserViewModel` in the same folder, which expose a `ShowUsersViewModel` property typed as `IShowUsersViewModel`.
- **Depends on** types from other layers it re-exposes:
  - `UserModel` (`UserManagement/Model`) — the display model for a single user, with observable `FirstName`/`LastName` properties.
  - `IUserService` (`BusinessLayer`) — the service that fetches and manages users; the implementation marks its `UserService` property with `[Import]`.
  - `ILoggingService` (`Logging`) — logging, likewise injected via `[Import]` in the implementation.
  - `IAsyncRelayCommand` (CommunityToolkit.Mvvm) — the standard MVVM command type for async handlers.

### Behavior & Details

The interface has no logic; its shape defines what a consumer may rely on:

- `Users` — a read-only `ObservableCollection<UserModel>` bound to the user list in the UI. The implementation populates it when the view loads and appends to it when a `UserChangedMessage` of type `Added` arrives via the `WeakReferenceMessenger`.
- `UserService` and `LoggingService` — get/set properties whose setters exist only because MEF injects the imports into the implementation; consumers should treat them as read-only dependencies.
- `LoadedCommand` — an `IAsyncRelayCommand` generated by the `[RelayCommand]` attribute on the implementation's `OnLoadedAsync`. A view binds to it (typically on a `Loaded` event) to trigger the initial fetch.
- `OnLoadedAsync` — the public async method behind that command. In the implementation it awaits `UserService.GetActiveUsers()` and adds each result to `Users` as a new `UserModel` with `FirstName` and `LastName` copied from the returned `UserDto`. Note that the interface exposes the raw method in addition to the generated command, so callers can invoke it directly without going through the command.

Rough edges: the implementation only handles the `Added` case of `UserChangedMessage`; `Updated` and `Deleted` both throw `NotImplementedException`, so the `Users` collection will grow stale in those scenarios until implemented.

- The `LoggingService` import is declared but never used.
- `OnLoadedAsync` appends without clearing `Users`, so re-running the load command duplicates the whole list; only the initial load is expected by the current callers.

### Purpose

`IShowUsersViewModel` is the contract for the view model that displays the list of active users in the UserManagement module. It exists so that the parent view model (`IUserViewModel`) can hold a reference to the "show users" pane through an abstraction rather than the concrete `ShowUsersViewModel` class — the concrete class is resolved at runtime via MEF composition.

### Role in the Codebase

This file is part of the `UserManagement/ViewModel` folder, where each view model follows the pair pattern: an interface in its own file, and a concrete class that implements it and is exported with `[Export(typeof(...))]`. `IUserViewModel` declares a `ShowUsersViewModel` property of this interface type, so the main user-management view model composes the sub-views by their interfaces and MEF hands back the concrete implementations. If this interface were removed, `IUserViewModel` and `UserViewModel` would lose the type they use to hold the show-users pane.

### Relationships

- **Implemented by** `ShowUsersViewModel` (same folder), which additionally inherits from `ViewModelBase` and is tagged `[Export(typeof(IShowUsersViewModel))]`, so it is this interface's only implementation in the codebase.
- **Consumed by** `IUserViewModel` and `UserViewModel` in the same folder, which expose a `ShowUsersViewModel` property typed as `IShowUsersViewModel`.
- **Depends on** types from other layers it re-exposes:
  - `UserModel` (`UserManagement/Model`) — the display model for a single user, with observable `FirstName`/`LastName` properties.
  - `IUserService` (`BusinessLayer`) — the service that fetches and manages users; the implementation marks its `UserService` property with `[Import]`.
  - `ILoggingService` (`Logging`) — logging, likewise injected via `[Import]` in the implementation.
  - `IAsyncRelayCommand` (CommunityToolkit.Mvvm) — the standard MVVM command type for async handlers.

### Behavior & Details

The interface has no logic; its shape defines what a consumer may rely on:

- `Users` — a read-only `ObservableCollection<UserModel>` bound to the user list in the UI. The implementation populates it when the view loads and appends to it when a `UserChangedMessage` of type `Added` arrives via the `WeakReferenceMessenger`.
- `UserService` and `LoggingService` — get/set properties whose setters exist only because MEF injects the imports into the implementation; consumers should treat them as read-only dependencies.
- `LoadedCommand` — an `IAsyncRelayCommand` generated by the `[RelayCommand]` attribute on the implementation's `OnLoadedAsync`. A view binds to it (typically on a `Loaded` event) to trigger the initial fetch.

Note that the interface exposes the raw method in addition to the generated command, so callers can invoke it directly without going through the command.

Rough edges: the implementation only handles the `Added` case of `UserChangedMessage`; `Updated` and `Deleted` both throw `NotImplementedException`, so the `Users` collection will grow stale in those scenarios until implemented.
children.summary:
### Purpose

The `UserManagement/ViewModel` directory contains the MVVM layer for the user management feature. It defines the view models that manage state and logic for adding users and displaying the user list, as well as the top-level shell that composes them.

The files belong together because they implement a strict "interface + implementation" pattern for each logical view. Each concrete view model is exported to the MEF composition container via interfaces defined in the same folder. This allows the application hosts (WPF, WinForms, Console) to bind to stable contracts rather than concrete classes, while enabling MEF to inject dependencies like `IUserService` automatically.

### Software Components

The directory is divided into three functional pairs, plus a top-level aggregate:

*   **The Add User View**: Composed of [IAddUserViewModel.cs](UserManagement/ViewModel/IAddUserViewModel.md) and its implementation [AddUserViewModel.cs](UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.md). This component handles the form state for creating a new user. It extends `IUser` to directly expose `FirstName` and `LastName` properties, handles validation via `INotifyDataErrorInfo`, and executes the save logic through `SaveUserAsync`.
*   **The Show Users View**: Composed of [IShowUsersViewModel.cs](UserManagement/ViewModel/IShowUsersViewModel.md) and [ShowUsersViewModel.cs](UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.md). This component maintains the `ObservableCollection` of users displayed in the UI. It fetches data from the business layer on load and listens for `UserChangedMessage` events to update the list reactively when a new user is added.
*   **The Root Shell**: Composed of [IUserViewModel.cs](UserManagement/ViewModel/IUserViewModel.md) and [UserViewModel.cs](UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.md). This is the composition root for the feature. It exposes the two child view models above as read-only properties. It does not contain feature logic itself but acts as the single entry point for the application hosts, inheriting from `MainViewModelBase` to provide standard window lifecycle handling.

### Relationships

The components are linked through MEF composition attributes (`[Export]` and `[Import]`) and dependency injection. `UserViewModel` imports the interfaces `IAddUserViewModel` and `IShowUsersViewModel`. At runtime, the MEF container resolves these to the concrete `AddUserViewModel` and `ShowUsersViewModel` classes in the same folder.

Communication between the sibling view models occurs via `WeakReferenceMessenger`. When `AddUserViewModel` successfully saves a user, it broadcasts a `UserChangedMessage`. `ShowUsersViewModel` registers as a recipient for this message and appends the new user to its list, ensuring the UI stays in sync without direct references between the two classes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "UserManagement/ViewModel"
        UV[UserViewModel]
        IUV[IUserViewModel]
        AUV[AddUserViewModel]
        IAU[ IAddUserViewModel]
        SUV[ShowUsersViewModel]
        ISU[IShowUsersViewModel]
    end
    
    UV -.->|implements| IUV
    UV -->|imports| IAU
    UV -->|imports| ISU
    
    AUV -.->|implements| IAU
    SUV -.->|implements| ISU
    
    AUV -->|sends UserChangedMessage| SUV
```

### Rough edges

`ShowUsersViewModel` registers for `UserChangedMessage` but only handles the `Added` event type. Handlers for `Updated` and `Deleted` currently throw `NotImplementedException`, meaning the user list will not reflect changes or removals if those message types are ever sent. Additionally, the `OnLoadedAsync` method in `ShowUsersViewModel` appends to the `Users` collection without clearing it first, which would result in duplicate entries if the load command is executed multiple times.

# App.config

**Path:** `WinFormsApp1/App.config`

### Purpose

This is the .NET application configuration file for the WinForms client. Its one job is to supply the SQL Server connection string that the data-access layer uses to reach the `Users` database.

### Role in the Codebase

`App.config` is the runtime configuration file for the `WinFormsApp1` project. At build time it is transformed into `WinFormsApp1.exe.config` and read at startup by the .NET configuration system. It holds a single `<appSettings>` entry, `ConnectionString`, whose value is:

```
Server=localhost;Database=Users;Integrated Security=True;TrustServerCertificate=True;
```

This points at a local SQL Server instance (`localhost`), targets the `Users` database, authenticates via Windows credentials (`Integrated Security=True`), and disables server-certificate validation (`TrustServerCertificate=True`) — typical for a local development setup.

If the file or the key were removed, the application would fail to start: the consumer reads the setting with a non-null-asserted call (see below), so a missing key throws rather than degrading gracefully.

### Relationships

The value is consumed by `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs`, which does:

```csharp
public class ModelContext()
    : ModelContextBase(ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]!, ["Entity.Hibernate"]);
```

`ModelContext` passes the string to `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/ModelContextBase.cs`, which stores it as the `ConnectionString` property. From there it flows to `RepositoryFactory` and `SessionFactoryBuilder` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`, where it is used to build the NHibernate session factory. The WinForms `Program.cs` pulls `ModelContext` in via MEF (`[Export(typeof(IModelContext))]`), so this config file is the root of the whole data-access chain for this client.

Note the same connection-string value is duplicated verbatim in `ConsoleApp1/App.config` and `WpfApp1/App.config` — the three front-end projects in this solution each carry their own copy, so changing the database target requires editing each one.

### Behavior & Details

- The file contains only one `appSettings` key; there are no connectionStrings sections, binding redirects, or custom sections.
- Because `ModelContext` uses `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]!` with a null-forgiving operator, the application assumes the key always exists. There is no fallback value anywhere — removing or mistyping the key produces a `NullReferenceException` at startup when the `ModelContext` singleton is first created.

### Rough edges

- The connection string is hardcoded to `localhost` in three separate `App.config` files (WinForms, WPF, Console). Any environment change (different server, credentials, database name) must be made in every copy, and they have already drifted as a pattern risk rather than currently.

# WinFormsApp1.csproj

**Path:** `WinFormsApp1/WinFormsApp1.csproj`

### Purpose

This is the MSBuild project file for `WinFormsApp1`, the WinForms desktop host application in the solution. It declares the project as a Windows executable targeting `net10.0-windows` with Windows Forms and nullable reference types enabled, and wires it up to the three projects that supply its runtime behaviour. It contains no application logic itself.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the build definition for the application's entry point. The sibling source file `Program.cs` is what this project compiles: `Main()` uses `CompositionHelper.CreateCompositionContainer()` from `Common` to build an MEF composition container, then discovers all exported `IModuleController` instances, calls `Initialize()` on each followed by `Run()`, and returns `ExitCodes.Ok` (or `ExitCodes.Error` if no module is found). The `OutputType` of `WinExe` is what turns that code into a windowed desktop executable rather than a library.

Without this file, the `WinFormsApp1` namespace and its `Program` class cannot be built, and the application has no host for its modules.

### Relationships

The three project references determine what lands in the output directory, and the directory matters: `CompositionHelper.CreateCompositionContainer()` (in `Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs`) scans the directory containing the executing assembly and loads every assembly it finds there as an MEF catalog. So the referenced assemblies are not just compile-time dependencies — the runtime discovery of modules depends on them being copied to the output folder.

- `..\Common\Common.csproj` — provides `CompositionHelper`, `ExitCodes`, and the composition infrastructure `Program.cs` uses.
- `..\Mvvm.Winforms\Mvvm.Winforms.csproj` — the WinForms flavour of the MVVM layer (it itself references `..\Mvvm\Mvvm.csproj`).
- `..\UserManagement\UserManagement.csproj` — a feature module; it pulls in `BusinessLayer`, `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`, and `Logging` transitively, which is how data access and logging end up in the WinForms app's deployment.

### Behavior & Details

- `OutputType` is `WinExe`, producing a Windows GUI executable with no console window.
- `TargetFramework` is `net10.0-windows`, matching the other projects in the solution, so the whole tree builds with the same runtime.
- `UseWindowsForms`, `Nullable`, and `ImplicitUsings` are all enabled here; the `System.ComponentModel.Composition` package used by `Program.cs` is not referenced directly in this project but comes transitively via `Common` and `UserManagement`.
- There are no explicit package references or other item groups; everything the app needs at build time flows through the three project references.

# WinFormsApp1/Program.cs

This is a source file defining a single logical unit: the `Program` class, the application's entry point.

### Purpose

`Program` is the bootstrap for the WinForms host of this solution. It exists to do one job: build a MEF (`System.ComponentModel.Composition`) container, pull out every exported `IModuleController`, start them up, and let them drive the UI. All actual application behaviour lives in the module controllers (such as `WinFormsApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs`); this class only orchestrates their lifecycle and defines what happens when the process is starting up or a crash is occurring.

It also pins the whole assembly to Windows via the `[assembly: SupportedOSPlatform("windows")]` attribute, since the host is WinForms-based.

### Role in the Codebase

This is the executable's entry point (`static int Main`) for the `WinFormsApp1` project. Nothing in the project runs without it: the WinForms window never opens unless `Program.Main` composes the container and calls `Run()` on the module controllers.

The repository contains parallel hosts — the solution also has `WpfApp1` and `ConsoleApp1` directories — which use the same module mechanism through their own entry points. This file is the WinForms half of that pattern: same container building, same two-phase module startup, but `Run()` ends in `Application.Run(...)` of a WinForms view instead of a WPF or console loop.

If this file were removed, the `WinFormsApp1` project would have no entry point and could not build as an executable.

### Relationships

- `Common.Composition.CompositionHelper` (`Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs`) — creates the `CompositionContainer`. `Program` calls the parameterless `CreateCompositionContainer()`, which builds an aggregate catalog from all assembly files next to the `Common` assembly (plus the entry assembly) and composes it. The WinForms host therefore relies on the host's `bin` folder containing the assemblies that export views, view models, and module controllers.
- `Mvvm.IModuleController` (`Mvvm/IModuleController.cs`) — the module lifecycle contract: `Initialize()`, `Run()`, `Shutdown()`. The only implementation in this project is `WinFormsApp1.Controller.DefaultModuleController`, exported with `[Export(typeof(IModuleController))]`; it is constructed by MEF with the imported `IMainView<DialogResult, int>` and `IMainViewModel`.
- `Common.ExitCodes` (`Common/ExitCodes.cs`) — supplies the process exit values: `Ok` (`0`) and `Error` (`-1`).
- Standard WinForms/COM+ infrastructure: `ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize()`, `[STAThread]`, `Application.Run` (inside the module controller), `MessageBox`, and the .NET MEF API from `System.ComponentModel.Composition`.

### Behavior & Details

The `Main` flow, in order:

1. `ApplicationConfiguration.Initialize()` applies WinForms app defaults (DPI awareness etc.).
2. `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException` is subscribed to. Despite the adjacent comment claiming exceptions should not be handled in Debug mode, the handler is wired unconditionally — it runs in Debug builds too.
3. The container is created via `CompositionHelper.CreateCompositionContainer()` and kept in the static `_container`.
4. `GetExportedValues<IModuleController>()` is called inside a try/catch. Only `ReflectionTypeLoadException` is caught: in that case each `LoaderExceptions` message is written to the console and the process exits with `ExitCodes.Error` (`-1`). Any other exception (e.g. `CompositionException` from unsatisfied imports) propagates and terminates the process with an unhandled exception.
5. If zero modules were exported, a "No module found." error dialog is shown and the process exits with `ExitCodes.Error`.
6. Two-phase startup: `Initialize()` is called on every module first, then `Run()` on every module. `DefaultModuleController.Initialize()` is empty, and its `Run()` calls `Application.Run((Form)MainView)` — so `Main` blocks in the message loop of the first running module.
7. When the message loop ends, `Main` returns `ExitCodes.Ok` (`0`).

Note that `Shutdown()` is defined by `IModuleController` but is never called by `Program`.

**Unhandled exception handling.** `AppDomainUnhandledException` casts `e.ExceptionObject` to `Exception` and calls `HandleException`, which does two things: logs the full exception via `Trace.TraceError`, and — only if the exception is *not* terminating — shows a modal error box with the German text "Es ist ein Fehler aufgetreten." (An error has occurred). For a terminating exception the process dies after the trace write; the message box is deliberately skipped because it would be useless. This handler only catches exceptions that escaped to the AppDomain level (e.g. from non-UI threads); exceptions thrown on the UI thread are handled by WinForms' own machinery, and a `CompositionException` thrown synchronously in `Main` simply becomes an unhandled startup crash.

### Rough edges

- The comment says exceptions should not be handled in Debug mode, but the `UnhandledException` subscription is not guarded by a Debug/Release check — the comment and the code disagree.
- `Shutdown()` is part of the `IModuleController` contract but `Program` never calls it, so modules are left with no clean shutdown path from the host.
- The unhandled-exception dialog is in German while the "No module found." dialog is in English; UI strings in this host are inconsistently localized.
- The nullable static `_moduleControllers` is only assigned inside the try block; if a `ReflectionTypeLoadException` is caught, the early return is fine, but the code has no defensive handling for `Main` being entered a second time (which the WinForms runtime doesn't do, but the statics give no protection).

# WinFormsApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs

### Purpose

This class is the WinForms application's entry-point controller. It wires together the main form and the main view model via MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework) and drives the application's lifetime: initializing, showing the form, and closing it. It exists so that `Program.Main` can treat the WinForms host as a swappable "module" behind the framework-defined `IModuleController` interface in `Mvvm`.

### Role in the Codebase

The WinForms project is one of several host projects in this repository (a sibling `WpfApp1` contains an analog with the same name). The framework in `Mvvm` (`IModuleController`, `IMainViewModel`, `IMainView<TDialogResult, TDimension>`) is host-agnostic, and each host contributes its own module controller.

`Program.cs` builds a `CompositionContainer`, pulls out every exported `IModuleController` (this class, via its `[Export(typeof(IModuleController))]`), calls `Initialize()` on each, then `Run()` on each. Without this class there would be no exported controller in the WinForms host, and `Main` would exit with the "No module found." error.

### Relationships

- `IModuleController` (defined in `Mvvm/IModuleController.cs`) — the interface this class implements. Its three methods define the application lifecycle: `Initialize()`, `Run()`, `Shutdown()`.
- `IMainView<DialogResult, int>` (defined in `Mvvm/IMainView.cs`) — the WinForms-specific main view interface. In this project, the concrete export is `UserForm` (`WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.cs`).
- `IMainViewModel` (defined in `Mvvm/IMainViewModel.cs`) — the main view model interface. The concrete export in the currently included projects is `UserViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`).
- `Program.cs` — the direct caller: it resolves this class from the composition container and invokes `Initialize()` and `Run()` in that order.

The constructor is marked `[ImportingConstructor]`, so MEF resolves `UserForm` and `UserViewModel` by their respective `[Export]` attributes and injects them.

### Behavior & Details

**Constructor.** Assigns the injected view and view model to the `protected` properties, then sets `MainView.DataContext = mainViewModel`. For `UserForm`, setting `DataContext` is the trigger that builds all of its WinForms `DataBindings` against the view model's sub-view models.

**`Initialize()`** — Declared `virtual` with an empty body. It exists as a hook for derived classes that need to do pre-UI setup (loading configuration, warming caches, etc.). The base implementation does nothing.

**`Run()`** — Calls `Application.Run((Form)MainView)`. This both shows the form and starts the WinForms message loop. It blocks until the form closes, at which point `Main` proceeds to its return. Note that the interface types `IMainView` and `IMainViewModel` both expose `CloseWindow`/`Close`/`Shutdown`, but none of those are invoked here — the lifetime is entirely driven by the user closing the form.

**`Shutdown()`** — Calls `MainView.Close()`. Notably, `Program.cs` never calls `Shutdown()` on any module controller. The form is closed implicitly when the user closes it (which unblocks `Application.Run`), and `Program` exits afterward. The method is therefore only relevant if a future caller of `IModuleController` (e.g. the `Mvvm.Wpf` host) actually drives the shutdown path.

**`virtual` and `protected`.** `Initialize`, `Run`, and `Shutdown` are all `virtual`, and `MainView`/`MainViewModel` are `protected`. This signals the class is designed as a base for module-specific controllers that need access to the main view/view model but want to override the lifecycle behavior. No subclass exists in the current WinForms project; the class is used as-is.

### Rough edges

- `Program.cs` never calls `Shutdown()`, so `Shutdown()` in this class is dead code in the WinForms host. It is only meaningful if some other caller of `IModuleController` invokes the full lifecycle (the `Mvvm.Wpf` host does call `Shutdown()` in reverse order, but that is a different host project).
- `Run()` casts `MainView` to `Form`. This is safe today because the only exported `IMainView<DialogResult, int>` is `UserForm : Form`, but the interface `IMainView<TDialogResult, TDimension>` does not guarantee the underlying type is a `Form`. A non-`Form` implementation would throw an `InvalidCastException` at runtime.
- `IMainViewModel` declares `Shutdown(int exitCode)` and `CloseWindow()`, but this controller never calls them; the view model's own shutdown contract is not exercised from this class.

children.summary:
### Purpose

This directory serves as the WinForms host adapter for the application. It contains the single controller that bridges the generic Mvvm framework with the specific WinForms user interface. Its sole responsibility is to manage the application lifecycle within this specific UI technology, allowing `Program.cs` to treat the WinForms host as a swappable module.

### Software Components

The directory contains one primary component:

*   **`DefaultModuleController.cs`**: This is the concrete implementation of the `IModuleController` interface. It is exported via MEF so that the application entry point can discover and instantiate it. This class acts as the glue between the abstract framework interfaces and the concrete WinForms types (`UserForm` and `UserViewModel`). It handles the initialization, execution, and theoretical shutdown of the WinForms application loop.

### Relationships

`DefaultModuleController` depends heavily on the `Mvvm` framework project. It implements `IModuleController`, which dictates the `Initialize`, `Run`, and `Shutdown` lifecycle methods. It receives `UserForm` and `UserViewModel` via constructor injection, relying on their `[Export]` attributes to satisfy the interface contracts defined in `Mvvm`.

The dependency direction is strictly one-way: `Program.cs` calls into this controller, which in turn calls into the View and ViewModel. The controller does not define the logic for the form or the data; it merely orchestrates their presentation and lifetime. Because this directory contains only one file with no internal sub-components, the "relationship" is primarily external: this file is the isolated point of contact between the generic `Program` entry point and the specific WinForms implementation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "WinFormsApp1/Controller"
        DMC[DefaultModuleController]
    end
    
    subgraph "Mvvm Framework"
        IMC[IModuleController]
    end
    
    subgraph "External Dependencies"
        UserForm[UserForm]
        UserViewModel[UserViewModel]
        Program[Program.cs]
    end
    
    DMC -.->|implements| IMC
    DMC -->|injects/references| UserForm
    DMC -->|injects/references| UserViewModel
    Program -->|calls| DMC
```

### Rough edges

*   `DefaultModuleController` contains a `Shutdown()` method that is never called by `Program.cs`, making it dead code in this specific host context.
*   The `Run()` method performs a hard cast of `MainView` to `Form`, which assumes the concrete implementation is always a WinForms `Form` and will throw an exception if the injected view does not inherit from it.

### Purpose

`UserForm.resx` (`WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.resx`) is the resource file paired with the `UserForm` designer-generated code. It is an `.resx` XML file, not a source file — it holds the declarative, designer-managed state for the form's controls, and the designer tooling generates and rewrites it; it should not be edited by hand.

### Role in the codebase

It sits alongside `UserForm.cs` and `UserForm.Designer.cs` in `WinFormsApp1/View`. The `.Designer.cs` file (the "partial" half of `UserForm`) calls `InitializeComponent()`, which loads this resource at design and compile time to reconstruct control metadata such as `ToolTips`, `ErrorProvider` layout, and other designer-serialised properties. Removing it would break `InitializeComponent()` regeneration and the designer's ability to round-trip the form.

### Relationships

- Consumed by `UserForm.Designer.cs`, which calls `InitializeComponent()`; that method reads this file's entries (e.g. the `errorProvider.TrayLocation` metadata) to reconstruct the form's component state.
- The single `<data>`-less `<metadata name="errorProvider.TrayLocation">` entry describes where the form's `errorProvider` component sits in the designer's component tray (position `17, 17`). `UserForm.cs` uses that `errorProvider` at runtime to show validation errors from `AddUserViewModel` on `txtFirstName` and `txtLastName`.

### Behavior & Details

- The bulk of the file is the standard Microsoft ResX header: schema, version (`2.0`), and reader/writer class references (`System.Resources.ResXResourceReader` / `ResXResourceWriter` from `System.Windows.Forms` 4.0). This is boilerplate present in every `.resx` file.
- No `<data>` entries are defined, so this form has no string, image, or object resources — only designer metadata.
- The sole non-boilerplate entry is:
  ```xml
  <metadata name="errorProvider.TrayLocation" type="System.Drawing.Point, System.Drawing, ...">
    <value>17, 17</value>
  </metadata>
  ```
  This records the `errorProvider` component's position in the designer's component tray, so the form opens with the component in a known place the next time the designer loads it.

# WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.Designer.cs

### Purpose

This file is the WinForms designer-generated half of `UserForm` — the main window of a user-management application. It declares the form's nine controls and lays them out in `InitializeComponent()`: a "Current Users" group holding the `lstUsers` list box on the left, and an "Add New User" group on the right with `txtFirstName`, `txtLastName`, `btnSave`, and their labels, plus an `ErrorProvider` for validation tooltips. It contains no business logic; all behaviour lives in the hand-written partial class `UserForm.cs`.

### Role in the codebase

`WinFormsApp1` is an MVC-style WinForms app where `View/UserForm.cs` + this file + `UserForm.resx` together compose the single window shown by `DefaultModuleController`. That controller imports `UserForm` via the `[Export(typeof(IMainView<DialogResult, int>))]` attribute in `UserForm.cs`, sets its `DataContext` to `IMainViewModel`, and calls `Application.Run` on it. Remove this file and `UserForm` no longer compiles — its constructor calls `InitializeComponent()`, and `UserForm.cs` references controls (`txtFirstName`, `lstUsers`, `errorProvider`, etc.) whose fields are declared here.

### Relationships

- **`UserForm.cs`** (same directory): the other half of this partial class. It wires up data bindings, event handlers, and `ErrorProvider` usage against the fields and `InitializeComponent()` defined here.
- **`Mvvm`** (external project referenced from `UserForm.cs`): supplies the `Mvvm.Form` base class, so the inherited members (`DataContext`, `Dispose(bool)`, the form plumbing) come from there, not from this file.
- **`UserManagement.Model` / `UserManagement.ViewModel`**: the view model types bound to the controls in `UserForm.cs`; this file only names the controls those bindings target.
- **`UserForm.resx`**: satellite resource file for the form, generated alongside this one.

### Behavior & Details

- The class is `partial` and `internal` to the `WinFormsApp1.View` namespace, extending the `Mvvm`-library `Form` base. The only logic in this file is the `Dispose(bool)` override, which disposes the `IContainer components` field when `disposing` is true — the standard pattern so the `ErrorProvider` (the only component created with a container) is released cleanly.
- `InitializeComponent()` instantiates each control, sets its static properties (positions, sizes, tab order, caption text), and parents them: `lstUsers` into `groupBox1`; `btnSave`, `txtLastName`, `label2`, `txtFirstName`, `label1` into `groupBox2`; both group boxes into the form. `errorProvider.BlinkStyle` is `NeverBlink`, so validation errors show a persistent icon without blinking.
- The control field names carry the contract `UserForm.cs` depends on: `txtFirstName`/`txtLastName` are the `FirstName`/`LastName` bindings' targets and the controls the `ErrorProvider` errors are attached to; `lstUsers` shows the user list formatted as `"FirstName LastName"`; `btnSave` triggers `SaveUserCommand`. Renaming any field in this file breaks `SetupBindings` in `UserForm.cs`.
- Like all WinForms designer files, the contents of `InitializeComponent()` are regenerated by the Visual Studio designer — edit the form in the designer, not by hand here.

### Rough edges

- The form's `Text` is still the default `"Form1"`, so the window's title bar never reflects that it is the user-management form.

### Purpose

The `WinFormsApp1/View` directory contains the primary user interface for the user management application. It holds the `UserForm`, which serves as the main window for viewing and adding users. These files belong together because they constitute the complete visual presentation layer of the MVC architecture, specifically the "View" that interacts with the user directly.

### Software Components

This directory consists of a single logical component: the `UserForm`.

*   **`UserForm`**: The main window of the application. It is implemented as a partial class split across two files. The component displays a list of current users and provides input fields for adding new users. It handles data binding between the UI controls and the underlying view model, as well as validation error display.

### Relationships

The `UserForm` component is composed of three interdependent files that must exist together to function.

1.  **`UserForm.cs`**: This is the hand-written portion of the partial class. It contains the business logic for the view, including data bindings, event handlers (such as the save button click), and validation logic using the `ErrorProvider`. It imports the view model and exposes the form as the main view to the controller.
2.  **`UserForm.Designer.cs`**: This is the auto-generated portion of the partial class. It defines the control fields (like `txtFirstName`, `lstUsers`) and the `InitializeComponent()` method that constructs the layout. It depends on `UserForm.cs` to provide the class identity, but `UserForm.cs` depends on this file for the field declarations and initialization logic. You cannot rename or remove controls in `UserForm.cs` bindings without updating this file, and vice versa.
3.  **`UserForm.resx`**: This is the resource file paired with the designer code. It holds metadata for designer-managed components, such as the tray location of the `errorProvider`. It is consumed by `UserForm.Designer.cs` during design-time and compilation.

The `UserForm` inherits from a `Mvvm.Form` base class (external dependency) to handle MVVM plumbing like `DataContext` management. It depends on `UserManagement.Model` and `UserManagement.ViewModel` projects for the data structures it binds to. The controller (`DefaultModuleController`) in a separate project imports `UserForm` via the `Export` attribute to run the application.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "WinFormsApp1/View"
        UserFormCS[UserForm.cs]
        UserFormDesigner[UserForm.Designer.cs]
        UserFormResx[UserForm.resx]
    end

    MvvmBase[Mvvm.Form Base Class]
    ViewModel[UserManagement.ViewModel]

    UserFormCS -.->|Extends| MvvmBase
    UserFormCS -->|Partial Class| UserFormDesigner
    UserFormDesigner -->|Uses Metadata| UserFormResx
    UserFormCS -->|Binds To| ViewModel
```

### Rough edges

The form's `Text` property is still set to the default `"Form1"` in `UserForm.Designer.cs`, so the window title bar does not accurately reflect its purpose as the user management form.

## Contents
- [UserForm.Designer.cs](WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.Designer.md)
- [UserForm.cs](WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.md)
- [UserForm.resx](WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.resx.md)

# WpfApp1/AssemblyInfo.cs

### Purpose

This file carries the WPF `ThemeInfo` assembly attribute for the `WpfApp1` desktop application. It tells the WPF resource lookup engine where to find theme-specific and generic resource dictionaries for this assembly, which is what lets controls and resources resolve `ThemeDictionary` and `GenericDictionary` correctly at runtime.

### Role in the Codebase

`WpfApp1` is the WPF executable project of the solution (see `WpfApp1/WpfApp1.csproj`: `OutputType` `WinExe`, `UseWPF` enabled, `net10.0-windows`). This file is the standard, template-generated `AssemblyInfo.cs` that WPF project scaffolding emits; it is not hand-maintained application code. The application itself is declared in `WpfApp1/App.xaml` (`WpfApp1.App`, derived from `Mvvm.Wpf`'s `MvvmApplication`), and its behavior lives elsewhere in the project and its referenced `Common`, `Mvvm.Wpf`, and `UserManagement` projects.

If the file were removed, nothing in application logic breaks — there are no application resources here — but WPF would fall back to default dictionary lookup locations, which matters only if theme or generic resource dictionaries are ever added to the assembly.

### Relationships

- Depends on `System.Windows` (the WPF framework), specifically the `ThemeInfo` attribute and `ResourceDictionaryLocation` enum from the framework, not from this repository.
- Consumed implicitly by the WPF runtime and by anything in `WpfApp1` that relies on resource dictionary lookup. It has no callers in the repository's own code; it is pure metadata compiled into the assembly.

### Behavior & Details

- `[assembly: ThemeInfo]` sets two lookup locations for this assembly:
  - First argument `ResourceDictionaryLocation.None` — no theme-specific resource dictionary location is declared. Theme dictionaries are therefore not searched for in this assembly, per the standard fallback chain (page → application → theme).
  - Second argument `ResourceDictionaryLocation.SourceAssembly` — the generic resource dictionary, if one exists, is expected in the `Themes/Generic.xaml` dictionary of this assembly itself (the default WPF convention).
- The attribute has no runtime side effects beyond registering this metadata on the assembly; no classes, methods, or state are defined here.

### Purpose

`WpfApp1/App.xaml` is the XAML half of the application class `WpfApp1.App`. It does one job: declare that the app's root object is a `MvvmApplication` (from the `Mvvm.Wpf` library, defined in `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`) rather than a plain WPF `Application`. Its only content is an empty `<MvvmApplication.Resources>` element, which is a WPF convention — resource dictionaries could be merged here, but this app defines none.

Because the class code-behind (`App.xaml.cs`) contains no constructor, the `x:Class` pairing means the app uses `MvvmApplication`'s parameterless constructor, which in turn scans all assemblies loaded with the application (default `SearchOption.TopDirectoryOnly`) and exports nothing ignored — i.e., standard MEF composition over everything in the app's folder.

### Role in the Codebase

This file is the app's entry point declaration. Without it, `App` would be a plain `Application` and none of the startup machinery in `MvvmApplication` would run. The actual work happens in the base class and in module controllers such as `DefaultModuleController` (`WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs`), whose `IModuleController` export MEF discovers during startup.

### Relationships

- Inherits (via `x:Class="WpfApp1.App"` and the matching `partial class App : MvvmApplication` in `App.xaml.cs`) from `Mvvm.Wpf.MvvmApplication`, which extends `System.Windows.Application`.
- Consumed implicitly by the C# compiler, which generates the App's constructor and `InitializeComponent` from this markup.

### Behavior & Details

Nothing to document beyond the root element type — the empty `Resources` section has no behavioural effect.

### Purpose

`WpfApp1/WpfApp1.csproj` is the MSBuild project file for the WPF front-end of the solution — the only WPF executable in `Demo.slnx`. It exists to compile the small `WpfApp1` folder (`App.xaml`, the exported `DefaultModuleController`, and the `UserView` window) into a Windows executable and to wire up its dependencies on the MVVM, composition, and business-logic projects.

This is build configuration, not a component of the application architecture. It contains no application logic of its own.

### What it configures

- **Output and platform** — `WinExe` targeting `net10.0-windows`, with `UseWPF` enabled, so the result is a WPF desktop app with no console window. `Nullable` and `ImplicitUsings` are both enabled.
- **NuGet dependency** — `Microsoft.Xaml.Behaviors.Wpf` 1.1.142, providing the WPF behavior classes available to XAML in this project.
- **Project references** — the three libraries the app is built on:
  - `Common` — general infrastructure (composition helpers, converters, diagnostics) used by `Mvvm.Wpf` and this project.
  - `Mvvm.Wpf` — provides `MvvmApplication`, the base class of `WpfApp1.App`. That base class sets up a MEF composition container, discovers exported `IModuleController` instances, and drives their `Initialize`/`Run`/`Shutdown` lifecycle.
  - `UserManagement` — the business-logic project whose `MainViewModel` and views this shell presents.

### Role in the Codebase

This file is the build entry point for the app's host shell. The code it compiles is thin by design: `App.xaml.cs` defines `App : MvvmApplication` with no members, and the composition container scans the output directory at startup for exported modules. Because `UserManagement` (and its own project references) is copied to the output alongside the app, its exports are discovered without being named in any code.

If the project file were removed, the WPF host would not build; the rest of the solution (e.g. `Mvvm.Winforms`, `Mvvm.Console`) could still build the same modules for their own hosts.

### Relationships

Consumers of this project file are the build system and the other solution members it references:

- `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs` — the base class of `WpfApp1.App`; this project must reference `Mvvm.Wpf` for `App.xaml` to compile.
- `Common` — referenced directly here (needed because `Mvvm.Wpf`'s types surface `Common` types in this project's code paths) and transitively by `Mvvm.Wpf`.
- `UserManagement` — referenced so its view-model and MEF exports land in the WPF app's output directory, where `MvvmApplication` discovers them at runtime.

Note the reference direction: `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs` scans assemblies in the working directory at runtime, so the project references here are what actually make the `UserManagement` modules visible to the container — the runtime discovery only works because this file pulls those assemblies into the output.

# WpfApp1/App.xaml.cs

### Purpose

This file is the code-behalf half of the WPF application's entry point. It defines `WpfApp1.App`, the concrete `Application`-derived class that launches the app. All real work — module discovery, composition, startup, shutdown, and exception handling — is delegated to its base class `MvvmApplication` in the `Mvvm.Wpf` project. The class body here is empty; the file exists so the compiler and XAML tooling can tie the `x:Class="WpfApp1.App"` declaration in `App.xaml` to a C# type that inherits `MvvmApplication` (which itself inherits `System.Windows.Application`).

The file also declares `[assembly: SupportedOSPlatform("windows")]` at the top. Since the project is `net10.0-windows`, this silences the TFM analyzer for Windows-specific APIs used throughout the app; it's an assembly-level attribute, so it effectively applies to the whole project.

### Role in the Codebase

`App` is the executable entry point of the `WpfApp1` project (`OutputType` is `WinExe` in `WpfApp1.csproj`). It is the `partial class` whose other half is generated from `WpfApp1/App.xaml` at build time; the XAML file's root element is `<mvvm:MvvmApplication x:Class="WpfApp1.App">`, so the generated part provides the `Main`-related infrastructure while this source part supplies the class declaration and its base type.

Removing this file (or its class declaration) would break the build, because the XAML-generated partial half has no type to merge with, and the app would have no `Application` subclass to run.

### Relationships

- **`MvvmApplication`** (`Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`): the base class. `App` overrides nothing and adds no members, so its entire runtime behaviour comes from `MvvmApplication`:
  - On startup it builds a MEF `CompositionContainer` from the assemblies in its directory (minus ignore lists), loads all exported `IModuleController`s, calls `Initialize()` on each, then `Run()` on each.
  - If no modules are found, or a `ReflectionTypeLoadException` occurs while resolving them, it shows an error and shuts down with `ExitCodes.Error`.
  - It hooks `DispatcherUnhandledException` and `AppDomain.UnhandledException`, logging via `Trace.TraceError` and showing a modal error dialog for non-terminating exceptions.
  - On exit it calls `Shutdown()` on the module controllers in reverse order and disposes the container.
- **`WpfApp1.csproj`**: references `Common`, `Mvvm.Wpf`, and `UserManagement`. Because `MvvmApplication`'s default constructor scans the app directory for assemblies to compose, the `UserManagement` project reference is what lets a module shipped in that assembly be discovered and started at runtime. Callers of this class: none directly — the OS/runtime instantiates `App` as the WPF startup object.

### Behavior & Details

- The class is `public partial` and inherits `MvvmApplication` with its default constructor semantics (no module assemblies specified, no ignore list, `SearchOption.TopDirectoryOnly`), meaning module discovery scans only the application's own directory.
- No behavior of its own: no `OnStartup`/`OnExit` overrides, no event handlers, no static members. Anything you'd expect to change at app startup (module set, search scope, ignored assemblies) would go in this class by passing a `MvvmApplication(string[] moduleAssemblies, string[] ignoreAssemblies, SearchOption)`-style argument — currently it isn't.

### Rough edges

- `[assembly: SupportedOSPlatform("windows")]` is duplicated: it appears both here and in `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`, which is harmless but redundant.
- The base class's error messages are partly in German (`"Es ist ein Fehler aufgetreten."` / `"Fehler"`), so `App` inherits non-English UI text on exception.

### Purpose `WpfApp1` is the WPF desktop application project within the solution. It serves as the executable host shell that launches the application, bootstraps the MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework) composition container, and displays the main user interface. The contents belong together because they form the thin WPF-specific layer required to run the `UserManagement` business logic on the WPF platform, adhering to the MVVM pattern defined by the `Mvvm.Wpf` library. ### Software Components The source code in this directory is divided into two main responsibilities: application bootstrapping and UI presentation. * **Application Entry Point**: Defined by [`App.xaml`](WpfApp1/App.xaml.md) and [`App.xaml.cs`](WpfApp1/App.xaml.cs.md). This component declares `WpfApp1.App` as a subclass of `MvvmApplication`. It contains no logic of its own; its sole purpose is to enable the base class's MEF scanning and lifecycle management. * **Lifecycle Controller**: Located in `Controller/`, specifically `DefaultModuleController.cs`. This class implements `IModuleController` and acts as the bridge between the host application and the business logic. It is responsible for initializing, running, and shutting down the main window. * **User Interface**: Located in `View/`, specifically `UserView.xaml` and `UserView.xaml.cs`. This component provides the main window for the "User Management" feature. # WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs

### Purpose

`DefaultModuleController` is the WPF application's bootstrapping controller. It implements `IModuleController` (defined in `Mvvm/IModuleController.cs`) with the minimal lifecycle the app needs: wire the main view to its view model, show the window, and close it on exit. It exists so the WPF host application has a concrete `IModuleController` export that `MvvmApplication` can discover and drive at startup.

### Role in the Codebase

The WPF app's host is `MvvmApplication` (`Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`), which derives from `System.Windows.Application`. During `OnStartup` it builds a MEF `CompositionContainer`, loads all exported `IModuleController` values, calls `Initialize()` on each, then `Run()` on each. During `OnExit` it calls `Shutdown()` in reverse order. This class is one of the controllers in that list — in this project, the only `IModuleController` export in the `WpfApp1` assembly, so it is effectively the single boot path of the WPF app.

Its counterpart in the WinForms project, `WinFormsApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs`, plays the same role with WinForms types (`IMainView<DialogResult, int>`).

If this class were removed, the container would find no `IModuleController` exports from `WpfApp1` and `MvvmApplication` would show "No module found." and shut down.

### Relationships

- **MEF wiring.** The class carries `[Export(typeof(IModuleController))]`, and its constructor is marked `[ImportingConstructor]`. The MEF container (created in `MvvmApplication.OnStartup`) satisfies the two constructor parameters:
  - `IMainView<bool?, double>` — exported by `UserView` (`WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml.cs`), a `Window` that also exports `IMainView<bool?, double>`.
  - `IMainViewModel` — exported by `UserViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`), which carries `[Export(typeof(IMainViewModel))]` in addition to its `IUserViewModel` export.
- **Interfaces.** It implements `IModuleController` from `Mvvm/IModuleController.cs` (`Initialize`, `Run`, `Shutdown`). `IMainView<TDialogResult, TDimension>` comes from `Mvvm/IMainView.cs` and inherits from `IDialogView<TDialogResult>`; here the dialog result is `bool?` and dimensions are `double`, matching WPF's unitless, double-based geometry. `IMainViewModel` comes from `Mvvm/IMainViewModel.cs`.

### Behavior & Details

- **Constructor.** Stores the injected `mainView` and `mainViewModel` in the protected `MainView` and `MainViewModel` properties, and sets `MainView.DataContext = mainViewModel`, binding the window to its view model. Everything else in the class is lifecycle plumbing.
- **`Initialize()`.** Empty. Kept as an override point — a subclass can do module setup (e.g. loading data, preparing services) before the view is shown.
- **`Run()`.** Calls `MainView.Show()`, displaying the main window. This is what actually makes the app visible.
- **`Shutdown()`.** Calls `MainView.Close()` to tear down the window.
- All three methods are `virtual`, so a derived controller can extend the lifecycle without changing how `MvvmApplication` drives it.

Because `MainView` and `MainViewModel` are `protected` rather than `public`, they are exposed for derived controllers to use, not for external callers. Callers of this class are the MEF container (construction) and `MvvmApplication` (lifecycle calls) only.

### Rough edges

- `Run()` uses `Show()`, not `ShowDialog()` or `Show()` followed by a result read, even though the view's dialog-result type is `bool?`. The `bool?` result is never observed anywhere in this controller or `MvvmApplication`; the dialog-result generics appear to be carried over from the `IDialogView` contract rather than used by the boot path.
- The WPF app relies on exactly one `IMainViewModel` export (`UserViewModel`). If more than one assembly exporting `IMainViewModel` were composed in, the constructor's `IMainViewModel` import would fail at composition time — there is no named or constrained import here to disambiguate.

# WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml.cs

### Purpose

This code-behind file is the C# half of the `UserView` window — the main "User Management" window of the WPF application. It does almost nothing on its own: it registers the window as an MEF export so the application's controller can find, show, and close it without ever naming the concrete type. The actual UI layout, bindings, and styling live in the paired `UserView.xaml` file.

### Role in the Codebase

`UserView` is the presentation entry point of the WPF app. The startup flow is:

1. `App` (`WpfApp1/App.xaml.cs`, derived from `MvvmApplication`) boots MEF composition.
2. `DefaultModuleController` (`WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs`) is the exported `IModuleController`. Its importing constructor receives an `IMainView<bool?, double>` and an `IMainViewModel`; it assigns the view model to the view's `DataContext` and calls `MainView.Show()` in `Run()`.
3. `UserView` is the only `IMainView<bool?, double>` export in the WPF project (the WinForms app has its own parallel `UserForm` implementing `IMainView<DialogResult, int>`), so this is the class MEF hands to the controller.

If the `[Export]` attribute or the interface implementation were removed, MEF would fail to satisfy the controller's constructor and the application would not launch.

### Relationships

- **`IMainView<bool?, double>`** (`Mvvm/IMainView.cs`): the contract this class implements. It inherits `IDialogView<bool?>` (`Mvvm/IDialogView.cs`) and `IView` (`Mvvm/IView.cs`). Concretely, `UserView` fulfils: `DataContext` (from `IView`, satisfied by `Window`), `Show()`/`Close()`/`Closing`/`Closed` (inherited from `Window`), `DialogResult` and `Left`/`Top`/`Width`/`Height` (satisfied by `Window` properties typed compatibly with `bool?` and `double`). Nothing here overrides any of that — it all comes for free from `Window`.
- **`[Export]`** (`System.ComponentModel.Composition`): makes `UserView` discoverable to the MEF container used by the `Mvvm` framework.
- **`UserView.xaml`**: the markup counterpart. The `x:Class="WpfApp1.View.UserView"` attribute in the XAML and the `partial` keyword here join them into one class; the XAML's data bindings (e.g. `ShowUsersViewModel.Users`, `AddUserViewModel.SaveUserCommand`, the `Loaded` event trigger that invokes `LoadedCommand`) are all resolved against whatever `DefaultModuleController` assigns as `DataContext` — the `IMainViewModel` export, `UserViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`).

The only caller in this repository is `DefaultModuleController`, which depends on the interface, not the class.

### Behavior & Details

- The class is `partial`; the other part (generated from `UserView.xaml` at build time) contains the `InitializeComponent()` method that the constructor calls to wire up the visual tree. The constructor performs no other work.
- The generic arguments encode how this app's dialog/position contract is typed: `bool?` for the dialog result, `double` for the view's position and size — matching WPF's `Nullable<bool> Window.DialogResult` and `double`-based `Left`/`Top`/`Width`/`Height`. The WinForms twin uses `DialogResult`/`int` instead, which is why the two apps need separate exports rather than sharing one.
- Because no member is implemented in this file at all, behaviour changes almost never require touching it. Only the export type or the interface conformance would be reasons to edit it.

### Rough edges

- `IMainView<TDialogResult, TDimension>` is a weakly typed contract: the "dimension" parameters (`Left`, `Top`, `Width`, `Height`) are all the same type, and the dialog result is an unconstrained generic. This forces each host app to pick an arbitrary type pairing (`bool?`/`double` here, `DialogResult`/`int` in WinForms), which is why the exports cannot be shared across the two projects.

### Purpose

`WpfApp1/View` serves as the presentation layer entry point for the WPF application. Its primary responsibility is to provide the main visual interface that the application controller displays to the user. The contents belong together because they constitute a single WPF window component, split between markup (`XAML`) and code-behind (C#), following standard WPF conventions.

### Software Components

The directory contains one main component: the `UserView` window. This window acts as the host for the "User Management" functionality.

- **`UserView`**: Defined jointly by [UserView.xaml](WpfApp1/View/UserView.md) and [UserView.xaml.cs](WpfApp1/View/UserView.md). The C# file acts as a lightweight wrapper that registers the window as a MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework) export. It implements the `IMainView<bool?, double>` interface but contains no specific business logic; all UI structure, bindings, and styling are defined in the XAML file.

### Relationships

The dependency flow is strictly from the application controller to this view. `DefaultModuleController` (located in `WpfApp1/Controller`) does not reference `UserView` directly. Instead, it imports the `IMainView<bool?, double>` interface. MEF resolves this import to the `UserView` class because it is the only class in the WPF project exporting that specific interface signature.

Once resolved, the controller assigns the `UserViewModel` as the `DataContext` for the view. All data bindings within `UserView.xaml` (such as commands and user lists) resolve against this view model. The code-behind file `UserView.xaml.cs` is critical for this discovery process; if the `[Export]` attribute or interface implementation were removed, MEF would fail to locate a view to display, preventing the application from launching.

        DMC[DefaultModuleController]
    end
    
    subgraph WpfApp1_View
        UV[UserView]
    end

        IMV[IMainView<bool?, double>]
    end

    IMV -->|resolved by MEF| UV
