# Demo.slnx

**Path:** `Demo.slnx` (repository root)

This is a .NET solution file in the XML-based `.slnx` format. It defines the solution that groups all 16 projects in this repository so they can be built, opened in Visual Studio or VS Code, and built together.

### Purpose

The solution file exists so the repo's many small, layered projects can be opened and built as a single unit instead of one at a time. It carries no logic of its own — its only job is the project list (plus, where present, a GUID per project, used for stable identification across renames and moves).

### Role in the Codebase

This is the top-level entry point for the whole repository. Every project directory at the root — `BusinessLayer`, `Common`, `Mvvm`, `DataAccessLayer`, `UserManagement`, the three UI hosts, and the test project — is registered exactly once in this file. All 16 registered `Path` entries match the 16 `*.csproj` files that exist, so there are no stale or orphaned entries. If the solution file were removed, each project could still be built on its own from its own `.csproj` (project references in the `.csproj` files are what carry the real dependency graph), but you would lose the single-window build/open experience.

The projects in the solution group into a few layers, and the reference graph in the `.csproj` files shows how they stack:

- **Core libraries:** `Common`, `Dto`, `Logging`, `Mvvm`, `DataAccessLayer`, `Entity.Hibernate` (Hibernate ORM entities), `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` (persistence, built on `Entity.Hibernate`).
- **Business logic:** `BusinessLayer` references `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`, `Dto`, `Entity.Hibernate`, and `Logging`.
- **UI hosts:** `ConsoleApp1`, `WinFormsApp1`, and `WpfApp1` are runnable hosts; `Mvvm.Console`, `Mvvm.Winforms`, and `Mvvm.Wpf` are MVVM infrastructure per UI framework, each referencing `Mvvm` (for example, `Mvvm.Console` references `Mvvm` and uses `System.ComponentModel.Composition` for plugin-style assembly loading).

# Demo

## Overview

**Demo** is a .NET solution that demonstrates a layered, MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework)-based MVVM architecture for Windows desktop applications. It solves the problem of building UI-agnostic business logic that can be hosted by multiple front-end technologies (WPF, WinForms, and Console) without code duplication.

The repository is designed for developers looking to understand how to structure enterprise-style C# applications using strict dependency inversion. Its distinctive feature is the use of MEF for plugin-style discovery and composition, allowing the core business logic to remain completely decoupled from specific UI frameworks. The system includes a sample "User Management" feature to demonstrate data persistence, validation, and inter-view communication across these different host environments.

## Repository Description

A demonstration of a modular .NET application using MEF, MVVM, and NHibernate, supporting WPF, WinForms, and Console hosts.

## Architecture Overview

The system follows a strict layered architecture where dependency flow is strictly top-down, from UI hosts to business logic and data access. The primary design pattern is **plugin-based composition** via MEF.

A request enters through a host application (`WpfApp1`, `WinFormsApp1`, or `ConsoleApp1`). The host bootstraps a `CompositionContainer` using the `CompositionHelper` from the `Common` project. This container scans the output directory for assemblies and discovers classes marked with MEF attributes. The host then resolves an `IModuleController` (specifically `DefaultModuleController`), which orchestrates the lifecycle (`Initialize`, `Run`) of the application modules.

The core feature is the `UserManagement` module, which contains the ViewModels. These ViewModels depend on the `BusinessLayer` for logic and `DataAccessLayer` for data. The `BusinessLayer` contains `UserService`, which handles domain logic and translates `UserDto` objects into persistent entities. Persistence is handled by `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`, which uses NHibernate to communicate with a SQL Server database.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Host Applications"
        WPF[WpfApp1]
        WF[WinFormsApp1]
        CON[ConsoleApp1]
    end

    subgraph "UI Frameworks & Infrastructure"
        MVVM_WPF[Mvvm.Wpf]
        MVVM_WF[Mvvm.Winforms]
        MVVM_CON[Mvvm.Console]
        MVVM_CORE[Mvvm]
        COMMON[Common]
    end

    subgraph "Feature Module"
        UM[UserManagement]
    end

    subgraph "Business Logic"
        BL[BusinessLayer]
    end

    subgraph "Data Access"
        DAL[DataAccessLayer]
        DAL_HIB[DataAccessLayer.Hibernate]
        ENT_HIB[Entity.Hibernate]
        DTO[Dto]
        LOG[Logging]
    end

    DB[(SQL Server)]

    WPF -->|Inherits/Uses| MVVM_WPF
    WF -->|Inherits/Uses| MVVM_WF
    CON -->|Uses| MVVM_CON
    
    MVVM_WPF -->|Implements| MVVM_CORE
    MVVM_WF -->|Implements| MVVM_CORE
    MVVM_CON -->|Implements| MVVM_CORE
    
    WPF & WF & CON -->|Bootstraps| COMMON
    WPF & WF & CON -->|References| UM
    
    UM -->|Consumes| MVVM_CORE
    UM -->|Calls| BL
    UM -->|Uses| DTO
    UM -->|Uses| LOG

    BL -->|Implements| DAL
    BL -->|Uses| DTO
    BL -->|Uses| LOG
    BL -->|Uses| ENT_HIB

    DAL_HIB -->|Implements| DAL
    DAL_HIB -->|Maps| ENT_HIB
    DAL_HIB -->|Writes/Reads| DB
```

## Main Components

*   **UI Hosts (`WpfApp1`, `WinFormsApp1`, `ConsoleApp1`)**: These are thin executable shells. They initialize the MEF container, discover the `DefaultModuleController`, and manage the application lifecycle. They contain no business logic, only bootstrap code and framework-specific adapters (like `MessageService` implementations in `Mvvm.Wpf`, etc.).
*   **`UserManagement`**: The core feature module implementing the MVVM pattern. It contains `UserViewModel`, `AddUserViewModel`, and `ShowUsersViewModel`. These components use `FluentValidation` for input checks and `WeakReferenceMessenger` to communicate state changes (e.g., user added) without direct coupling.
*   **`BusinessLayer`**: Contains the domain services, primarily `UserService`. It acts as the bridge between the UI ViewModels and the Data Access Layer. It handles the mapping of `UserDto` to `User` entities and manages NHibernate sessions via a `RepositoryFactory`.
*   **`DataAccessLayer` & `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`**: `DataAccessLayer` defines the abstract contracts (`IRepository`, `IUnitOfWork`, `IEntity`), while `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` provides the concrete NHibernate implementation. This separation ensures the business layer is not coupled to a specific ORM.
*   **`Mvvm` & `Common`**: `Mvvm` provides the framework-agnostic base classes (`ViewModelBase`, `IView`, `IMessageService`) that all ViewModels inherit from. `Common` provides the `CompositionHelper` which is the engine for MEF assembly scanning and container building, along with shared utilities like `ExtendedGuard` for validation.
*   **`Dto` & `Entity.Hibernate`**: `Dto` defines the data transfer objects (`UserDto`) and validation rules shared between UI and Business layers. `Entity.Hibernate` defines the NHibernate-mapped `User` entity and its Fluent mappings, determining the database schema.
*   **`Logging`**: A unified logging facade wrapping Serilog and `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging`. It is injected via MEF into the `BusinessLayer` and `UserManagement` modules to provide consistent diagnostic output.

## Features

*   **Multi-Platform Hosting**: The same business logic and ViewModels run on WPF, WinForms, and Console hosts via MEF.
*   **MEF-Based Plugin Architecture**: Modules are discovered and composed at runtime, allowing for modular extension.
*   **Framework-Agnostic MVVM**: Core ViewModels are decoupled from UI specifics, using interfaces for view interaction and messaging.
*   **Fluent Validation**: Input validation is handled via `FluentValidation` in the `Dto` layer, surfacing errors to the UI via `INotifyDataErrorInfo`.
*   **NHibernate Persistence**: Database operations are abstracted behind repositories, using NHibernate for SQL Server interaction with schema auto-updating.
*   **Unified Logging**: Centralized Serilog-backed logging service injected via MEF across layers.

## Technology Stack

*   **Language**: C# (targeting .NET 10)
*   **UI Frameworks**: WPF, Windows Forms, Console
*   **Architecture Pattern**: MVVM, Layered Architecture
*   **Dependency Injection/Composition**: MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework)
*   **ORM**: NHibernate (with Fluent NHibernate)
*   **Validation**: FluentValidation
*   **Logging**: Serilog, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging
*   **Database**: SQL Server
*   **Testing**: MSTest, Moq
*   **Community Toolkit**: `CommunityToolkit.Mvvm` (for `ObservableObject`)

## Use Cases

*   **Learning MEF Composition**: Developers looking to understand how to use `System.ComponentModel.Composition` for plugin-based application design in .NET.
*   **Multi-UI Development**: Teams needing to share business logic and ViewModels across different Windows UI technologies (e.g., migrating from WinForms to WPF) without rewriting the core logic.
*   **NHibernate Repository Pattern**: Implementers wanting to see a concrete example of abstracting ORM concerns behind interfaces (`IRepository`, `IUnitOfWork`) in a C# application.
*   **MVVM with Validation**: Developers seeking a reference implementation of MVVM that integrates `FluentValidation` and handles data errors in ViewModels.

# RepositoryFactory.cs

**Path:** `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`

### Purpose

`RepositoryFactory` exists to make business-layer services able to obtain NHibernate-backed repositories without knowing anything about how the database session is created. It is the composition root for the persistence stack: it wires a connection string and the mapping assembly from `IModelContext` into the NHibernate infrastructure, and exposes repository instances to the rest of the business layer through the `IRepositoryFactory` contract.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is a thin, MEF-activated glue class in the `BusinessLayer` project. It does no business logic of its own — it closes over the generic, infrastructure-level `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` (defined in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`) by pinning `TKey` to `int`, and adds the `IRepositoryFactory` identity so that the layer only depends on its own interface.

It is exported to the MEF container via `[Export(typeof(IRepositoryFactory))]` and constructed through its `[ImportingConstructor]`, so it is never instantiated directly in code. Services like `UserService` (`BusinessLayer/UserService.cs`) take `IRepositoryFactory` in their constructor and call `Create()` to get a disposable repository per operation. If this class were removed, the container would have no export satisfying `IRepositoryFactory`, and every business service that depends on it would fail to compose.

### Relationships

- **Base class:** `HibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` — a concrete generic class in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` whose `protected` constructor takes a connection string and an array of mapping-assembly names and builds an NHibernate `ISessionFactory` using FluentNHibernate (SQL Server, with a schema update). `RepositoryFactory` inherits its entire lifecycle from there and adds no members of its own beyond the constructor.
- **Implemented interface:** `IRepositoryFactory` (`BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`), which is an empty marker interface over `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`). That interface in turn extends `IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>`, so `Create()` returns a stateless-session-backed `IHibernateRepository<int>`.
- **Import:** `IModelContext` (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IModelContext.cs`), resolved at composition time to the layer's `ModelContext` (`BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs`), which supplies the `ConnectionString` from app config and `MappingAssemblies` as `["Entity.Hibernate"]`.
- **Callers:** MEF-composed business services that import `IRepositoryFactory` — currently `UserService`.

### Behavior & Details

- The constructor forwards `context.ConnectionString` and `context.MappingAssemblies` to the base NHibernate factory, which does all real work: FluentNHibernate configuration for a SQL Server 2012 provider, a `SchemaUpdate` on startup, loading fluent mappings from the named assemblies, and building the session factory.
- Because the base constructor runs on construction, the NHibernate session factory is built exactly when MEF composes `RepositoryFactory`. The base class also guards against a second construction with a static `IsInitialized` flag and throws `InvalidOperationException` ("Already initialized") if a second instance is ever requested, and wraps any setup failure in a `DataAccessException`.
- `Create()` (inherited) returns a new `IRepository<int>` per call over a freshly opened stateless session; callers dispose the repository after use (as `UserService` does with `using var repository = ...`).
- Note that `HibernateRepositoryFactory.Drop()` is a `NotImplementedException` stub, so there is no working teardown path for the session factory in the current code.

### Rough edges

- `ModelContext` is defined as `public class ModelContext()` — a primary constructor taking no parameters that are actually used; the arguments (`ConnectionString`, `MappingAssemblies`) come from the `ModelContextBase` base-class constructor instead. This compiles in C# 12, but it looks like a leftover and is worth confirming is intentional.
- The one-instance-per-process enforcement in the base class relies on a static flag, so a second composition (e.g., a second container or a test re-composing the graph) throws rather than sharing or rebuilding.
- `Drop()` is unimplemented, so the session factory lifecycle has no symmetric teardown to its construction.

# BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs

### Purpose

This file defines `IRepositoryFactory`, the BusinessLayer's own, key-free contract for creating NHibernate repositories. It exists so that business services (like `UserService`) can depend on a factory abstraction without knowing that repositories are backed by NHibernate/Hibernate, or that the repository key type is `int`.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a small type alias / specialization interface inside the `BusinessLayer` namespace. It derives from `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` (defined in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`), which itself derives from the generic `DataAccessLayer.IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>` and adds `Create()` returning `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`.

By fixing `TKey` to `int` and dropping the generic parameter, this interface gives the business layer a stable, non-generic seam for repository creation. If it were removed, `UserService` and `RepositoryFactory` would need to reference the generic `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` directly, leaking the key type and the DataAccessLayer's Hibernate-specific naming into the business layer.

### Relationships

- **Extends** `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` (from `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`), which inherits from `DataAccessLayer.IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>`. So members inherited through the chain include:
  - `IHibernateRepository<int> Create()` — from `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`.
  - `void Drop()` — from the generic base `IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>`.
- **Implemented by** `RepositoryFactory` (same folder, `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`), which also extends `HibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` and is MEF-exported as `IRepositoryFactory`.
- **Consumed by** `UserService` (`BusinessLayer/UserService.cs`), which takes `IRepositoryFactory` in its `[ImportingConstructor]` and calls `_repositoryFactory.Create()` to open repositories for queries and unit-of-work transactions.

### Behavior & Details

The interface declares no new members of its own; it contributes only the type-level specialization (fixing `TKey` to `int`) and a non-generic name that business-layer code can reference. All contract behavior comes from the inherited members:

- `Create()` returns a new `IHibernateRepository<int>` (in practice a `HibernateRepository<int>` over a stateless session, per `HibernateRepositoryFactory.Create`). Callers treat it as disposable (`using var repository = _repositoryFactory.Create();`).
- `Drop()` is declared in the generic base but is never implemented meaningfully — `HibernateRepositoryFactory.Drop()` throws `NotImplementedException`, so callers in the business layer don't use it.
- Because `TKey` is constrained to `struct` in the base interfaces, `int` satisfies the constraint; that's why the specialization uses `int` (matching the integer primary keys of the entities, e.g. `User`).

One practical caveat for anyone implementing this: the underlying `HibernateRepositoryFactory` constructor enforces a process-wide single initialization (a static `IsInitialized` flag), so only one factory/session factory can be created per process.

# BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs

### Purpose

`ModelContext` is the MEF export that supplies the application's database connection settings: the connection string and the list of assembly names that contain ORM mapping files. It exists because the business layer needs a concrete, discoverable `IModelContext` that consumers can import without knowing where the configuration comes from.

The whole class is a single parameterless constructor — the type has no members of its own.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a small DI/MEF composition piece inside `BusinessLayer`. The `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` project defines the contract (`IModelContext`), the abstract base (`ModelContextBase`), and the ORM machinery; this file is the concrete binding for this application, filling in the actual connection string and mapping assembly.

### Relationships

- **Base class:** `ModelContextBase` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/ModelContextBase.cs`. That abstract class stores `ConnectionString` and `MappingAssemblies` as read-only properties, so this class inherits both.
- **Exported contract:** `IModelContext` (defined in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IModelContext.cs`). The `[Export(typeof(IModelContext))]` attribute makes MEF provide this class to any part that imports `IModelContext`.
- **Caller:** `RepositoryFactory` in `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs` imports `IModelContext` in its `[ImportingConstructor]` and passes `context.ConnectionString` and `context.MappingAssemblies` on to its `HibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` base. That is the only current consumer found in the codebase.
- **Configuration:** The connection string is read from `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]`, so the value is whatever `app.config`/`web.config` supplies under that key.

### Behavior & Details

The single parameterless constructor does two things:

- Reads `AppSettings["ConnectionString"]` and passes it (with the `!` null-forgiving operator) as the `connectionString` argument to `ModelContextBase`. If the setting is missing, the constructor receives `null`; nothing here validates it, so a misconfigured app will fail later, when a connection is actually attempted.
- Passes `["Entity.Hibernate"]` as the `mappingAssemblies` argument, telling the Hibernate ORM that entity mapping files live in the `Entity.Hibernate` assembly. Note that `ModelContextBase`'s own commented-out line adds `"DataAccessLayer"` and `"DataAccessLayer.Hibernate"` to this list in some deployments — the base class keeps its list as passed, so this export maps only `Entity.Hibernate`.

Because the constructor takes no parameters, MEF can compose it unconditionally; all its configuration comes from `AppSettings` at construction time. Changing the connection string or mapping assemblies is done entirely through configuration and this one call, respectively — no code change in the data-access layer is needed.

### Rough edges

- `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]!` asserts non-null without checking; a missing app setting is a silent `null` until the connection string is used.
- The `["Entity.Hibernate"]` literal hard-codes the mapping assembly for this app; adding a mapping assembly requires editing this file rather than the configuration.

# BusinessLayer/UserService.cs

### Purpose

`UserService` is the business-logic component for user management in this MEF-composed application. It implements `IUserService` (defined in `BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`) and provides two operations: listing users (`GetActiveUsers`) and creating a user (`AddUser`). It exists so the view-model layer can talk to the persistence layer through a stable interface without knowing NHibernate or the repository types.

### Role in the codebase

The class lives in `BusinessLayer/`, sits between the `UserManagement` view-models and the NHibernate-based data access layer, and is wired up through MEF: `[Export(typeof(IUserService))]` publishes it, and `[ImportingConstructor]` takes its one dependency, `IRepositoryFactory` (implemented by `RepositoryFactory` in the same folder). If it were removed, `AddUserViewModel` and `ShowUsersViewModel` could no longer load or create users, and MEF composition would fail to satisfy their `[Import]` of `IUserService`.

- **`IUserService`** (`BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`) — the contract this class implements, also declaring the `LoggingService` property.
- **`IRepositoryFactory`** (`BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`) — inherits `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>` from `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`, which returns an `IHibernateRepository<int>` (NHibernate, `IDisposable`) from `Create()`. `UserService` creates one repository per operation and disposes it with `using`.
- **`User`** (`Entity.Hibernate/User.cs`) — the NHibernate entity; its public `User(firstName, lastName)` constructor also sets `IsActive = true`.
- **`UserDto`** (from the `Dto` namespace) — the shape crossing the layer boundary; `UserDto` and `User` share `Id`, `FirstName`, `LastName`.
- **`ILoggingService`** (`Logging/ILoggingService.cs`) — used to log save failures.
- **`BusinessLayerException`** (`BusinessLayer/BusinessLayerException.cs`) — a simple `Exception` wrapper with `(message, inner)`.
- **Callers** — `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs` calls `GetActiveUsers()` on load; `AddUserViewModel.cs` calls `AddUser()` from its save command and catches `BusinessLayerException`. `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` mocks `IUserService` rather than using this class directly.

**`GetActiveUsers()`** — Creates a repository, runs a LINQ query over `GetQueryable<User>()`, projects each entity to a `UserDto` (id, first name, last name only), and materializes it with `ToListAsync()`. Despite the name, the query contains no `IsActive` filter, so it returns every user in the table, not only active ones.

**`AddUser(UserDto user)`** — Runs in three steps:

1. Validates the input with `CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics` `Guard` — `FirstName` and `LastName` must be non-null and non-whitespace. These guards throw a generic `ArgumentException` (not `BusinessLayerException`), so callers cannot distinguish bad input from save failures by exception type.
2. Opens a transaction via `repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction()` and saves a new `User` entity.
3. On success commits; on any exception it rolls back, logs the error through `LoggingService`, and rethrows as `BusinessLayerException("Error saving user", e)`. The comment in the code states this is the only exception type callers should ever see from this service.

The `LoggingService` property is public with a setter (part of `IUserService`) and is meant to be injected by the composition container rather than the constructor. Note that in the constructor it is set to `null!` and the property carries no `[Import]` attribute, so whether it is ever populated depends entirely on the host's MEF configuration. If the property is not set, `AddUser` will throw a `NullReferenceException` inside its own `catch` block when it tries to log, masking the original error.

- `GetActiveUsers` does not filter by `IsActive`; it returns all users, contradicting its name.
- `LoggingService` is not MEF-injected by this class (no `[Import]`); anything relying on the error path must guarantee the property is set externally, or a save failure becomes a `NullReferenceException` from within the service's own `catch`.
- `AddUser`'s `Guard` calls throw `ArgumentException`, so validation failures bypass the "callers only ever see `BusinessLayerException`" contract stated in the code.

# `BusinessLayer/BusinessLayerException.cs`

This file defines `BusinessLayerException`, the single exception type used by the `BusinessLayer` project to signal that a business operation failed.

### Purpose

The class exists so business-logic failures are distinguishable from other kinds of errors. It inherits from the .NET `System.Exception` (a framework type, not defined in this repository), and its only addition is its *identity*: catching it tells a caller that the failure originated in the business layer and wrapped an underlying cause, rather than being a validation error, infrastructure fault, or framework exception.

### Role in the Codebase

`BusinessLayerException` is the error contract of the `BusinessLayer` project (`BusinessLayer/BusinessLayerException.cs`). Its main producer is `BusinessLayer/UserService.cs`: when `UserService.AddUser` fails while saving a user, the method rolls back the transaction, logs the original error, and rethrows it wrapped in a `BusinessLayerException` — the code comment there ("only throw a BusinessException") marks this as an intentional rule for that service.

Downstream, `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs` catches `BusinessLayerException` explicitly in its save command. Note, however, that that catch block currently just does `throw;` — it rethrows unchanged, so today it distinguishes nothing yet; it is a placeholder for handling the business-layer failure separately from other exceptions. `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` constructs the exception directly (`new BusinessLayerException("Database connection failed", new Exception())`) and asserts that `SaveUserCommand` throws exactly this type, so the type is also part of the tested behaviour contract.

Removing this class would break `UserService`, `AddUserViewModel`, and the test project compilation, and more importantly remove the marker that lets callers tell business failures apart from other exceptions.

### Behavior & Details

The class has exactly one constructor:

```csharp
public BusinessLayerException(string message, Exception inner) : base(message, inner)
```

- It requires **both** a message and an inner exception. There is no parameterless or message-only constructor, so every `BusinessLayerException` carries the original fault as `InnerException`. Code that wants to throw it with no cause (as the test does) must explicitly pass one, e.g. `new Exception()`.
- The constructor does nothing but forward both arguments to the `Exception` base constructor. No state is added; there is nothing to serialize or configure beyond the standard exception members.

Because the only constructor demands an `inner`, this exception is exclusively a *wrapper*: it is meant to be thrown around a caught exception, never on its own.

### Rough edges

- `AddUserViewModel` catches `BusinessLayerException` and rethrows it with no additional handling, so the dedicated catch currently has no observable effect and the type's purpose of separating business failures is only realized at the `UserService` boundary.
- The class omits a `SerializationInfo`-based (deserialization) constructor, which is the conventional third constructor on a custom `Exception` subclass; `BusinessLayerException` therefore cannot be recreated by the serializer after crossing an AppDomain/assembly boundary.

*   **Repository Infrastructure:** The [RepositoryFactory](BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.md) manages the NHibernate session factory. It acts as a thin wrapper around the generic Hibernate factory, fixing the key type to `int`. # Common/Common.csproj

`Common/Common.csproj` — the MSBuild project file for the `Common` class library in `Demo.slnx`.

### Purpose

Build definition for the shared `Common` project. It targets `net10.0-windows` and is configured as a WPF project (`UseWPF`), so the project can reference WPF/XAML facilities even though it is a class library, not an application. It also enables nullable reference types and implicit usings.

The single package dependency is `System.ComponentModel.Composition` (v10.0.6), which provides the MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework) types used by `Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs` to discover and compose plugin assemblies at runtime. Note this package is referenced at the same version by several sibling projects (`Mvvm`, `Mvvm.Console`, `Mvvm.Wpf`, `Logging`, `UserManagement`) — the MEF-based plugin architecture spans the solution, and this file is the piece of it that lets the `Common` MEF helpers compile.

### Role in the Codebase

This is a build manifest, not application code. Removing it would drop the `Common` project from `Demo.slnx` and break the four projects that reference it (`ConsoleApp1`, `Mvvm`, `WinFormsApp1`, `WpfApp1`). It has no runtime behavior of its own.

### Relationships

- **Produces**: the `Common` assembly, containing the helpers under `Common/` (`Composition/CompositionHelper.cs`, `Reflection/AssemblyHelper.cs`, `Diagnostics/ExtendedGuard.cs`, `Converter/DebugConverter.cs`, `ExitCodes.cs`).
- **Consumed by**: `ConsoleApp1`, `Mvvm`, `WinFormsApp1`, and `WpfApp1` via project references.
- **External dependency**: the `System.ComponentModel.Composition` NuGet package — the only one.

### Behavior & Details

- `TargetFramework` is `net10.0-windows`, so the assembly can only load in Windows-targeted hosts; every dependent project inherits this constraint transitively.
- `UseWPF=true` pulls in WPF framework references for a library project, which is what allows this assembly to be shared with the WPF apps (`WpfApp1`, `Mvvm.Wpf` ecosystem) in the solution.
- Because the `System.ComponentModel.Composition` reference lives here as well as in the Mvvm/Logging/UserManagement projects, changing the MEF package version should be done consistently across all of those csproj files to avoid type-identity mismatches in the composition container.

### Rough edges

- The package pinning of `System.ComponentModel.Composition` is duplicated across at least six project files rather than centralized (e.g., via Directory.Packages.props), so version drift is easy.
- `UseWPF=true` on a shared class library makes WPF a hard build-time dependency for all four consuming projects, console or WinForms included.

### Purpose

`Common/ExitCodes.cs` defines the process exit codes the application returns when it cannot run. It exists so that the several application entry points in this solution report their outcomes with named, consistent values instead of bare integers, letting anything inspecting the process (a test harness, a supervisor, a developer reading a return code) tell "started fine" apart from "failed to start" without magic numbers.

### Role in the Codebase

The class lives in the `Common` project, the shared utility project every other project in the solution references. It is a small helper, not an architectural component: a `public static class` with three compile-time constants. Nothing else in `Common` depends on it; it only depends in the reverse direction — the host applications consume its constants when they must terminate.

If it were removed, the two hosts that reference it (`WinFormsApp1/Program.cs`, `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`) would fail to compile, since they reference the constants directly rather than hard-coding the numbers.

### Relationships

- **`Common/ExitCodes.cs`** (this file) — defines the constants in namespace `Common`. No imports, no base types.
- **`WinFormsApp1/Program.cs`** — the WinForms host's `Main` returns `ExitCodes.Ok` on successful module startup and `ExitCodes.Error` when module loading fails (`ReflectionTypeLoadException`) or no `IModuleController` is found.
- **`Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`** — the WPF host's `OnStartup` calls `Current.Shutdown(ExitCodes.Error)` in the same two failure cases.

`ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` is a host too but never references these constants; it signals failure by throwing instead of returning a code.

### Behavior & Details

Three constants, all compile-time (`const`), so their use in return statements and `Shutdown` calls is resolved at compile time:

- `Ok = 0` — the conventional "success" exit status, returned by `WinFormsApp1`'s `Main` after all modules have been initialized and started.
- `Error = -1` — a generic "startup failed" status, used when the MEF composition container cannot load module types or no module controllers were exported.
- `InsufficientPrivileges = -2` — currently defined but not referenced anywhere else in the repository. It is available for a host to return when it needs to distinguish a permission failure from a generic error, but no host does so today.

Two caveats worth knowing:

- The negative values are not what an OS process actually reports. On Windows, process exit codes are 32-bit unsigned values, so a process exiting with `-1` surfaces as `0xFFFFFFFF` (4294967295) and `-2` as `4294967294`. Any external code that checks the exit code must either compare against those wrapped values or treat "anything non-zero" as failure. Within the process, the constants are fine.
- Only `Ok` and `Error` are in use. The constant set is a fixed vocabulary — a new failure class (e.g. using `InsufficientPrivileges`) requires every host's failure paths to agree on which value to return, since the callers are not centralized.

### Rough edges

`InsufficientPrivileges` has no callers in the repository, so it is either reserved for a host that does not (yet) exist in this solution or dead code. There is no central place where a host maps a specific failure to one of these codes — each entry point picks the constant inline, so the vocabulary is only as consistent as the hosts' discipline.

### Purpose

The `Common` package serves as the shared foundation for the solution, housing low-level utilities, composition logic, and interop helpers that are consumed by all application hosts. Its contents belong together because they represent cross-cutting concerns—such as dependency injection bootstrapping, process exit semantics, and Windows-specific graphics conversion—that do not belong to a single feature but are required by the `Mvvm`, `WinForms`, and `Console` applications alike.

### Software Components

This directory contains source code organized into distinct utility clusters, each addressing a specific technical need.

**Composition and Bootstrap**
The [Composition](Common/Composition.md) subdirectory holds the entry-point logic for the application's plugin architecture. [CompositionHelper](Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.md) is the central actor here; it scans the application directory for assemblies and builds a MEF `CompositionContainer`. This allows host applications to resolve modules like `IModuleController` automatically at startup without manual registration.

**Reflection and Metadata**
The [Reflection](Common/Reflection.md) subdirectory provides [AssemblyHelper](Common/Reflection/AssemblyHelper.md), a static class for inspecting assembly metadata and file locations. It handles the verbose `System.Reflection` boilerplate, offering methods to retrieve company/product names and load application icons. Notably, `CompositionHelper` relies on this class to identify which files are valid assemblies.

**Windows Interop and Imaging**
The [Windows](Common/Windows/Media/Imaging.md) subdirectory contains [BitmapSourceHelper](Common/Windows/Media/Imaging/BitmapSourceHelper.md), which bridges GDI+ and WPF imaging formats. It converts `System.Drawing.Bitmap` objects into WPF `BitmapSource` instances and vice versa, handling the unmanaged memory management required for these conversions.

The [Diagnostics](Common/Diagnostics.md) subdirectory offers [ExtendedGuard](Common/Diagnostics/ExtendedGuard.md), a static utility for argument validation. It complements standard guard clauses with specific collection checks, such as asserting that a list does or does not contain a particular item. This is primarily used by the MVVM layer to enforce view-model registration rules.

Two standalone files handle specific, isolated responsibilities:
*   [DebugConverter](Common/Converter/DebugConverter.md) in [Converter](Common/Converter.md) is a WPF value converter that triggers a debugger break when invoked. It serves as a diagnostic tool for inspecting data bindings during development.

The dependency flow within the `Common` package is largely unidirectional, with utility components supporting the composition bootstrap.

# Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs

### Purpose

`CompositionHelper` is a static helper that builds a MEF (`System.ComponentModel.Composition`) `CompositionContainer` from all loadable assemblies next to the running application. It exists so that the application's modules can be discovered and wired up automatically at startup: instead of registering each export/import by hand, the container is populated from every `.dll` and `.exe` in the application directory (or its subdirectories), and the app then pulls out whatever it needs — in practice the `IModuleController` exports — from it.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is the composition bootstrap for the solution. It lives in `Common` and is consumed by the host applications:

- `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs` calls `CreateCompositionContainer(moduleAssemblies, ignoreAssemblies, searchOption)` in `OnStartup`, then resolves `IModuleController` exports, calls `Initialize()` and `Run()` on them, and disposes the container in `OnExit`.
- `WinFormsApp1/Program.cs` calls the no-argument overload in `Main` and follows the same module-controller pattern.
- `ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` calls it with an ignore list and resolves a specific view-model export (`IUserViewModel`) directly.

If it were removed, the hosts would have no way to assemble the container from the directory of assemblies, and module discovery would have to be replaced by explicit registration.

### Relationships

- Depends on `Common.Reflection.AssemblyHelper` (in `Common/Reflection/AssemblyHelper.cs`), used only for its `Extensions` constant, the `string[] { ".dll", ".exe" }` that determines which files in the directory are considered candidate assemblies.
- Everything else is from `System.ComponentModel.Composition.Hosting` (external, .NET's MEF): `AggregateCatalog`, `AssemblyCatalog`, `CompositionContainer`, `CompositionBatch`.
- The returned `CompositionContainer` is what all hosts use for `GetExportedValues<...>`; callers treat it as disposable (both hosts dispose it on shutdown).

### Behavior & Details

There are two parameterless/thin overloads that just delegate to the real implementation `CreateCompositionContainer(string[] moduleAssemblies, string[] ignoreAssemblies, SearchOption searchOption)`. All three share one behavior; the overloads only let callers skip the list(s) they don't need.

The full overload works in four stages:

1. **Collect candidate files.** It takes the directory of `Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly()` (i.e. the directory containing the `Common` assembly, which in practice is the application's output directory) and enumerates files matching `*` + each extension in `AssemblyHelper.Extensions` (`*.dll`, `*.exe`) using the given `searchOption` (`TopDirectoryOnly` by default, or `AllDirectories` if a caller wants subdirectories).

2. **Load and catalog each file.** For every file not in `ignoreAssemblies` (matched case-insensitively by file name), it calls `Assembly.LoadFrom`. Two bookkeeping rules apply:
   - If the loaded assembly's location is already in the catalog set, it throws `InvalidOperationException` ("Assembly ... is already loaded") — this throw is inside the per-file `try`, so it is caught and only printed to the console; the loop then moves on.
   - Otherwise it adds an `AssemblyCatalog` to the `AggregateCatalog` and records the assembly's location (lower-cased) in a `HashSet`.
   - Any other exception (a corrupt file, a bad assembly such as the `ConsoleApp1.exe` case in the sample, etc.) is also caught and its message is written to `Console.WriteLine` — a failing assembly is silently skipped from the container rather than aborting startup.

3. **Guarantee the Common and entry assemblies are present.** After the file scan, it adds the executing assembly and, if different, the entry assembly (`Assembly.GetEntryAssembly()`) to the catalog, again only if their locations aren't already recorded. This matters because the scan depends on the `Common` assembly sitting next to the executable, and the entry assembly's location can in edge cases not be one of the enumerated files.

4. **Load module assemblies and self-export the container.** For each name in `moduleAssemblies` it loads the assembly with `Assembly.LoadFrom` and adds it to the catalog. Note this stage is *not* in a try/catch: an unloadable module assembly, or one already present, throws `InvalidOperationException` and propagates to the caller. Finally it creates the `CompositionContainer`, adds the container itself as an exported value via a `CompositionBatch` (so other components can import the container), composes the batch, and returns the container.

A caveat worth knowing: `moduleAssemblies` entries are loaded with `Assembly.LoadFrom` but the catalog entry is built from the *name string*, not the loaded `Assembly` object (unlike the file-scan stage). The comment in the code refers to App.config as the source for module assemblies, but in the current code no caller actually passes a non-empty `moduleAssemblies` — `WpfApp1.App` inherits `MvvmApplication`'s parameterless constructor, so both arrays are empty in practice.

### Rough edges

- Failures in the file-scan loop are only written to the console (`Console.WriteLine`), which in a WPF app goes nowhere a user sees; a missing or broken module assembly can make exports silently absent until a later `GetExportedValues` fails or finds nothing.
- The "already loaded" `InvalidOperationException` thrown inside the `try` is swallowed by its own `catch`, so a genuine duplicate-assembly problem produces just a console line.

### Purpose

`DebugConverter` (`Common/Converter/DebugConverter.cs`) is a WPF `IValueConverter` used for debugging data bindings. When you attach it to a binding, every time the binding asks for a converted value, it logs the values in play and drops you into the debugger — so you can watch what's flowing through a binding you suspect is broken.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the only converter in the `Common/Converter` folder. It exists purely as a diagnostic aid: you temporarily point a binding at it (via a resource key), observe the binding traffic in the debugger, then remove it. It has no production behavior — both directions simply pass the value through unchanged.

### Relationships

- It implements `System.Windows.Data.IValueConverter` (a WPF/WindowsBase type), so it can be instantiated as a XAML resource and referenced from bindings.
- It is consumed from WPF views: `WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml` declares it as `<converter:DebugConverter x:Key="MyDebugConverter" />` and uses it in a binding, though the current usage on a `TextBox` is commented out. Callers are therefore XAML files that reference it by a static resource key.
- It uses `System.Diagnostics.Debug` for the log output.

### Behavior & Details

- `Convert(value, targetType, parameter, culture)`: writes a line to the debug output via `Debug.WriteLine` showing the bound value, target type, and parameter, then calls `Debugger.Break()`, then returns `value` unchanged. This is the side effect that makes the converter useful: if you don't have a debugger attached, the break is a no-op and the converter is just a pass-through.
- `ConvertBack(value, targetType, parameter, culture)`: returns the value as-is with no logging or breaking. So the converter only triggers when the binding pushes a value *to* the view, not when it reads back from the view.

Because the class is `public` with a parameterless constructor, it can be instantiated in XAML without any special registration.

# Common/Diagnostics/ExtendedGuard.cs

### Purpose

`ExtendedGuard` is a small static helper that asserts a collection does or does not contain a given item, throwing an `ArgumentException` when the assertion fails. It complements the preconditions in the third-party `CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics.Guard` class, which handles null/whitespace checks but offers no collection-containment checks.

### Role in the Codebase

It sits under `Common/Diagnostics`, the project's shared guard/argument-checking helpers, and is consumed from the Mvvm layer. It has no other dependencies. Removing it would break the child-ViewModel bookkeeping in `ViewModelBase` (below), which relies on it to detect double-registration and unregistration of unregistered view models.

### Relationships

The only in-repo caller is `Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs`:

- `ViewModelBase.RegisterChildViewModel` calls `ExtendedGuard.NotContains(_childViewModels, viewModel, nameof(viewModel))` before adding a child, so a view model cannot be registered twice.
- `ViewModelBase.UnregisterChildViewModel` calls `ExtendedGuard.Contains(...)` before removing a child, so you cannot unregister a view model that was never registered.

Both call sites combine it with `Guard.IsNotNull(viewModel)` from CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics.

### Behavior & Details

Two methods, both on the static class:

- `Contains<T>(ICollection<T> collection, T item, string name)` — throws `ArgumentException` if `collection` does not contain `item`.
- `NotContains<T>(ICollection<T> collection, T item, string name)` — throws `ArgumentException` if it does.

The `name` parameter is meant to identify the offending item in the error message for the caller's convenience. Both containment checks use `ICollection<T>.Contains`, so equality is whatever the item type's `Equals` does (for view models, reference equality by default).

### Rough edges

The thrown messages hard-code a literal `'{name}'` instead of interpolating the `name` argument (e.g. `"... does not contain '{name}'"`), so the parameter is accepted but never actually appears in the exception message. As written, the message gives no hint about which collection or item failed.

It lives in the `Common` project under `Common/Reflection/`, alongside `Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs` — a shared-infrastructure folder the rest of the solution (`Mvvm`, `Mvvm.Wpf`, `Mvvm.Winforms`, the app projects) builds on. It is a helper with no state, no construction, and no project-specific logic; every member is a pure function of the `Assembly` you hand it (or of the executing/entry assembly).

If it were removed, `CompositionHelper` and `MainViewModelBase` would break, and the metadata accessors would have to be re-implemented at every call site.

Dependencies are all framework: `System.Reflection`, `System.IO`, `System.Drawing`, `System.Text`. Nothing in this repository is referenced by `AssemblyHelper` itself.

- `Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs` uses `AssemblyHelper.Extensions` when enumerating `*.dll` and `*.exe` files next to the executing assembly to build its MEF `AggregateCatalog`.
- `Mvvm/MainViewModelBase.cs` calls `AssemblyHelper.LoadApplicationIcon()` in its constructor to set the WPF window's `Icon` from the entry assembly.

The attribute accessors (`GetAssemblyCompany`, `GetAssemblyProduct`, `GetAssemblyCopyright`, `GetAssemblyTrademark`, `GetAssemblyCulture`, `GetAssemblyVersion`, `GetAssemblyFileVersion`, `GetPublicKeyToken`) have no in-repository callers at present; they are a general-purpose API for whoever needs assembly metadata (about `AssemblyHelper` itself, or about assemblies loaded by `CompositionHelper`).

- **`GetAssemblyFileName(assembly)`** — returns `new Uri(assembly.Location).LocalPath`. This normalizes the location into a real file path rather than a `file:///` URI; it is the base for the other two file helpers.

- **`GetApplicationDirectory()`** — the directory containing the *executing* assembly's file. Note the nullable return: if the assembly has no resolvable location, `FileInfo`'s `DirectoryName` can be `null`, which is propagated.

- **`GetAssemblyFileExtension(assembly)`** — file extension of the assembly's location, e.g. `".dll"`.

- **`LoadApplicationIcon()`** — takes the *entry* assembly (`Assembly.GetEntryAssembly()`), not the executing one, and reads the embedded resource named `<entryAssemblySimpleName>.App.ico` via `GetManifestResourceStream`. The name is constructed from `assembly.GetName().Name + ".App.ico"`, so the resource name in your entry assembly must match its simple assembly name exactly (e.g. assembly `MyApp` → resource `MyApp.App.ico`). - **`GetAssemblyCompany` / `GetAssemblyProduct` / `GetAssemblyCopyright` / `GetAssemblyTrademark` / `GetAssemblyCulture`** — each reads one `Assembly*Attribute` with `Attribute.GetCustomAttribute` and returns the attribute's value, or `string.Empty` when the attribute is absent. - **`GetPublicKeyToken(assembly)`** — pulls `assembly.GetName().GetPublicKey()` and formats the whole public key as a lowercase hex string (two hex digits per byte, in order). Returns `string.Empty` if the assembly is not strong-named. Note this is the *public key*, not the key token — it is the long form, not the 16-byte token you typically see in a `.dll`'s identity.

- `GetAssemblyFileName` assumes `assembly.Location` is a file URI. For dynamically generated or in-memory-only assemblies, `Location` is `string.Empty` and `new Uri("").LocalPath` returns `""`; the downstream `FileInfo("").DirectoryName` would be `null` for `GetApplicationDirectory` and `GetAssemblyFileExtension` would throw. - `GetAssemblyVersion` and `GetAssemblyFileVersion` return the attribute's declared `Version` string, not the runtime `AssemblyName.Version` — for `AssemblyVersionAttribute` that is the same thing, but the implementation goes through the attribute rather than `assembly.GetName().Version`, so any subtle divergence (e.g. attribute not present but version still in metadata) would surface as `string.Empty`.

### Purpose

The `Common/Windows/Media/Imaging` directory serves as a bridge between GDI+ (`System.Drawing`) and WPF (`System.Windows.Media.Imaging`) image formats. It provides static utility methods to convert `Bitmap` objects to WPF `BitmapSource` instances and vice versa, allowing WPF UI elements to consume images generated by Win32 or GDI+ code without requiring callers to manage interop handles manually.

### Software Components

This directory contains a single source file: `BitmapSourceHelper.cs`. This file defines the `BitmapSourceHelper` class, a stateless static helper that encapsulates the plumbing for image format conversion.

The class exposes four primary entry points:
*   **`LoadImage`** and **`LoadBitmap(Bitmap)`**: Convert GDI+ images into WPF `BitmapSource` objects. The `LoadBitmap` method specifically uses `GetHbitmap` and `Imaging.CreateBitmapSourceFromHBitmap` to create the WPF object.
*   **`LoadBitmap(string)`** and **`LoadBitmap(Stream)`**: Load images directly from file paths or streams into WPF `BitmapSource` objects using `BitmapImage` with `CacheOption.OnLoad` to ensure the data is fully decoded and cached in memory.
*   **`SaveBitmap`**: Converts a WPF `BitmapSource` back into a GDI+ `Bitmap` by encoding the source to a BMP in a memory stream.

[BitmapSourceHelper.cs](Common/Windows/Media/Imaging/BitmapSourceHelper.md) is the only component here; it does not depend on other files in this directory but relies on standard .NET Framework/WPF libraries for the actual conversion logic.

### Relationships

`BitmapSourceHelper` acts as a leaf-level utility. It does not depend on other custom code within the repository, but it is consumed by higher-level components that need to display non-WPF native images in a WPF context.

For example, `Mvvm/MainViewModelBase` utilizes `BitmapSourceHelper.LoadBitmap` to load the application icon from an assembly resource and assign it to the window's `Icon` property. This pattern suggests that any module handling native icon resources or GDI+ generated thumbnails should route through this helper to avoid duplicating the `GetHbitmap`/`DeleteObject` interop logic.

The dependency flow is strictly one-way:
1.  Callers (e.g., ViewModels) request a conversion.
2.  `BitmapSourceHelper` performs the conversion using BCL APIs.
3.  The resulting WPF `BitmapSource` or GDI+ `Bitmap` is returned to the caller.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Caller"
        VM[Mvvm/MainViewModelBase]
    end

    subgraph "Common/Windows/Media/Imaging"
        BSH[BitmapSourceHelper]
    end

    subgraph "System Libraries"
        GDI[System.Drawing]
        WPF[System.Windows.Media.Imaging]
        Interop[System.Windows.Interop.Imaging]
    end

    VM -->|loads icon| BSH
    BSH -->|uses| GDI
    BSH -->|uses| WPF
    BSH -->|uses| Interop
```

### Rough edges

`BitmapSourceHelper.LoadBitmap(Bitmap)` creates a GDI handle via `GetHbitmap` but does not call `DeleteObject` to release it, resulting in a native handle leak for every conversion. Additionally, `SaveBitmap` forces all output to BMP format via `BmpBitmapEncoder`, which may not be desirable if the caller expects a different image format for the returned `Bitmap`.

# `Common/Windows/Media/Imaging/BitmapSourceHelper.cs`

### Purpose

`BitmapSourceHelper` is a small static class that converts images between GDI+ (`System.Drawing.Image` / `Bitmap`) and WPF's `BitmapSource` type system. WPF UI elements bind to `BitmapSource`; Win32/GDI+ icon and image code produces `Bitmap`. This class is the glue in both directions, so callers don't have to know the interop plumbing (`GetHbitmap`, `Imaging.CreateBitmapSourceFromHBitmap`, `BmpBitmapEncoder`) themselves.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a shared helper under `Common/Windows/`, the WPF-side of a cross-cutting `Common` namespace. It holds no state — every method is a pure conversion — and it is the only file in its directory. Callers that need to feed a `Bitmap`-based image into WPF, or round-trip a WPF image back to GDI+, go through it instead of repeating the conversion code.

### Relationships

- **Consumed by `Mvvm/MainViewModelBase`** — its constructor loads the application icon via `AssemblyHelper.LoadApplicationIcon()`, converts it with `BitmapSourceHelper.LoadBitmap(icon.ToBitmap())`, and assigns the result to the window's `Icon` property. That is the caller that makes the class's purpose concrete: getting a non-WPF image onto a WPF window.
- **System APIs it leans on** (all from the BCL / WPF, not the repo):
  - `System.Windows.Interop.Imaging.CreateBitmapSourceFromHBitmap` — the actual GDI+ → WPF bridge used by `LoadBitmap(Bitmap)`.
  - `BmpBitmapEncoder` / `BitmapFrame` — used by `SaveBitmap` to serialize a `BitmapSource` to PNG… specifically to BMP, in a memory stream.

### Behavior & Details

Four conversion entry points, all null-tolerant (a null input yields a null result except where noted):

- **`LoadImage(Image? source)`** — takes any GDI+ `Image` and wraps it in a `new Bitmap(source)` before delegating to `LoadBitmap(Bitmap)`. Use this when you only have an `Image` (e.g. from an icon handle) and don't need the `Bitmap` itself.

- **`LoadBitmap(Bitmap? source)`** — the core GDI+ → WPF conversion. It extracts the bitmap's HBITMAP handle via `GetHbitmap()` and hands it to `CreateBitmapSourceFromHBitmap` with an empty `Int32Rect` and `FromEmptyOptions()`. One caveat: `GetHbitmap()` returns a GDI handle that is never freed here (no corresponding `DeleteObject`), so callers that convert many images through this method should be aware each call leaks one HBITMAP until process exit.

- **`SaveBitmap(BitmapSource? source)`** — the reverse direction: encodes the `BitmapSource` as a BMP in a `MemoryStream`, rebuilds a GDI+ `Bitmap` from the stream, and wraps it once more in a fresh `Bitmap`. The double wrap discards the intermediate and guarantees an owned `Bitmap` rather than one still tied to the stream. The encoder is a `BmpBitmapEncoder`, so the intermediate representation is always BMP regardless of the source's native format.

- **`LoadBitmap(string filename)` / `LoadBitmap(Stream stream)`** — load a file directly into a WPF `BitmapSource`. These go through a different path than the `Bitmap` overloads: they construct a `BitmapImage` with `BeginInit`/`EndInit` and set `CacheOption = BitmapCacheOption.OnLoad`. That flag is important — it forces the full image data to be decoded and cached in memory during `EndInit`, so the returned `BitmapImage` no longer depends on the stream (or file) staying open. Note the file-based overload opens the stream with `File.OpenRead` inside a `using` block, so the file handle is released by the time the method returns, which is only safe because of the `OnLoad` cache option.

Two small asymmetries are worth knowing: the `Image`/`Bitmap` overloads are nullable-annotated and return `BitmapSource?`, while the `string`/`Stream` overloads declare a non-nullable `BitmapSource` and will throw (`FileNotFoundException` / `ArgumentException`) on bad input instead of returning null.

### Rough edges

- `LoadBitmap(Bitmap)` never releases the HBITMAP obtained from `GetHbitmap()` — a native handle leak per call (see above).
- `SaveBitmap` always routes through BMP encoding even when the caller might want a lossless format like PNG, so quality/format of the round-tripped image is fixed regardless of the `BitmapSource` it started from.

### Purpose

`ConsoleApp1/App.config` (path: `ConsoleApp1/App.config`) is the application configuration file for the `ConsoleApp1` host executable. It exists to supply the SQL Server connection string that the composition-based data layer needs at runtime.

### Role in the Codebase

The file holds a single `appSettings` entry, `ConnectionString`, pointing at a local SQL Server instance: `Server=localhost;Database=Users;Integrated Security=True;TrustServerCertificate=True;`. It is the runtime counterpart of the `BusinessLayer` and `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` projects: `ModelContext` in `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs` reads this exact key at construction time via `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings["ConnectionString"]` and hands it to `ModelContextBase`, which uses it to build the Hibernate session factory (`SessionFactoryBuilder`). Without this file — or without the `ConnectionString` key — `ModelContext` receives `null` (the code uses the null-forgiving operator `!` rather than checking) and the session factory build fails, so no part of the user-management demo in `ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` can run.

The same key and value are duplicated in `WinFormsApp1/App.config` and `WpfApp1/App.config`, which means each host application carries its own copy of the connection string rather than sharing one configuration source.

### Relationships

- **Consumer:** `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs` is the only reader of this key. It resolves the app settings through `System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager`, which picks up the entry from the active executable's `App.config`.
- **Downstream chain:** `ModelContextBase` (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/ModelContextBase.cs`) stores the string in its `ConnectionString` property; `HibernateRepositoryFactory` and `SessionFactoryBuilder` in the same project apply it to Hibernate's configuration.
- **Host:** `ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` builds a `CompositionContainer` via `CompositionHelper.CreateCompositionContainer(["ConsoleApp1.exe"])` (from `Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs`), which discovers exported parts from the loaded assemblies — including `ModelContext` — and triggers the config read. The console app itself never reads the config file directly.

### Behavior & Details

- The connection uses Windows integrated security (`Integrated Security=True`) against a `localhost` server and a database named `Users`; `TrustServerCertificate=True` skips TLS certificate validation, typical of a local development setup.
- The value is a plain literal with no `<connectionStrings>` section, environment-variable substitution, or per-environment overrides. Changing the database location means editing this key in every host's `App.config` that shares it.

The entry point of the console application — `Main` builds a MEF (Managed Extensibility Framework) dependency-injection container from the assemblies in the application directory, pulls in the user-management view models, and runs a small demo: it saves the same user 100 times, then loads all active users and prints each one to the console. # `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`

### Purpose

This interface defines the read-only query contract for repositories in the `DataAccessLayer` namespace. It exists so that the rest of the codebase can depend on a database-agnostic set of query operations rather than a specific ORM, letting `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` supply the Hibernate-based implementation.

### Role in the Codebase

`IRepository<TKey>` sits at the core of the data access abstraction. It is implemented by `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`, which extends it with write capability (`Save`) and a unit-of-work, so this interface is deliberately query-only. `IRepositoryFactory` in the same directory also constrains the repositories it hands out to this interface. If it were removed, the Hibernate layer and the factory contract would both lose their base contract.

Note the split in responsibilities: `IRepository<TKey>` covers reading, while `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` adds `Save<TEntity>` and `UnitOfWork`. Code that only reads entities can depend on `IRepository<TKey>` alone.

### Relationships

- **`IEntity<TKey>`** (same directory, `DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs`): the marker interface every entity must implement — a single `TKey Id { get; }` property. Every method here constrains `TEntity` to `class, IEntity<TKey>` on top of it.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepository<TKey>`**: the concrete implementation, reached through `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`, which adds `IDisposable` plus `Save` and `UnitOfWork` to this contract.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** and **`IRepositoryFactory`**: factories that produce repositories bound to this contract.
- **Callers**: `BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs` wires `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`, so the business layer is the layer that consumes repositories created from this contract.

### Behavior & Details

The generic parameter `TKey` (constrained to `struct`) is the identifier type for entities stored in this repository. The `in` (contravariant) variance declaration is unusual for an interface with no parameter-only positions; in practice it restricts assignability rather than adding flexibility, so do not rely on variance when substituting `TKey` types.

All seven members are constrained the same way: `TEntity : class, IEntity<TKey>`. There are no `TKey`-typed parameters on any member — `TKey` only flows through `TEntity`'s `Id`.

The methods group into three patterns:

- **Deferred queryables** — `GetQueryable<TEntity>(Expression<Func<TEntity, bool>> predicate)` and the parameterless `GetQueryable<TEntity>()`. These return `IQueryable<TEntity>`, so the expression tree is not evaluated at the call site; the consuming context (an active session in the Hibernate implementation) executes the query when it is enumerated or passed on to further LINQ operations. This is the escape hatch for callers who need to compose additional queries.
- **Single-result lookups** — `Single<TEntity>(criteria)`, `SingleOrDefault<TEntity>(criteria)`, and `FindOne<TEntity>(criteria)`. `Single` and `SingleOrDefault` follow the standard LINQ naming: `Single` returns `TEntity` (and throws if zero or more than one match), `SingleOrDefault` returns `TEntity?` (nullable, so it can represent "no match"). `FindOne` is a sibling of the same idea, also returning `TEntity?` — its distinction from `SingleOrDefault` is not encoded in the contract and lives in whichever implementation and calling convention the codebase uses.
- **Collection results** — `Find<TEntity>(criteria)` and `GetAll<TEntity>()`, both returning `IEnumerable<TEntity>`. `GetAll` has no predicate; `Find` narrows by expression.

Because the return types for `Find`, `GetAll`, and the `GetQueryable` overloads are `IQueryable`/`IEnumerable` rather than concrete lists, the interface does not commit to eager vs. deferred execution at this level — that depends on the implementation (the Hibernate-backed one) and on how the caller enumerates the result.

A few caveats worth knowing before you implement or extend this:

- No `IDisposable` here. `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` adds it, so code that holds a repository directly against `IRepository<TKey>` cannot dispose it — disposal is an `IHibernateRepository` concern.
- `TKey` is contravariant (`in`) despite never appearing in a parameter position. This is legal but almost certainly unintentional; treat it as if there were no variance modifier.
- `Single`/`SingleOrDefault`/`FindOne` overlap heavily; pick whichever name your implementation actually differentiates, rather than assuming the LINQ semantics for all three.

### Rough edges

- The `in` variance on `TKey` is unearned (no input positions) and may mislead readers about substitutability.
- `FindOne` and `SingleOrDefault` have near-identical signatures, and the interface gives no signal of how they differ in behaviour.
- No write path and no lifecycle (`IDisposable`) are part of this contract — a consumer holding only `IRepository<TKey>` cannot save or release resources; both live one layer down in `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`.

# DataAccessException.cs

`DataAccessLayer/DataAccessException.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `DataAccessException`, the exception type the data access layer uses to surface persistence failures. It exists so that consumers of the data access layer can distinguish "something went wrong talking to the data store" from any other kind of exception, without having to inspect underlying driver or ORM exceptions.

### Role in the Codebase

`DataAccessException` is the shared failure signal of the `DataAccessLayer` project. It is a thin marker exception with no logic of its own — its value is purely in the type. Callers that depend on data access can `catch (DataAccessException)` to handle any persistence-layer failure uniformly, regardless of which repository or provider produced it. If the class were removed, that catch point would disappear and callers would have to handle raw ORM/driver exceptions instead.

### Relationships

- `DataAccessException` inherits from `System.Exception` (the standard .NET exception base class); nothing beyond the constructor is overridden.
- It currently has one throw site in the repository: `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs` wraps any failure while building the Hibernate session factory with `throw new DataAccessException("Error initializing Hibernate repository factory", e)`, preserving the original failure as the inner exception.
- No code in the repository currently catches `DataAccessException`; today it is a one-directional contract — thrown by the data access layer, awaiting a consumer.

### Behavior & Details

The class has a single constructor, `DataAccessException(string message, Exception inner)`, which forwards both arguments straight to the base `Exception` constructor. Two consequences follow:

- **There is no parameterless constructor and no message-only constructor.** Callers must always supply a message and an inner exception. Code that wants to throw `DataAccessException` without an underlying cause (e.g. `throw new DataAccessException("msg")`) will not compile — adding such a constructor is a deliberate extension point if that ever becomes needed.
- **The original failure is preserved.** Because the second argument is always passed as the inner exception, the stack trace and message of the root cause (e.g. a SQL or NHibernate error) remain accessible via `InnerException` after the exception propagates up.

The class has no properties, state, or other members; serializing or inspecting it behaves exactly like a plain `Exception`.

Rough edges: the only constructor forces an inner exception to be present, which is fine for wrapping but makes the type awkward to use for purely programmatic data-access failures (validation, misconfiguration) where no underlying exception exists.

# DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs

## Purpose

`IUnitOfWork` is the provider-agnostic contract for managing database transactions in this codebase. It exists so that business logic (e.g., `UserService` in `BusinessLayer/`) can begin, commit, and roll back transactions without knowing which ORM or data access implementation is actually being used.

## Role in the Codebase

This file sits in the `DataAccessLayer` directory alongside other abstraction interfaces (`IRepository<TKey>`, `IRepositoryFactory`). It defines the transactional "unit" boundary for all data access: a caller starts a transaction, performs one or more repository operations, then commits or rolls back as a single atomic unit.

The concrete implementation is `HibernateUnitOfWork` (in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/`), which wraps an NHibernate `IStatelessSession`. A thinner sub-interface, `IHibernateUnitOfWork`, extends `IUnitOfWork` to add an overload of `BeginTransaction` that accepts an explicit `IsolationLevel`.

If this interface were removed, there would be no provider-agnostic way to express transactional boundaries, and callers would be forced to depend on the NHibernate-specific implementation directly.

## Relationships

- **Inherited by:** `IHibernateUnitOfWork` (DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateUnitOfWork.cs) — adds `BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel isolationLevel)`.
- **Implemented by:** `HibernateUnitOfWork` (DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateUnitOfWork.cs) — the only concrete implementation in the repository.
- **Exposed through:** `IHibernateRepository.UnitOfWork` property, which returns an `IHibernateUnitOfWork`.
- **Consumed by:** `UserService` (BusinessLayer/UserService.cs) calls `repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction()`, `CommitTransaction()`, and `RollBackTransaction()` to wrap user-save operations in a transaction.

`IUnitOfWork` itself extends `System.IDisposable` (standard .NET), so a unit of work is expected to release its underlying session/transaction resources when disposed.

## Behavior & Details

The interface declares four members:

| Member | Contract |
|---|---|
| `bool IsInTransaction { get; }` | Read-only flag: `true` when a transaction has been opened and not yet committed or rolled back. |
| `void BeginTransaction()` | Opens a new transaction. The `HibernateUnitOfWork` implementation starts with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted` by default and throws `InvalidOperationException` if a transaction is already open. |
| `void CommitTransaction()` | Commits the open transaction. Throws `InvalidOperationException` if no transaction is active. On failure, the implementation rolls back before rethrowing. |
| `void RollBackTransaction()` | Rolls back the open transaction. Throws `InvalidOperationException` if no transaction is active. |

### Typical usage pattern

```csharp
using var repository = _repositoryFactory.Create();
repository.UnitOfWork.BeginTransaction();
try
{
    await repository.Save(entity);
    repository.UnitOfWork.CommitTransaction();
}
catch
{
    repository.UnitOfWork.RollBackTransaction();
    throw;
}
```

Callers (such as `UserService.AddUser`) are responsible for the try/catch and for deciding whether to rethrow or wrap the exception. The unit of work itself does not swallow errors.

### Rough edges

- The `CommitTransaction` failure path in `HibernateUnitOfWork` calls `RollBackTransaction()`, but if that rollback also throws, the original exception is lost (the rollback exception propagates instead). This is an implementation detail outside this interface, but it is relevant to anyone relying on the "commit or throw" contract.
- `Dispose` on `HibernateUnitOfWork` sets `_isDisposed = true` only when a transaction existed at disposal time, which means calling `Dispose` twice with no transaction open leaves the flag unset. Again, this lives in the implementation, not the contract.

# DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs

### Purpose

This file defines `IEntity<TKey>`, the marker contract for anything the data access layer treats as an entity: a type that has an `Id` of a struct type. It exists so that the generic repository and unit-of-work types can constrain their `TEntity` parameters to "things with an identity" without knowing the concrete shape of each domain entity.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the base contract of the `DataAccessLayer` project, sitting next to the abstract base class `Entity<TKey>` (in `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs`) that implements it. Every repository operation in this project is gated on this contract — for example `IRepository<TKey>.GetQueryable<TEntity>(...)` and `FindOne<TEntity>(...)` in `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs` all declare `where TEntity : class, IEntity<TKey>`, as does `HibernateRepository` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`. If this interface were removed, those constraints and `Entity<TKey>`'s implementation clause would stop compiling.

### Relationships

- Implemented by `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs`'s `Entity<TKey>`, which is the abstract base class concrete domain entities are expected to derive from.
- Referenced as a generic constraint throughout `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`, `IRepositoryFactory.cs`, `IUnitOfWork.cs`, and the Hibernate implementation, so the data-access layer can be written once against any entity type.
- Callers are any domain model that needs persistence: a concrete entity either derives from `Entity<TKey>` or implements this interface directly (which requires supplying its own `TKey Id { get; }`).

### Behavior & Details

- `TKey` is constrained to `struct`, so keys must be value types — `int`, `Guid`, `long`, etc. No reference-type keys.
- The interface is declared `out TKey` (covariant), allowing an `IEntity<int>` to be used where `IEntity<...>` is expected, and permitting `Entity<TKey>` to implement it with a property that is readable.
- `Id` has a getter only. A type implementing this interface directly must expose a read-only identity; it cannot set it through the interface. `Entity<TKey>` fills that gap by giving derived classes a `protected set`.
- Being a marker-style interface (a single property), it carries no behaviour of its own — its value is entirely as a constraint that unifies the repository layer around one idea of "entity".

# `DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`

## Purpose

This interface defines the contract for a component that produces repository instances and can tear them down. It exists so that consumers of the data access layer can obtain repositories through a factory abstraction instead of instantiating them directly, which decouples business-layer code from the mechanics of opening sessions.

## Role in the Codebase

The interface is the top of a small inheritance chain in the `DataAccessLayer` project:

1. `IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>` (this file) — generic contract.
2. `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs` — binds `TRepository` to `IHibernateRepository<TKey>`, so callers only write `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`.
3. `IRepositoryFactory` in `BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs` — closes `TKey` to `int`, the application's actual key type.

The concrete implementation is `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`; the composed instance is `RepositoryFactory` in `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs`.

If this file were removed, both `IHibernateRepositoryFactory` and the generic binding it depends on would break, and the business layer's factory interface chain would have nothing to inherit from.

## Relationships

- **Extends nothing**; its constraint references `IRepository<TKey>` from `DataAccessLayer/IRepository.cs`, the generic query API (`GetQueryable`, `Single`, `Find`, `GetAll`, etc.) that created repositories implement.
- **Implemented (indirectly) by** `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`, which provides the `Create()` and `Drop()` implementations. Note that it implements `Create()` through an explicit interface-implementation cast (the line reading `IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>.Create()`), so this interface's members are what that file is answering to.
- **Consumers:** Business-layer services take the business-layer `IRepositoryFactory` (e.g., `UserService` in `BusinessLayer/UserService.cs` receives it via its constructor) and call `Create()` to get a repository.

## Behavior & Details

- **`Create()`** — returns a new `TRepository`. The concrete implementation opens a stateless NHibernate session per call, so each returned repository is independent and should be disposed by the caller.
- **`Drop()`** — intended to release anything the factory holds. In the only concrete implementation, `HibernateRepositoryFactory.Drop()`, this is currently `throw new NotImplementedException()`; no call site invokes it, so it is effectively a placeholder for future teardown.

Two caveats worth knowing before relying on this contract:

- **The `out` variance on `TRepository` is not actually honored.** `TRepository` is an output position (only a return type), so `out` looks right, but the constraint `where TRepository : IRepository<TKey>` puts it in an *in* position — generic variance in C# requires that no constraint on a covariant parameter reference the parameter, so this combination is not valid C# (the compiler rejects `where T : SomeInterface<out U>` for a covariant `U`). The code as written therefore signals that the variance attribute was likely added by mistake; it has no effect beyond the compiler error it implies.
- **`Drop()` is aspirational.** Since no implementation can actually honor it yet, do not design shutdown paths around calling `Drop()`.

## Rough edges

- The `out` variance modifier on `TRepository` conflicts with the `IRepository<TKey>` constraint and is not valid C# as written.
- `Drop()` has no working implementation anywhere (`NotImplementedException`), making half of the contract unusable.
