# `DataAccessLayer/Entity.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines `Entity<TKey>`, the abstract base class that gives every persisted entity in the system its identity. It exists so that all domain entities share a single, uniform `Id` property with a consistent contract, without each entity having to declare its own key.

### Role in the Codebase

`DataAccessLayer` is a small contract-and-abstraction project: interfaces for repositories (`IRepository.cs`, `IRepositoryFactory.cs`, `IUnitOfWork.cs`), the entity marker interface `IEntity<TKey>` (`IEntity.cs`), plus `DataAccessException` and `SortOrder`. This class is the concrete half of the entity-identity contract: `IEntity<TKey>` declares the interface, and `Entity<TKey>` is the base class real entities inherit from. If it were removed, concrete entities (e.g. `Entity.Hibernate/User.cs`, `User : Entity<int>`) would lose their shared `Id` implementation and would have to define keys individually.

### Relationships

- **`IEntity<TKey>`** (defined in `DataAccessLayer/IEntity.cs`) — the interface this class implements. It declares only `TKey Id { get; }` and has an `out` variance modifier, so `IEntity<int>` values flow into read-only collections and repository queries.
- **Subclasses in the entity projects** — e.g. `User : Entity<int>` in `Entity.Hibernate/User.cs` is the pattern: each concrete entity picks a struct key type and inherits `Id`.
- **`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepository.cs`** — the repository methods are constrained to `IEntity<TKey>` (the interface, not this class), so anything exposing an `Id` of the right key type works with the data-access layer, but this class is the intended way for entities to satisfy that constraint.

### Behavior & Details

- `Entity<TKey>` is abstract, so it can only be subclassed. The `where TKey : struct` constraint restricts key types to value types (e.g. `int`, `Guid`).
- The constructor is `protected` and sets `Id = default!` (the C# null-forgiving operator applied to `default(TKey)`, e.g. `0` for `int`). Subclasses must be constructible without arguments (see `User`'s comment about NHibernate requiring a parameterless constructor), and that requirement chains from here.
- `Id` is `public virtual` with a `protected set` — meaning only the class itself or derived classes can assign it, never application code or the repositories from outside the hierarchy. Declaring it `virtual` leaves room for a persistence provider or subclass to override the accessor if needed, though the known subclasses (`User`) do not.
- `[Serializable]` on the class marks it for binary/serialization compatibility, and `[Browsable(false)]` on `Id` keeps the key property out of designer/property-grid tooling.
- Nothing is stored or cached: there is no state beyond the key, no side effects, and no failure modes of its own. A new `User` therefore starts with `Id == 0` until the provider assigns a real key.

### Rough edges

`IEntity<TKey>`'s `Id` setter is intentionally absent, yet `Entity<TKey>` marks `Id` `virtual` — a derived class could in principle override the property with a public setter, breaking the "identity is not settable from outside" contract. Nothing in this codebase does so, but the compiler will not stop a subclass from doing it.

### Purpose

The `DataAccessLayer` project defines the abstract contracts for data persistence in this codebase. It provides the core interfaces for querying, managing transactions, and defining entity identities, allowing the application to remain decoupled from specific Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) providers.

These files belong together because they form a dependency-free foundation: they contain no logic, only definitions. By keeping the abstraction layer separate from implementation details (like NHibernate, which lives in `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate`), higher-level business logic can depend on these stable contracts without needing to know how the data is actually stored or retrieved.

### Software Components

This directory contains four distinct functional areas, all defined as interfaces or base types to enforce loose coupling:

**Entity Identity**
This group defines what counts as a "entity" for the persistence layer.
*   [IEntity](DataAccessLayer/IEntity.md) (`IEntity.cs`): The marker interface requiring a read-only `Id` of type `TKey`.
*   [Entity](DataAccessLayer/Entity.md) (`Entity.cs`): The abstract base class that implements `IEntity`, providing a standard `Id` property that concrete domain models (like `User`) inherit from.

**Querying**
This group defines how data is retrieved.
*   [IRepository](DataAccessLayer/IRepository.md) (`IRepository.cs`): The primary read-only contract. It exposes methods for finding single entities (`FindOne`, `Single`) and collections (`Find`, `GetAll`), as well as `IQueryable` access for composed LINQ queries. It is strictly query-oriented; it does not include save or delete operations.

**Factory & Lifecycle**
This group defines how repositories are instantiated.
*   [IRepositoryFactory](DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.md) (`IRepositoryFactory.cs`): The contract for creating and dropping repository instances. It abstracts the creation of stateless sessions, ensuring that each repository instance is independent.

**Transactions & Errors**
This group defines operational control and failure signaling.
*   [IUnitOfWork](DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.md) (`IUnitOfWork.cs`): The contract for managing transactional boundaries (`Begin`, `Commit`, `Rollback`). It ensures that business operations can be treated as atomic units regardless of the underlying provider.
*   [DataAccessException](DataAccessLayer/DataAccessException.md) (`DataAccessException.cs`): A wrapper exception type that standardizes how persistence errors are propagated to consumers, hiding the underlying ORM/driver specifics.
*   [SortOrder](DataAccessLayer/SortOrder.md) (`SortOrder.cs`): A simple enum (`Ascending`/`Descending`) intended as a shared vocabulary for sorting, though it is currently unused by the other interfaces in this directory.

### Relationships

The components in this directory form a strict dependency hierarchy where the factory produces repositories, repositories expose the unit of work, and all entities conform to the entity contract.

`IRepositoryFactory` is the entry point for consumers. It creates instances of `IRepository` (specifically `IHibernateRepository` in the concrete layer). Once a repository is created, it exposes an `IUnitOfWork` instance, which the caller uses to wrap database operations in a transaction. All query methods in `IRepository` and the identity checks in `IEntity` rely on the `TKey` generic parameter being a `struct`, ensuring consistent key handling across the layer.

`DataAccessException` acts as the unified error boundary. While defined here, it is typically thrown by the concrete Hibernate implementations to wrap lower-level driver errors, allowing business layers to catch a single type for all persistence failures.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph DataAccessLayer
        EF[IRepositoryFactory]
        ER[IRepository]
        EU[IUnitOfWork]
        EI[IEntity]
        EC[Entity]
        EX[DataAccessException]
        SO[SortOrder]
    end

    EF -->|Creates| ER
    ER -->|Exposes| EU
    EC -->|Implements| EI
    ER -.->|Constrains TEntity| EI
    EX -.->|Thrown by| EF
```

*Note: `SortOrder` is currently isolated from the other components in this directory as no interface currently accepts it as a parameter.*

### Rough edges

*   `IRepositoryFactory` includes a `Drop()` method that has no working implementation in the concrete layers, making it effectively unusable for shutdown logic.
*   `SortOrder` is defined but not referenced by any other interface or class in this directory, leaving its intended usage ambiguous.

- [DataAccessLayer.csproj](DataAccessLayer/DataAccessLayer.md)
- [Entity.cs](DataAccessLayer/Entity.md)
- [IEntity.cs](DataAccessLayer/IEntity.md)

# DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepositoryFactory.cs

### Purpose

This file defines `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`, the contract for a factory that produces Hibernate-based repositories. It exists to give callers a stable interface for requesting NHibernate-backed repositories while hiding the session factory and configuration details inside the concrete implementation.

### Role in the Codebase

It is the Hibernate-specific factory contract inside the `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate` namespace. The generic, engine-agnostic contract is `IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>` in `DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`, which declares `Create()` and `Drop()` and constrains `TRepository` to `IRepository<TKey>`. This interface specializes that contract to the Hibernate repository type, so the business layer can ask for a factory without depending on any concrete data-access implementation.

### Relationships

- **`IRepositoryFactory<TRepository, TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`): the base interface. It declares `Create()` and `void Drop()`. This interface inherits both; `Drop()` carries over unchanged, and `Create()` is hidden via `new` with a more specific return type of `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` instead of the base `TRepository` type argument.
- **`IHibernateRepository<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/IHibernateRepository.cs`): the repository type returned by `Create()`. It extends `IRepository<TKey>` and `IDisposable` and adds `Save<TEntity>` and a `UnitOfWork` property.
- **`HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`** (`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateRepositoryFactory.cs`): the concrete implementation. It builds the NHibernate `ISessionFactory` in its constructor, and its `Create()` returns a `HibernateRepository<TKey>` wrapping a stateless session. Because `TRepository` is an out-variance (`out TRepository`) position, that implementation satisfies this interface.
- **`BusinessLayer.IRepositoryFactory`** (`BusinessLayer/IRepositoryFactory.cs`): a non-generic marker interface that simply extends `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<int>`. This is the form the business layer would actually hold and resolve, so this interface is what business-layer code indirectly depends on.

### Behavior & Details

- `TKey` is constrained to `struct`, matching the base `IRepositoryFactory`.
- The `new IHibernateRepository<TKey> Create()` declaration **hides** rather than overrides the base `Create()` (interfaces cannot override). A caller holding an `IHibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` reference gets the specific `IHibernateRepository<TKey>` return type; a caller holding only the base `IRepositoryFactory<IHibernateRepository<TKey>, TKey>` reference gets the base return type and must cast if it wants the Hibernate-specific members like `Save` or `UnitOfWork`.   - `GetQueryable()` — unfiltered, as `IQueryable`.

  - `Find` — deferred filtered `IEnumerable`; `FindOne` — `FirstOrDefault`, so null on no match rather than an exception.

### Purpose

`DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/HibernateUnitOfWork.cs` defines `HibernateUnitOfWork`, the NHibernate-backed unit of work for this data access layer. It wraps a single `IStatelessSession`'s transaction lifecycle — begin, commit, rollback, dispose — so repository consumers can bracket their database operations in a transaction without dealing with NHibernate's `ITransaction` directly.

### Role in the Codebase

This is the concrete `IUnitOfWork` implementation for the NHibernate persistence layer, paired with the sibling `HibernateRepository<TKey>` in the same directory. The repository's `UnitOfWork` property creates it on demand: `_unitOfWork ??= new HibernateUnitOfWork(_session)` — i.e., each repository instance lazily creates one unit of work over the stateless session the factory (`HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>`) opened for it. If removed, `HibernateRepository`'s `UnitOfWork` property and `IUnitOfWork` would have no concrete implementation to hand out.

### Relationships

- **`IHibernateUnitOfWork`** (same directory): the interface this class implements. It extends `IUnitOfWork` (defined in `DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs`, which declares `IsInTransaction`, `BeginTransaction()`, `RollBackTransaction()`, `CommitTransaction()`, and `IDisposable`) and adds one member, `BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel isolationLevel)`.
- **`IUnitOfWork`** (`DataAccessLayer/IUnitOfWork.cs`): the base interface; its members are implemented verbatim here.
- **`IDataAccessLayer.Hibernate.HibernateRepository<TKey>`**: the main caller — it owns a `readonly IStatelessSession` and passes it to the unit of work's constructor.
- **NHibernate** (external library): the `IStatelessSession` and `ITransaction` types and their `BeginTransaction`/`Commit`/`Rollback` semantics come from the NHibernate assembly, not this repository.

### Behavior & Details

- **Constructor** takes an `IStatelessSession` and stores it. No transaction is started at construction time; one must call `BeginTransaction` first.
- **`BeginTransaction()`** delegates to the overload with `IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted`.
- **`BeginTransaction(IsolationLevel)`** calls `_session.BeginTransaction(isolationLevel)` and stores the result in `_transaction`. It throws `InvalidOperationException` if a transaction is already running, so at most one transaction can be active per unit of work.
- **`CommitTransaction()`** commits, then releases (disposes and nulls) the transaction. If the commit throws, it rolls back and rethrows the original exception — the rollback here is defensive cleanup around a failed commit.
- **`RollBackTransaction()`** throws `InvalidOperationException` when no transaction is running; otherwise it rolls back and releases the transaction.
- **`IsInTransaction`** is simply `_transaction != null`, so it is true from the call to `BeginTransaction` until commit or rollback completes.
- **`Dispose()`** is virtual. Note that it only disposes the current transaction — it does not roll it back. A disposed unit of work with an uncommitted transaction therefore silently discards it; nothing is rolled back on the database. It also does not clear `_transaction` to null afterward, and `_isDisposed` is only set when a transaction was pending at disposal time.

### Rough edges

- The `CommitTransaction` pre-check error message says "Cannot roll back a transaction..." even though the method commits — a copy/paste leftover that will mislead anyone reading the exception.
- `Dispose()` does not set `_isDisposed` when no transaction is active, and it doesn't null `_transaction`, so `_isDisposed` and the actual state of the object are not reliably consistent.
- The class is not thread-safe, and `_transaction` has no `volatile`/locking; this is fine as long as each unit of work is confined to one thread of use, but nothing enforces that.

**Path:** `DataAccessLayer.Hibernate/SessionFactoryBuilder.cs`

## Purpose

`SessionFactoryBuilder` is a static helper that builds an NHibernate `ISessionFactory` from a connection string and a list of mapping-assembly names. It is intended as a shared factory for the session infrastructure that repositories (`HibernateRepository<TKey>`) and the unit of work depend on.

In practice, it is currently dead code: `BuildSessionFactory` is not called anywhere in the repository. The same configuration is instead duplicated inline in the constructor of `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` (via the `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs` → `BusinessLayer/RepositoryFactory.cs` chain, where `IModelContext.ConnectionString` and `MappingAssemblies` are passed to the factory's constructor). If you want new code to use this class, nothing stops you from calling `SessionFactoryBuilder.BuildSessionFactory(...)` directly — it is public. If you remove the file, nothing breaks today, but the duplicated configuration in `HibernateRepositoryFactory` remains the only working path.

- Depends on external libraries only: Fluent NHibernate (`Fluently.Configure()`, `MsSqlConfiguration.MsSql2012`), NHibernate (`ISessionFactory`, `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver`), and `NHibernate.Tool.hbm2ddl.SchemaUpdate`. No other project file is referenced.
- `mappingAssemblies` are resolved at runtime with `Assembly.Load(mappingAssembly)`, so the entries are assembly names, not file paths. The live counterpart in this codebase passes `["Entity.Hibernate"]` (see `BusinessLayer/ModelContext.cs`), so the mapping assemblies contain Fluent NHibernate maps such as `UserMap`.

1. Configures the database with `MsSqlConfiguration.MsSql2012`, the supplied `connectionString`, `MicrosoftDataSqlClientDriver`, and `ShowSql()` (SQL statements are logged to the console/stdout).
2. For each name in `mappingAssemblies`, loads the assembly and adds its Fluent mappings via `FluentMappings.AddFromAssembly`.
3. Runs `SchemaUpdate(cfg).Execute(false, true)` through `ExposeConfiguration`. This auto-updates the database schema to match the mappings on every build — the `true` flag means updates are executed, `false` means no script is written to disk.

- The entire Fluent NHibernate configuration is duplicated between `SessionFactoryBuilder.BuildSessionFactory` and the `HibernateRepositoryFactory<TKey>` constructor, and only the factory's copy is actually used by the application. **Path:** `Dto/UserDto.cs`

### Purpose

`UserDto` is the plain data object (DTO) that carries user information across the project's layer boundary. It exists so the UI and business layers exchange user data without depending on the persistence layer's `User` entity directly.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a data model in the `Dto` namespace, sitting alongside its contract, `IUser` (`Dto/IUser.cs`). It has no logic of its own — no methods, no validation — and is constructed, read, and passed around by other layers.

- **Implements `IUser`** (`Dto/IUser.cs`), which declares `FirstName` and `LastName`. The `Id` property here is an addition beyond the interface — the interface only captures the name fields.
- **Consumed by the business layer:** `IUserService.GetActiveUsers()` (`BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`) returns `List<UserDto>`, and `AddUser(UserDto user)` accepts one. - **Produced by the UI layer:** `AddUserViewModel` (`UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`) builds a `UserDto` from form input and passes it to `UserService.AddUser`.

- `Id` is an `int`, set by the persistence layer (populated when `UserService` maps an entity in `GetActiveUsers`). Callers should treat it as read-only — `AddUser` ignores it when creating the entity.

`UserDto` implements `IUser`, which only declares `FirstName` and `LastName`, so the `Id` property is invisible through the interface. Any code taking an `IUser` (e.g. to display or persist a user) has no way to get the `Id` without casting back to `UserDto`.

It acts as the neutral middle ground between the UI and business layers, ensuring that the presentation and service tiers exchange user data without depending directly on the persistence layer's entities. The contents are grouped together because the data types (like `UserDto`) and their validation logic (`Validation/`) are tightly coupled and consumed jointly by the higher-level features.

# Dto/Validation/UserValidator.cs

### Purpose

`UserValidator` is a FluentValidation validator for `IUser` (`Dto/IUser.cs`). It encodes the one business rule the user-management feature has for user data: both the first name and the last name must be non-empty. It exists so that UI viewmodels can check user input against a shared, reusable rule set instead of hand-rolling checks.

### Role in the Codebase

It lives in the `Dto` assembly under `Validation/`, next to the `IUser` and `UserDto` types it validates. It is a leaf helper with no other responsibilities — no entry point, no state, no side effects. Nothing breaks at compile time if it is removed, but the viewmodels that construct it (see below) lose their input validation.

### Relationships

- **Base type:** `AbstractValidator<T>` from the FluentValidation library (external, third-party). Inheriting it is all that's required to make this validator usable through `IValidator<IUser>`.
- **Validated type:** `IUser` from `Dto/IUser.cs`, which defines exactly two properties: `FirstName` and `LastName`. The class also implements it, via `UserDto` in `Dto/UserDto.cs`, so the validator applies to both.

Any other viewmodel can do the same.

The constructor declares two rules:

- `RuleFor(x => x.FirstName).NotEmpty().WithMessage("Firstname is required.")`
- `RuleFor(x => x.LastName).NotEmpty().WithMessage("Lastname is required.")`

The `ValidateProperty` overload also relies on FluentValidation's `IncludeProperties` option, so the property names in the rules must match the viewmodel's property names — `FirstName` and `LastName` do.

- The rules only cover `FirstName` and `LastName`, but the base class's `HasErrors` property is `Count != 0` over the whole dictionary of property names — combined with the base's `ValidateAllProperties` clearing it first, that's consistent, but note `HasErrors` alone (without a prior `ValidateAllProperties`) would report stale errors from a previous `ValidateProperty` call for a different property. This file is the Fluent NHibernate mapping for the `User` entity. It exists to tell NHibernate how the `User` domain object (defined in `Entity.Hibernate/User.cs`) corresponds to a relational table in SQL Server, so that the ORM can read and write `User` records transparently.

It also runs `SchemaUpdate` against the configuration, so the `Users` table and its columns are created/updated automatically at startup based on the rules in this class. If this mapping were removed, `User` entities could no longer be persisted or loaded through NHibernate, and schema auto-update would no longer manage the `Users` table.

- **`ClassMap<User>`** (FluentNHibernate.Mapping, external library): the base class whose constructor body is the mapping itself. The `Map`, `Id`, and `Table` calls are Fluent NHibernate's fluent API.

# `Logging/ILoggingService.cs`

### Purpose

This interface is the project's logging contract. It extends `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger` with a set of convenience methods so callers can write a log line in one call — `logger.LogWarning("Failed to save {Id}", id)` — without building an `EventId`, choosing a level-specific `ILogger.Log` overload, or wrapping anything. The reason it exists alongside `ILogger` is ergonomics: `ILogger` only exposes the generic `Log<TState>(LogLevel, EventId, TState, Exception?, formatter)` method, which is awkward to call by hand. This interface turns "log this at this level, maybe with this exception" into a directly callable method for each level.

### Role in the Codebase

`ILoggingService` is the abstraction that the rest of the application logs through; `Logging/LoggingService.cs` is its concrete implementation (backed by Serilog, writing to a rolling daily file and to the debug console). The interface is injected via MEF — `LoggingService` is marked `[Export(typeof(ILoggingService))]` — and the consuming classes declare an `ILoggingService LoggingService { get; set; }` property and import it.

Callers found in the repository that depend on it:

- `BusinessLayer/UserService.cs` (via `BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`) — e.g. `LoggingService.LogError(e, "Error saving user")` in its save path
- `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs` (via `IAddUserViewModel`)
- `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs` (via `IShowUsersViewModel`)

If the interface were removed, those classes could no longer declare their logger dependency, and the MEF export/import contract between `LoggingService` and its consumers would break.

### Relationships

- **Base type:** `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILogger` (from the Microsoft.Extensions.Logging package, not this repo). That is why the interface must also be implemented for `Log<TState>`, `IsEnabled`, and `BeginScope<TState>` — those come from `ILogger` and are satisfied by `LoggingService` delegating to its internal `ILogger`, not by the convenience methods declared here.
- **Implementation:** `Logging/LoggingService.cs` (`LoggingService : ILoggingService`).
- **Dependency injection:** MEF (`System.ComponentModel.Composition`). The `[Export(typeof(ILoggingService))]` on `LoggingService` and the `ILoggingService` properties on the consuming classes are how it is wired up.
- **Callers** assign messages and exceptions directly, e.g. `LoggingService.LogError(e, "Error saving user")`, which maps to the `LogError(Exception?, string?, params object?[])` overload.

### Behavior & Details

The interface declares no state or logic — it is purely a set of method signatures — but the shape of those signatures is the contract the whole codebase programs against.

For each of the six `LogLevel` values — `LogTrace`, `LogDebug`, `LogInformation`, `LogWarning`, `LogError`, `LogCritical` — there are four overloads, varying in which optional pieces a caller supplies:

1. `(EventId eventId, Exception? exception, string? message, params object?[] args)` — full form
2. `(EventId eventId, string? message, params object?[] args)` — with an event id but no exception
3. `(Exception? exception, string? message, params object?[] args)` — with an exception but no event id
4. `(string? message, params object?[] args)` — message only

`message` uses standard string-formatting placeholders (`{0}`, `{1}`, …) filled by `args`, the same convention as the underlying `ILogger`. All parameters except `message` are nullable; a caller may pass `null` for the exception, the event id, or even the message.

In addition, three `Log` overloads take the `LogLevel` explicitly for cases where the level is not fixed at compile time: `Log(LogLevel, string?, params object?[])`, `Log(LogLevel, EventId, string?, params object?[])`, and `Log(LogLevel, Exception?, string?, params object?[])`.

Because it extends `ILogger`, a consumer of this interface can also use the generic `Log<TState>(LogLevel, EventId, TState, Exception?, Func<TState, Exception?, string>)`, `IsEnabled(LogLevel)`, and `BeginScope<TState>(TState)` — the implementation delegates those to its inner Serilog-backed `ILogger`.

One thing to note for maintainers: the overload sets are not uniform across the `Log` family — the explicit-level `Log` overloads lack the `(LogLevel, EventId, Exception?, string?, …)` combination, so a caller wanting both an event id and an exception at a dynamic level must drop down to the inherited `ILogger.Log<TState>` form.

### Rough edges

- The four-overload pattern is repeated six times, one per level, and the explicit-level `Log` overloads omit a few combinations (e.g. no `EventId` + `Exception` variant). Adding a new combination requires touching both the interface and `LoggingService`.
- `message` is typed `string?` yet the methods are used as format strings; there is no `IFormatProvider`/culture parameter, so formatting follows the default culture.

### Purpose

`Mvvm/IModuleController.cs` defines `IModuleController`, a three-method lifecycle contract for application modules: `Initialize()`, `Run()`, and `Shutdown()`. Its job is to give every UI host in this solution (the WinForms and WPF apps) one common way to discover and drive all application modules without the host knowing what any specific module does.

### Role in the Codebase

This is a small contract interface in the `Mvvm` project, which holds the shared MVVM abstractions (`IViewModel`, `IMainViewModel`, `IMessageService`, `ViewModelBase`, and so on). `IModuleController` is the module-discovery seam of the whole application: hosts find modules by querying the MEF `CompositionContainer` for exports of this type, then drive them in a fixed order.

The enforced lifecycle is two-phase:

1. `Initialize()` is called on every module first — modules can set up resources, wire dependencies, etc.
2. `Run()` is called on every module only after all modules have initialized, so one module may rely on another's initialized state.
3. `Shutdown()` is called at exit, in the reverse order of the controllers, so dependents tear down before their dependencies.

If this interface were removed, both hosts (`WinFormsApp1/Program.cs` and `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs`) would have no way to enumerate or start the application's modules.

### Relationships

- **Implementations:** `WinFormsApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs` and `WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs` both implement the interface and are registered with MEF via `[Export(typeof(IModuleController))]`. Both make all three methods `virtual`, so a concrete app can derive from `DefaultModuleController` and override the lifecycle steps (e.g. add `Initialize()` work) instead of implementing the interface from scratch.
- **Consumers:** `WinFormsApp1/Program.cs` resolves `[.. _container.GetExportedValues<IModuleController>()]` in `Main()` and calls `Initialize()` on all controllers, then `Run()` on all controllers. `Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs` does the same in `OnStartup`, and additionally calls `Shutdown()` on `ModuleControllers.Reverse()` in `OnExit`.
- **No other dependencies:** the interface has no imports beyond the `Mvvm` namespace it belongs to.

### Behavior & Details

The interface itself contains no logic; the behavior comes from the convention its consumers implement:

- Resolution happens once at startup. Both hosts treat a failed resolution (`ReflectionTypeLoadException`) as fatal — they print the loader exceptions and exit with an error — and they also treat "zero controllers found" as an error rather than starting an empty application.
- Controllers are stored in array order. That order is whatever MEF returns, so there is no explicit way to prioritize one module over another; the reverse-order shutdown simply mirrors that order.
- The WinForms host (`Program.cs`) never calls `Shutdown()`. `Application.Run` blocks inside `Run()` and the process exits when the main form closes, so teardown of modules is left to process termination. Only the WPF host performs the `Shutdown()` pass, in `OnExit`.

### Rough edges

`Shutdown()` is part of the contract, but the WinForms host never invokes it — any cleanup work a WinForms module puts in `Shutdown()` silently never runs.

### Purpose

`Mvvm/ValidatableViewModelBase.cs` defines `ValidatableViewModelBase<T>`, an abstract base class for ViewModels whose properties are validated with [FluentValidation](https://fluentvalidation.net/) and whose error state is surfaced to the UI through the standard WPF/WinForms `INotifyDataErrorInfo` contract. It exists so that a ViewModel doesn't have to hand-roll error bookkeeping: the class holds the current validation errors, fires `ErrorsChanged` when they change, and lets derived ViewModels call `validator.Validate(...)`-backed helpers directly.

### Role in the Codebase

It lives in the `Mvvm` project, which holds the framework-level ViewModel plumbing (`ViewModelBase`, this class) shared by the UI front-ends in `Mvvm.Wpf`, `Mvvm.Winforms`, and `Mvvm.Console`. A concrete ViewModel that wants property validation inherits from it and passes in a FluentValidation validator via the primary constructor — for example `AddUserViewModel : ValidatableViewModelBase<IUser>(new UserValidator())` in `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`.

The comment at the top of the class notes that this is an example base class, and that for projects that already use CommunityToolkit.Mvvm's own validation, `ObservableValidator` can be used instead.

### Relationships

- **Base class:** `ViewModelBase` (defined in `Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs`), which itself derives from CommunityToolkit.Mvvm's `ObservableObject` and implements `IViewModel`. Inherited from `ViewModelBase`: `INotifyPropertyChanged` plumbing, design-mode detection, and child-ViewModel registration. Inherited from `ObservableObject`: the `ObservableObject` API. This class adds the `INotifyDataErrorInfo` interface, which is not implemented by `ViewModelBase`.
- **External dependency:** `FluentValidation.IValidator<T>` and its `Validate`/`ValidationResult` types.
- **Callers:** any ViewModel that wants `INotifyDataErrorInfo`-driven validation. In this repo, `AddUserViewModel` is the current example.

### Behavior & Details

The class is generic over the object type `T` being validated and receives a single `IValidator<T>` through its primary constructor. Derived classes pass in their concrete validator, e.g. `new UserValidator()` for `IUser`.

State is a single dictionary: `Dictionary<string, List<string>> _errors`, keyed by property name, holding the list of error messages for that property.

`INotifyDataErrorInfo` is implemented as follows:

- `GetErrors(propertyName)` — returns the list of messages for that property, or an empty enumerable. A `null` property name (the contract's "give me all errors" call) also returns an empty enumerable; see Rough edges.
- `HasErrors` — true as long as `_errors` is non-empty, i.e. as long as any property currently has at least one error.
- `ErrorsChanged` — the standard event; raise it after mutating `_errors` so the UI re-queries `GetErrors`/`HasErrors`.
- `OnErrorsChanged(DataErrorsChangedEventArgs)` — protected helper that wraps the event invocation so derived classes don't have to null-check.

The two validation entry points are:

- `ValidateAllProperties(T obj)` — clears `_errors` and runs `validator.Validate(obj)` over every rule. For each failed property, it appends the message into `_errors[propertyName]` and raises `ErrorsChanged` for that property. Because it starts by clearing, it's the right helper to call before a "save" action: it gives a fresh, whole-object result.
- `ValidateProperty(T obj, string propertyName)` — runs `validator.Validate(obj, options => options.IncludeProperties(propertyName))` so only rules for that property execute. If valid, the property's entry is removed from `_errors`; if not, the entry is replaced with the fresh list of messages. `ErrorsChanged` is raised for the property either way.

A typical derived ViewModel calls `ValidateProperty(this, nameof(Prop))` from an `OnPropChanged` hook and `ValidateAllProperties(this)` before a save, then checks `HasErrors` to decide whether to proceed — exactly what `AddUserViewModel` does in `SaveUserAsync`.

### Rough edges

- `GetErrors(null)` returns an empty enumerable. The `INotifyDataErrorInfo` contract documents the `null` argument as "return errors for all properties"; the `HasErrors` property exists as the substitute, and WPF's data-error template binding uses `GetErrors` per property, so this is workable, but consumers who call `GetErrors(null)` expecting every error will come back empty-handed.
- `ValidateProperty` only re-evaluates rules attached to the one property passed in. A FluentValidation rule that compares two properties (e.g. "confirm password must match password") won't be picked up here even when the other property changes — only `ValidateAllProperties` will exercise it. Callers have to know which rules cross properties and call `ValidateAllProperties` for those cases.

# Mvvm/DisposableViewModelBase.cs

### Purpose

`DisposableViewModelBase` is the abstract base class for ViewModels that own `IDisposable` resources (timers, subscriptions, sockets, and similar) and need them released deterministically when the ViewModel goes away. It supplies the classic dispose pattern — a public `Dispose()`, a `Dispose(bool)` that derived classes can override, a `Disposables` collection, a `CheckIfDisposed()` guard, and a `Disposed` event.

### Role in the Codebase

It sits in the `Mvvm` folder alongside the rest of the ViewModel base class family: `ViewModelBase`, `ValidatableViewModelBase<T>`, and `MainViewModelBase`. It is a mixin of the "lifecycle" concern into the inheritance chain, rather than a parallel hierarchy: a concrete ViewModel that needs disposal would derive from this class, gaining both `ViewModelBase` behaviour and disposal support.

Currently no class in the repository derives from it (its only references are its own declaration and finalizer), so it appears to be infrastructure in place for future ViewModels. Its contract is also exposed through `IDisposableViewModel`, so views or other infrastructure can depend on that interface rather than the concrete class.

### Relationships

- Extends `ViewModelBase` (defined in `Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs`), which itself extends CommunityToolkit.Mvvm's `ObservableObject` and implements `IViewModel`. Everything inherited from `ViewModelBase` — design-mode detection, child ViewModel registration, `OnClosing`/`OnClosed` — is available unchanged here.
- Implements `IDisposableViewModel` (defined in `Mvvm/IDisposableViewModel.cs`), a marker interface that is simply `IViewModel, IDisposable`. That is what makes the `Dispose()` call here the interface implementation.
- Callers would be concrete ViewModels deriving from this class, and any code holding an `IDisposableViewModel` reference and calling `Dispose()` on it.

### Behavior & Details

- Registering resources: add any `IDisposable` to the `Disposables` collection (a protected, read-only `Collection<IDisposable>`). When disposal runs, every entry is disposed in collection order. The base class does not clear or deduplicate the collection; that is left to whoever adds entries.
- Disposal sequence in `Dispose(bool)`:
  1. No-op entirely if `IsDisposed` is already `true` — disposal is idempotent.
  2. If `disposing` is `true` (explicit `Dispose()` call), dispose every item in `Disposables`. If `false` (finalizer path), managed disposables are deliberately left alone.
  3. Set `IsDisposed = true`.
  4. Raise `Disposed`.
- `Dispose()` calls `Dispose(true)` then `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)`, so the finalizer won't run for explicitly disposed instances.
- The finalizer calls `Dispose(false)`, covering only the unmanaged path — there is no actual unmanaged-resource hook in the base, so it exists purely so a future derived override has the full pattern to work with.
- `CheckIfDisposed()` throws `ObjectDisposedException` (named after the concrete runtime type) if called after disposal. Derived classes are expected to call it at the top of methods that touch released resources; nothing in the base enforces that.
- `IsDisposed` is public but has a private setter, so it can be observed from views but only changes via the dispose path. `[Browsable(false)]` hides it from design-time property grids.

### Rough edges

`Disposed` is raised after `IsDisposed` has already been set, so any handler that reacts to the event by calling back into the ViewModel will find `IsDisposed` already `true`, and handlers that run `CheckIfDisposed()` from within `Disposed` will throw.

### Purpose

**Mvvm/IViewModel.cs** — `Mvvm.IViewModel` is the root marker interface for every view model in this codebase. It exists to give the framework a single type that identifies "this is a view model" and to guarantee that all view models raise `INotifyPropertyChanged` so the UI bindings update automatically.

The interface has no members of its own; its entire substance is its base, `INotifyPropertyChanged` (the .NET BCL type `System.ComponentModel.INotifyPropertyChanged`). Implementing `IViewModel` therefore commits a class to exposing `PropertyChanged`, and that's the whole contract.

### Role in the Codebase

This interface is the root of the view-model type hierarchy in the `Mvvm` project, which is the shared MVVM framework layer that the `Mvvm.Wpf`, `Mvvm.Winforms`, and feature projects (e.g. `UserManagement`) all build on.

The concrete inheritance chain below it:

- `ViewModelBase` (abstract, `Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs`) implements `IViewModel` and inherits property-change support from the CommunityToolkit `ObservableObject`.
- `MainViewModelBase` and `DisposableViewModelBase` extend `ViewModelBase`; `ValidatableViewModelBase<T>` extends it as well and adds `INotifyDataErrorInfo`.

If `IViewModel` were removed, the abstract bases could still function through `ObservableObject` alone, but code that resolves or filters "any view model" by type would lose its common denominator. - **Depends on:** only `System.ComponentModel.INotifyPropertyChanged` — a .NET framework type, no project dependencies.
- **Extenders within this project:** `ViewModelBase`, plus via interface inheritance `IMainViewModel` and `IDisposableViewModel`.
- **Transitive implementers (callers/users):** feature view models such as `UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs` (`UserViewModel : MainViewModelBase, IUserViewModel`) and `ShowUsersViewModel : ViewModelBase, IShowUsersViewModel`. Anyone in the app layer that wants a uniform reference to "a view model" — for DI, lifecycle handling, or child-view-model bookkeeping — would program against `IViewModel`.

# `Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines a single enum, `MessageResult` — a platform-neutral type that represents the outcome of a yes/no-style question shown to the user. It exists so that the abstractions in the `Mvvm` core project can specify a question's return type without depending on any GUI framework, whose own result enums (`MessageBoxResult` in WPF, `DialogResult` in WinForms) differ from each other.

### Role in the Codebase

It is a small shared data type in the core `Mvvm` project, alongside the `IMessageService` interface that consumes it. It makes no decisions itself; it only names the possible outcomes of a question. If it were removed, `IMessageService`'s three `Show...Question` methods and every `MessageService` implementation could no longer compile, because they use `MessageResult` as their return type.

### Relationships

- **`IMessageService`** (same folder, `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`) declares `MessageResult ShowYesNoCancelQuestion(...)`, `ShowYesNoQuestion(...)`, and `ShowOkCancelQuestion(...)` as its question-returning methods. Callers of that interface use this enum to branch on the user's answer.
- **Implementations** in the satellite projects — `Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs`, `Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs`, and `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs` — cast their platform-specific dialog results to `MessageResult` and return them. The console implementation throws `NotImplementedException` for all three question methods, so this enum is only meaningful in GUI contexts.

### Behavior & Details

The members mirror the WinForms `DialogResult` values 0–7 (`None`, `OK`, `Cancel`, `Abort`, `Retry`, `Ignore`, `Yes`, `No`) plus `TryAgain = 10` and `Continue = 11`, which match the numeric values of `System.Windows.Forms.DialogResult`. That alignment is deliberate: the WinForms implementation simply does an unchecked cast `(MessageResult)MessageBox.Show(...)` and gets a correctly-named member for every `DialogResult` the message boxes can return.

The WPF implementation casts `MessageBoxResult` values (`No`, `Cancel`, `OK`) into this enum; those three values exist here with matching numeric values, so the cast is safe.

Practically, callers only ever observe the subset returned by the interface's three methods: `Yes`/`No`/`Cancel` from `ShowYesNoCancelQuestion`, `Yes`/`No` from `ShowYesNoQuestion`, and `OK`/`Cancel` from `ShowOkCancelQuestion`. The remaining members (`None`, `Abort`, `Retry`, `Ignore`, `TryAgain`, `Continue`) exist only to keep the numeric values cast-compatible with `DialogResult`; no method in this codebase can currently produce them.

### Rough edges

The WinForms implementations rely on an unchecked cast between a WinForms enum and this one. Any `DialogResult` member with a numeric value that is not a member of `MessageResult` would round-trip as a silently "wrong" value, and the cast breaks if either enum's values ever change. Today the values line up, but nothing in the code enforces that.

# `Mvvm/IView.cs`

## Purpose

This file defines `IView`, the root of the view-side contract in this repository's hand-rolled MVVM framework. Its single member, `object? DataContext { get; set; }`, gives the framework a platform-neutral way to attach a view model to a view: the view model is carried as a plain `object?` rather than a typed reference, because `IView` must be implementable by both WPF (`Window`) and WinForms (`Form`), and neither UI framework's base type can reference the other.

## Role in the codebase

`IView` is the base marker for the view interface hierarchy in the `Mvvm` project:

- `IDialogView<TDialogResult>` extends it and adds `DialogResult`, `Show()`, `Close()`, and `Closing`/`Closed` events.
- `IMainView<TDialogResult, TDimension>` extends `IDialogView` and adds `Left`/`Top`/`Width`/`Height`.

Any view in the repository that participates in the framework ultimately derives from `IView` through one of those. It is a shared contract rather than an implementation: removing it breaks the interface hierarchy and therefore every view class (`UserForm` in `WinFormsApp1`, `UserView` in `WpfApp1`) and the module controllers that consume them.

## Relationships

- **Consumed by views:** `UserForm` (`WinFormsApp1/View/UserForm.cs`) implements `IMainView<DialogResult, int>`; `UserView` (`WpfApp1/View/UserView.xaml.cs`) implements `IMainView<bool?, double>`. Both are exported via MEF (`[Export(typeof(IMainView<...>))]`) and composed by each app's `DefaultModuleController`.
- **`DataContext` is not a pure contract member.** For the WPF side it is inherited from `Window`; for the WinForms side, `UserForm` *overrides* `object? DataContext` from `Control` and uses the setter as the hook where it wires up its `DataBindings` and event handlers via `SetupBindings`. So in practice, setting `DataContext` on a view is the framework's mechanism for handing the view model to the view and triggering its bindings.

## Behavior & Details

There is no behavior in this file — it is a single-member interface with no default implementations. The one thing worth knowing:

- `DataContext` is nullable and untyped. View implementations are expected to cast it to their specific view model type inside the setter (as `UserForm` does with `(IUserViewModel?)value`). Nothing in the framework validates the type at the contract level; a wrong type surfaces only inside the implementing view.

## Rough edges

- `IView`'s `DataContext` collides with framework members: `WinForms.Control` and WPF's `UIElement` already define `object? DataContext`/`object DataContext`. Implementations therefore inherit or override members with the same name and signature from different base classes; `UserForm` must explicitly `override` the WinForms version. This works today but makes the interface's contract partially determined by whichever UI framework's base type the implementer chooses, which is invisible to anyone reading `IView` alone.

# `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`

### Purpose

This file defines the `IMessageService` interface, the contract for showing modal message boxes (information, warning, error, and yes/no-style questions) from MVVM code. It exists so that view models can display user-facing dialogs without referencing a specific UI framework: the same call site works whether the app is hosted in WPF, Windows Forms, or a console.

### Role in the Codebase

This interface is the abstraction at the top of a small messaging subsystem. The core `Mvvm` namespace holds only the contract (this file plus the `MessageResult` enum in `Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`); the concrete behavior lives in separate projects, one per host UI: `Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs`, `Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs`, and `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs`. Each of those classes is marked `[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]`, so the composition container (MEF) injects the implementation that matches the host UI. If this interface were removed, none of the three implementations could exist and every view model using `[Import] public IMessageService MessageService { get; set; } = null!;` would stop compiling.

### Relationships

- **Implementations** (each exports this type to the MEF container): `MessageService` in `Mvvm.Wpf`, `MessageService` in `Mvvm.Winforms`, `MessageService` in `Mvvm.Console`.
- **Consumers**: view models obtain it via MEF composition, for example `AddUserViewModel` in `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`, which calls `MessageService.ShowError(...)` when validation fails.
- **Tests**: `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` substitutes a `Mock<IMessageService>` (Moq) for the real service.
- **`MessageResult`**: the return type of the three question methods, defined in `Mvvm/MessageResult.cs` as an enum mirroring Win32 message-box results (`OK`, `Cancel`, `Yes`, `No`, ...).

### Behavior & Details

The interface groups nine methods in three pairs-plus-one, all with the same shape: a fire-and-forget method and one or two question methods.

- **`ShowMessage(string message)` / `ShowMessage(string message, string caption)`** — informational dialog. The caption-less overload delegates to the two-argument one; implementations supply a default caption (e.g. `"Message"` in the WPF version).
- **`ShowWarning(...)`** — same pattern, warning icon; the single-argument overload uses a default caption such as `"Warning"`.
- **`ShowError(...)`** — same pattern, error icon; default caption `"Error"`.
- **`ShowYesNoCancelQuestion(string message, string caption)`** — returns a `MessageResult` telling the caller which button was pressed; the implementation preselects `Cancel` as the default button.
- **`ShowYesNoQuestion(string message, string caption)`** — `Yes`/`No` buttons, `No` preselected.
- **`ShowOkCancelQuestion(string message, string caption)`** — `OK`/`Cancel` buttons, `Cancel` preselected.

Two conventions are worth knowing before writing against this interface:

1. **The question methods always take both `message` and `caption`.** Unlike the notification methods, there are no caption-less overloads for questions, so call sites must supply both arguments.
2. **Question results are compared against `MessageResult` values, not `bool`.** For example a caller checking a yes/no answer tests for `MessageResult.Yes` explicitly; a `Cancel` or click-away is any other value. This matters because all three implementations cast the platform's native result to `MessageResult`, so the enum values line up with the user's actual button choice.

Because the interface is platform-neutral and mocked in unit tests, view models should be written against it only — never directly against `System.Windows.MessageBox` or `System.Windows.Forms.MessageBox`.

Rough edges: the `MessageResult` enum includes values the interface can never return for its three question methods (`None`, `Abort`, `Retry`, `Ignore`, `TryAgain`, `Continue`), since it mirrors the full Win32 set. That is harmless, but a reader should not expect any of those values from a call to this interface.

# Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs

### Purpose

`ViewModelBase` is the abstract root of the application's MVVM view-model hierarchy. It exists so that every view model can share three concerns without each one re-implementing them: change notification (inherited from the CommunityToolkit `ObservableObject`), a parent–child view-model tree that propagates closing/closed events, and a reliable way to know whether the code is running inside the WPF designer.

### Role in the Codebase

This class is the base layer of the Mvvm folder's inheritance ladder:

- `DisposableViewModelBase`, `MainViewModelBase`, and `ValidatableViewModelBase<T>` all derive directly from `ViewModelBase` and add disposal, main-window handling, and FluentValidation support respectively.
- Concrete application view models can derive from it directly (e.g. `ShowUsersViewModel` in `UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs` does).

It is the piece the rest of the Mvvm infrastructure hangs on: `MainViewModelBase` specifically relies on its `IsInDesignMode` check to skip hooking up the window, and on `OnClosing()`/`OnClosed()` as the closing pipeline it drives from the main window's `Closing` event. Removing this class would break every base class and view model in the project.

### Relationships

- **Inherits `ObservableObject`** (CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, external library): provides property-change notification; concrete view models use its `[ObservableProperty]` support.
- **Implements `IViewModel`** (defined in `Mvvm/IViewModel.cs`): a marker interface that is itself empty except for extending `INotifyPropertyChanged`.
- **`Common.Diagnostics.ExtendedGuard`** (defined in `Common/Diagnostics/ExtendedGuard.cs`): supplies the `Contains`/`NotContains` guard methods; this file also uses the standard `Guard` from CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics.
- **Callers**: the other abstract bases in this folder and all concrete view models that extend them indirectly inherit the child-VM registration and design-mode detection described below.

### Behavior & Details

**Design-mode detection.** `IsInDesignModeStatic` lazily computes once and caches the result in the static `_isInDesignMode`. It reads WPF's standard `DesignerProperties.IsInDesignModeProperty` default value, and additionally treats any process whose name starts with `devenv` (Visual Studio) as design mode, since the designer property can report false while a live preview runs inside `devenv`. Once cached the value never changes, so a process that starts outside the designer will always report `false`. The instance property `IsInDesignMode` is a plain passthrough to the static member.

**Child view-model tree.** Each view model keeps a `List<ViewModelBase>` of registered children:

- `RegisterChildViewModel(viewModel)` adds a child, guarding that the argument is non-null and that it is not already registered (`ArgumentException` in either case).
- `UnregisterChildViewModel(viewModel)` removes a child, guarding that the argument is non-null and that it actually is registered.

**Closing pipeline.** Both methods are `protected virtual` and are intended to be driven by `MainViewModelBase`, which hooks `Application.Current.MainWindow.Closing` and calls them:

- `OnClosing()` folds the children's results with a *bitwise* AND (`&`), so every child's `OnClosing()` is always evaluated — even after one child has already returned `false` — and the result is `false` if any child refuses to close. A view model that needs to veto closing (for example to prompt for unsaved changes) overrides this to return `false`.
- `OnClosed()` walks the registered children in order and calls each child's `OnClosed()`, so cleanup hooks fire recursively through the whole tree.

Note that `MainViewModelBase.OnClosing(CancelEventArgs)` sets `e.Cancel = true` when the pipeline returns `false`, and calls `OnClosed()` only after the window actually closes. There is no automatic cleanup of the `_childViewModels` list — children must be unregistered explicitly, and `OnClosing()`/`OnClosed()` operate on whatever is currently registered.

**Registration invariant.** The guards enforce that a child appears in exactly one parent's list for its lifetime: registering twice or unregistering a child that was never registered throws `ArgumentException`.

### Rough edges

- `ExtendedGuard`'s error messages use `ArgumentException("...'{name}'...")`, but the `name` argument passed by `ViewModelBase` (`nameof(viewModel)`) is never interpolated, so the message literally reads `'{'name'}'`.
- `OnClosed()` has no counterpart that prunes the child list, so after a child view model is disposed the parent still holds a reference to it and will still call into it on the next close.

# Mvvm/IMainViewModel.cs

### Purpose

`IMainViewModel` is the contract for the main window's view model. It marks a view model as the one bound to the application's main window, and — beyond ordinary view-model behaviour — gives controllers the ability to close that window or shut the whole application down with an exit code. It exists so that host-specific code (module controllers in the WPF and WinForms host apps) can drive the application's lifecycle through an interface rather than a concrete view model class.

### Role in the Codebase

This interface is a small piece of the shared `Mvvm` namespace — the cross-platform view-model layer consumed by both host applications. It defines the role, not the behaviour: the only implementation is `MainViewModelBase` (in `Mvvm/MainViewModelBase.cs`), an abstract class that app-specific main view models derive from. Removing it would break every module controller in the host apps, which all depend on this type (see below).

### Relationships

- **Extends `IViewModel`** (defined in `Mvvm/IViewModel.cs`). `IViewModel` itself extends `INotifyPropertyChanged` and declares no members, so inheriting it simply marks this type as a change-notifying view model. `IMainViewModel` adds the window-lifecycle surface on top.
- **Implemented by `MainViewModelBase`** (`Mvvm/MainViewModelBase.cs`), which itself extends `ViewModelBase` (in `Mvvm/ViewModelBase.cs`). The interface is the point through which consumers see those implementations.
- **Consumed by the module controllers** in the host applications, which are composed via MEF:
  - `WinFormsApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs` receives `IMainViewModel` through its `[ImportingConstructor]`, stores it in `MainViewModel`, and assigns it as `MainView.DataContext`.
  - `WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController.cs` does the same.
  - App-specific view models advertise themselves as implementations with `[Export(typeof(IMainViewModel))]` (e.g. `UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`), which is what the MEF composition matches against.

### Behavior & Details

The interface declares one property and two methods:

- `ImageSource? Icon` — the window icon as WPF imaging. `MainViewModelBase` fills it in from the application's executable icon (via `AssemblyHelper.LoadApplicationIcon` and `BitmapSourceHelper.LoadBitmap`); it stays `null` if no icon loads, hence the nullable type.
- `CloseWindow()` — closes the main window. In `MainViewModelBase` this calls `Application.Current?.MainWindow?.Close()` and is a no-op in design mode. Note this goes through the window's `Closing` event, so a view model can still cancel the close (the base class routes it through `OnClosing`).
- `Shutdown(int exitCode)` — shuts down the whole application, propagating `exitCode`. In `MainViewModelBase` this calls `Application.Current?.Shutdown(exitCode)`.

One caveat for anyone relying on this contract: both methods depend on `Application.Current` at call time (WPF's `Application`, specifically). The interface does not say how the current `Application` is reached, and the base implementation's behaviour — and its no-op in design mode — is an implementation detail callers shouldn't need to know but do in practice.

### Purpose

The `Mvvm` project serves as the framework-agnostic core of the application's MVVM architecture. It provides the abstract base classes, interfaces, and shared types that define how ViewModels behave, how Views connect to them, and how application modules communicate with the user interface.

The contents belong together because they form the contract layer between the business logic (feature modules like `UserManagement`) and the specific UI technologies (WPF or WinForms). By centralizing the `ViewModelBase` hierarchy, the `IView` contract, and the `IMessageService` abstraction here, the project ensures that feature code remains testable and UI-agnostic, while the host applications only need to implement the specific glue code for their respective frameworks.

### Software Components

The components in this directory group into three functional layers:

**View-Model Base Hierarchy**
The foundation of the library is the inheritance chain starting at [ViewModelBase](Mvvm/ViewModelBase.md). It extends CommunityToolkit's `ObservableObject` to provide property change notification, design-mode detection, and a parent-child tree structure for managing nested ViewModels. Derived from this are three specialized bases:
*   [ValidatableViewModelBase](Mvvm/ValidatableViewModelBase.md) adds support for `FluentValidation` and surfaces errors via `INotifyDataErrorInfo`.
*   [DisposableViewModelBase](Mvvm/DisposableViewModelBase.md) implements the standard dispose pattern for ViewModels that manage unmanaged or external resources.
*   [MainViewModelBase](Mvvm/MainViewModelBase.md) handles the lifecycle of the application's main window, including icon loading and shutdown logic.

**View and ViewModel Contracts**
The interfaces define the boundary between the model and the view:
*   [IViewModel](Mvvm/IViewModel.md) is the root marker interface for all ViewModels, extending `INotifyPropertyChanged`.
*   [IMainViewModel](Mvvm/IMainViewModel.md) adds window-specific controls like `CloseWindow()` and `Shutdown()` to the ViewModel contract.
*   [IDisposableViewModel](Mvvm/IDisposableViewModel.md) marks ViewModels that must be explicitly disposed.
*   [IView](Mvvm/IView.md) defines the minimal view contract, primarily through the `DataContext` property which serves as the binding point for the ViewModel.
*   [IDialogView](Mvvm/IDialogView.md) and [IMainView](Mvvm/IMainView.md) extend `IView` with specific behaviors for dialogs and the main application window, respectively.

**Messaging and Module Lifecycle**
*   [IMessageService](Mvvm/IMessageService.md) abstracts the UI framework's message boxes, allowing ViewModels to display warnings, errors, and questions without referencing WPF or WinForms types directly.
*   [MessageResult](Mvvm/MessageResult.md) is an enum that standardizes the return values of user interactions (Yes/No/Cancel) across different UI frameworks.
*   [IModuleController](Mvvm/IModuleController.md) defines the lifecycle contract (`Initialize`, `Run`, `Shutdown`) for application modules, allowing hosts to start and stop features uniformly.

### Relationships

The dependency structure follows a strict layering: concrete application code depends on these abstractions, but these abstractions do not depend on the specific UI host. The `ViewModelBase` class is the central hub; it implements `IViewModel` and is the parent to the specialized bases. For instance, a concrete ViewModel like `UserViewModel` might derive from `MainViewModelBase` (which derives from `ViewModelBase`) and implement `IMainViewModel`.

The messaging subsystem relies on the [MessageResult](Mvvm/MessageResult.md) enum to translate platform-specific results into a common type. The `IModuleController` interface is the entry point for the host applications (WPF/WinForms), which use MEF to discover and drive the lifecycle of these modules. The `Common` project is a dependency for `Mvvm` (specifically for `ExtendedGuard` in `ViewModelBase`), but no other external dependencies exist within the `Mvvm` project itself beyond the NuGet packages for CommunityToolkit and FluentValidation.

### Purpose

`Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs` is the WinForms implementation of the cross-platform `IMessageService` interface. It wraps `System.Windows.Forms.MessageBox` so that view-models in the framework-agnostic `Mvvm` project can display messages, warnings, errors, and yes/no questions without ever touching WinForms types directly. The class is exported to MEF (`[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]`), so a container composes it into dependent view-models at runtime.

This is one of three interchangeable platform implementations of `IMessageService` in this repository — `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs` and `Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs` do the same job for console and WPF hosts. A host application picks one by referencing the matching project.

### Role in the Codebase

The `Mvvm.Winforms` project is a thin adapter layer. It targets `net10.0-windows` with `UseWindowsForms` enabled and references only the `Mvvm` project. Its entire purpose is to satisfy the `IMessageService` contract with WinForms' `MessageBox`. If it were removed, WinForms applications consuming this library would have no composable `IMessageService` to display dialogs.

### Relationships

- **`Mvvm.IMessageService`** — the interface this class implements (defined in `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`). All nine methods here are required by that contract.
- **`Mvvm.MessageResult`** — the enum returned by the question methods (defined in `Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`). Its values are deliberately numbered identically to WinForms' `MessageBoxButtons` enum, which is why the methods here can cast `MessageBox.Show`'s return value directly to `MessageResult`.
- **MEF consumers** — any view-model with an `[Import]` of `IMessageService` (e.g. `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`, which has an `IMessageService MessageService` property) receives this instance when the WinForms host composes the container.

- **Informational methods** (`ShowMessage`, `ShowWarning`, `ShowError`) each call `MessageBox.Show` with `MessageBoxButtons.OK` and the corresponding icon (`None`, `Warning`, `Error`). The single-argument overloads supply default captions: `"Message"`, `"Warning"`, `"Error"`.

- All methods are synchronous and block the UI thread while the dialog is open, as is standard for WinForms `MessageBox`.

# Mvvm.Wpf/MvvmApplication.cs

## Purpose

`MvvmApplication` is the base `Application` class for WPF hosts of this codebase's MVVM framework. It exists so a WPF app's `App` class (see `WpfApp1/App.xaml.cs`, which is literally `public partial class App : MvvmApplication` with no body) gets a full application lifecycle for free: composition-container creation, module discovery via MEF, ordered module startup, teardown on exit, and a global exception policy — without any of that code appearing in the consuming app.

It's the WPF counterpart of what `WinFormsApp1/Program.cs` and `ConsoleApp1/Program.cs` do imperatively (both call `CompositionHelper.CreateCompositionContainer(...)` and drive the same `Initialize()` → `Run()` → `Shutdown()` sequence themselves).

## Role in the Codebase

The `Mvvm.Wpf` project is a small library (this file plus `MessageService.cs`) that WPF applications reference. `MvvmApplication` is the piece an app plugs into by making its `App.xaml` root element `mvvm:MvvmApplication` (as `WpfApp1/App.xaml` does) and its code-behind derive from it. The app then supplies behaviour through ME

F exports in its own assemblies rather than code in `App`. Removing it would force every WPF host to re-implement container creation, the two-phase module start, reverse-order shutdown, and the exception handlers.

## Relationships

- **`System.Windows.Application`** (WPF framework type) — the base class. `MvvmApplication` adds nothing visible to WPF itself; it only overrides `OnStartup` and `OnExit` and adds constructors.
- **`Common.Composition.CompositionHelper`** (`Common/Composition/CompositionHelper.cs`) — builds the `CompositionContainer`. It scans the folder containing the *Common* assembly for files with assembly extensions, skips names in `ignoreAssemblies` (case-insensitive), and additionally loads whatever is passed in `moduleAssemblies` via `Assembly.LoadFrom`. A container failure here is caught and only `Console.WriteLine`d, so a WPF app gets no UI feedback from it.
- **`Mvvm.IModuleController`** (`Mvvm/IModuleController.cs`) — the contract with the app's modules: `Initialize()`, `Run()`, `Shutdown()`. Modules opt in with `[Export(typeof(IModuleController))]`, e.g. `WpfApp1/Controller/DefaultModuleController` (which in `Run()` shows the main view, and in `Shutdown()` closes it).
- **`Common.ExitCodes`** (`Common/ExitCodes.cs`) — supplies `ExitCodes.Error` (-1) for the two fatal startup paths.
- **Consumers** — WPF app `App` classes derived from it (the `App` in `WpfApp1`), typically via XAML, since WPF instantiates `Application` from XAML rather than from a constructor call.

## Behavior & Details

**Constructors.** The primary constructor takes `string[] moduleAssemblies`, `string[] ignoreAssemblies`, and an optional `SearchOption` (default `TopDirectoryOnly`), all stored as properties. The two public overloads delegate with an empty `moduleAssemblies`; one takes no arguments, the other only `ignoreAssemblies`. So the default behavior is: scan the app's own directory, exclude nothing, no explicitly named extra assemblies.

Note the parameter order is `moduleAssemblies` *then* `ignoreAssemblies`. The single-array overload is therefore `MvvmApplication(string[] ignoreAssemblies, ...)` — if a caller passes one array, it is treated as *ignore* names, not as assemblies to load. Easy to get backwards.

**Startup (`OnStartup`).** In order:

1. Register the two exception handlers (see below).
2. Create the `CompositionContainer` via `CompositionHelper`.
3. `GetExportedValues<IModuleController>()`. If that throws `ReflectionTypeLoadException`, each loader exception is written to `Console` and the app exits with `ExitCodes.Error` (console output is invisible in a WPF app, so this is effectively a silent early exit).
4. If zero modules were exported, show a "No module found." `MessageBox` and exit with `ExitCodes.Error`.
5. Call `Initialize()` on every module, then — in a second pass — `Run()` on every module. The split means every module is fully initialized before any module's `Run()` executes, which lets a module's `Run()` assume other modules' `Initialize()` already happened.

**Shutdown (`OnExit`).** `ModuleControllers.Reverse().Shutdown()` — modules shut down in the opposite order they started. Then `Container.Dispose()`. If startup failed before any modules ran, this loop is a no-op and the container (possibly null, if `OnStartup` returned before assigning it) is disposed only if non-null.

**Exception handling.** Two handlers cover the usual WPF split:

- `AppDispatcherUnhandledException` catches exceptions on the UI thread, calls the shared handler, then sets `e.Handled = true` — so the app survives any non-terminating UI exception.
- `AppDomain.UnhandledException` catches everything else; it cannot prevent termination.

Both funnel into `HandleException`, which `Trace.TraceError`s the exception and — only when not terminating — shows a modal error box. The UI string here is German ("Es ist ein Fehler aufgetreten." / "Fehler") while the no-modules message above is English, so localisation is inconsistent within the class.

There's a comment claiming the handlers are skipped in Debug mode so the debugger can break on exceptions; the code actually registers them unconditionally, so in Debug a WPF app will still show the error box and swallow UI exceptions rather than breaking.

## Rough edges

- The comment above the handler registration doesn't match the code: handlers are registered in all configurations, so the "don't handle in Debug" intent isn't implemented.
- The `ReflectionTypeLoadException` path reports to `Console`, which a WPF app has no console for — the user sees only a sudden exit.
- The single-`string[]` overload takes `ignoreAssemblies`, the opposite of what the parameter order in the primary constructor suggests; a reader of the signature alone will guess wrong.
- Error message language is mixed (German dialog, English "No module found.").

### Purpose

`Mvvm.Wpf/MessageService.cs` defines the WPF implementation of `IMessageService` (declared in `Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`), a small abstraction over native message boxes. It exists so that view models can show informational, warning, error, and question dialogs without referencing WPF types. View models depend on the interface; this class is what actually displays the `System.Windows.MessageBox` at runtime.

### Role in the Codebase

This is a platform adapter inside the `Mvvm.Wpf` project. That project is the WPF host layer of an MEF-based modular application: `MvvmApplication.cs` in the same folder builds a `CompositionContainer` from assemblies at startup, and every exported type in the loaded assemblies becomes available for import. `MessageService` is marked `[Export(typeof(IMessageService))]`, so the container wires it into anything that carries an `[Import]` of `IMessageService` — for example the `MessageService` property in `UserManagement/ViewModel/AddUserViewModel.cs`, which calls `MessageService.ShowError(...)` when validation fails.

The `Mvvm.Wpf` namespace is not imported in this file, which is why this file doesn't see the interface — it comes from the `Mvvm` namespace via the project reference in `Mvvm.Wpf.csproj`. The same pattern exists for other UI stacks: `Mvvm.Console/MessageService.cs` and `Mvvm.Winforms/MessageService.cs` export equivalent implementations for their own platforms. A given application only loads the host assembly for the stack it runs on, so its container resolves to exactly one of these exports.

### Relationships

- **Implements** `IMessageService` (`Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`) — the nine members here are exactly the interface's members.
- **Returns** `MessageResult` (`Mvvm/MessageResult.cs`), a plain enum that mirrors WPF's `MessageBoxResult` values (`None`, `OK`, `Cancel`, `Abort`, `Retry`, `Ignore`, `Yes`, `No`, `TryAgain`, `Continue`), so callers never see a WPF type.
- **Consumed via MEF**: view models and other components pull it in with `[Import] public IMessageService MessageService { get; set; }`. Unit tests instead mock the interface directly (see `TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs`).
- Depends on `System.Windows.MessageBox` from WPF — this is the only place the WPF dependency shows up in the type's surface, which is the point of the abstraction.

### Behavior & Details

The class is a thin, stateless wrapper. Every method maps one-to-one onto a `MessageBox.Show` call with `MessageBoxButton.OK` for the informational family, and the appropriate button set for questions.

- **Informational methods** (`ShowMessage`, `ShowWarning`, `ShowError`) return `void`. Each has a two-argument form and a one-argument overload that supplies a default caption: `"Message"`, `"Warning"`, and `"Error"` respectively. Icons are `None`, `Warning`, and `Error`; button is always `OK`.
- **Question methods** return `MessageResult`. There are no caption overloads here — every question method requires an explicit caption.
  - `ShowYesNoCancelQuestion` — buttons `YesNoCancel`, default result `Cancel`.
  - `ShowYesNoQuestion` — buttons `YesNo`, default result `No` (pressed via the `E` key or as a default button behavior in WPF).
  - `ShowOkCancelQuestion` — buttons `OkCancel`, default result `Cancel`.

Each question method casts the raw WPF `MessageBoxResult` to the local `MessageResult` enum. Both enums use identical numeric values, so the cast is safe in practice, but it means the two enums must stay in lockstep — a value added to WPF's enum that isn't mirrored in `MessageResult` would be silently lost in the cast.

A subtle detail: WPF's `MessageBox.Show` returns `MessageBoxResult.None` if the box is dismissed by some path that doesn't map to a button (rare, but possible in some dialog interactions). In that case the question methods return `MessageResult.None`, not the declared default — the `Cancel`/`No` parameters are only the *default button*, not a fallback return value. Callers that treat "not affirmative" as the safe branch should check `!= MessageResult.OK` / `!= MessageResult.Yes` rather than assuming the default is always returned.

There is no logging, no async surface, and no customization point (font, owner window, modal-vs-modeless) — the class is deliberately opaque: it only answers "show this message, get back this result."

- The `MessageBoxResult` → `MessageResult` cast couples the two enums silently; a future divergence in WPF's enum values would corrupt results without a compile-time error.
- Question methods lack the one-argument caption overloads their informational counterparts have, so callers writing `ShowYesNoQuestion("...", "…")` must always pass the caption — an asymmetry easy to trip over.

### Purpose

The `Mvvm.Wpf` project serves as the WPF-specific host layer for the repository's MEF-based MVVM framework. Its primary responsibility is to provide a ready-made application shell that handles container composition, module lifecycle management, and global exception handling, allowing WPF applications to focus on business logic rather than bootstrapping infrastructure.

Its contents belong together because they form a complete WPF binding for the shared `Mvvm` core: one component (`MvvmApplication`) manages the application startup and shutdown, while the other (`MessageService`) abstracts the platform-specific UI messaging. Together, they allow WPF hosts to plug into the framework via XAML inheritance and MEF exports, mirroring the patterns established in the `Mvvm.Console` and `Mvvm.Winforms` sibling projects.

This directory contains two distinct functional components, each defined in its own C# file:

*   **Application Lifecycle Management**: `MvvmApplication.cs` defines the base `Application` class that WPF apps inherit from. It encapsulates the complex startup sequence, including scanning assemblies for MEF exports, creating the composition container, and executing the ordered `Initialize` and `Run` phases of all modules. It also manages the reverse-order shutdown and registers global exception handlers for both the UI dispatcher and the application domain.
*   **UI Message Abstraction**: `MessageService.cs` implements the `IMessageService` interface from the core `Mvvm` project. It acts as a thin adapter that translates interface method calls into native `System.Windows.MessageBox` invocations. ### Purpose

`TestProject1/UserViewModelTest.cs` is the unit-test suite for the user-management ViewModels in the `UserManagement` project. It defines one MSTest class, `UserViewModelTest`, which exercises two pieces of behaviour in the real `UserViewModel` object graph: adding a user (with input validation and error surfacing, in `AddUserViewModel`) and loading the active user list (in `ShowUsersViewModel`). The `IUserService` and `IMessageService` dependencies are mocked with Moq so the tests verify the ViewModels' orchestration logic without touching a database or showing real dialogs.

The `TestProject1` project is the solution's test project (MSTest on `net10.0-windows`, Moq, referencing `BusinessLayer` and `UserManagement`). This class is its only test. The ViewModels under test are `MefExported` composition parts — normally wired up by MEF imports at runtime — so the tests construct them by hand and assign the `UserService`/`MessageService` properties directly, which is why the properties exist as settable `[Import]` properties in the source. Removing this file loses the coverage of the add-user validation path, the successful add path (collection update + field clearing), and the initial load path.

- **`UserViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/UserViewModel.cs`): the object under test. It is a `MainViewModelBase` that exposes `AddUserViewModel` and `ShowUsersViewModel` (MefImported in the app; instantiated manually here).

- **`ShowUsersViewModel`** (`UserManagement/ViewModel/ShowUsersViewModel.cs`): registers for `UserChangedMessage` in its constructor (an `Added` message appends to `Users`); `OnLoadedAsync` — exposed as `LoadedCommand` — fetches `UserService.GetActiveUsers()` and populates its `Users` collection.
- **`IUserService`** (`BusinessLayer/IUserService.cs`): mocked; provides `GetActiveUsers()` and `AddUser(UserDto)`.
- **`IMessageService`** (`Mvvm/IMessageService.cs`): mocked; the tests verify the exact `ShowError` call.
